1 
 
REPORT 
The Action Taken Report (ATR) of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing 
Committee on Science and Technology, Environment, Forests and Climate Change deals with 
the action taken by the Government on the recommendations/observations of the Committee 
contained in its ‘Three Hundred Eighty Seventh Report’ on ‘Demands for Grants (2025-26) of 
the Department of Atomic Energy’. The Report was presented to/ laid on the Table of both the 
Houses of Parliament on the 25th March, 2025. 
2. Action Taken Notes (ATNs) have been received from the Department of Atomic Energy 
in respect of all the 67 recommendations/observations contained in the ‘Three Hundred Eighty 
Seventh Report’. The replies of the Department of Atomic Energy have been categorized as 
follows:-  
Chapter I: Recommendations/Observations which have been accepted by the 
Government: Para Nos., 2.5, 2.7, 2.11, 2.13, 2.14, 2.15, 2.18, 2.19, 2.20, 2.21, 
2.22, 2.24, 2.25, 2.26, 2.30, 3.4, 3.5, 3.7, 3.9, 3.10, 3.13, 3.14, 3.16, 3.18, 3.22, 
3.23, 3.24, 3.27, 3.29, 3.30, 3.31, 3.33, 3.34, 3.35, 3.36, 3.37, 3.38, 3.41, 3.42, 
4.1, 4.2, 4.4, 4.5, 4.6, 5.3, 5.4, 6.3, 7.4, 7.5,7.6, 7.7, 7.8, 7.9, 7.10. 
 Total recommendations – 54 
Chapter II:    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to 
pursue in view of the Government’s replies: 
Para Nos., 2.3, 2.6, 2.10, 2.28, 2.29, 3.2, 3.3, 3.17, 3.20, 6.2, 8.5, 8.6, 8.7. 
     Total recommendations – 13 
Chapter III: Recommendations/Observations in respect of which replies of the 
Government have not been accepted by the Committee: NIL  
Chapter IV:   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the 
Government are still awaited: NIL 
3. The details of the ATNs have been analyzed in the succeeding Chapters. 
  

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
OVERALL BUDGETARY DETAILS FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25 (BE, RE & 
ACTUAL EXPENDITURE) AND ALLOCATION FOR THE FINANCIAL YEAR 2025-26 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.1 The Committee recommends that the DAE should adopt a more robust approach to 
financial planning and forecasting by incorporating detailed risk assessments and contingency 
allocations into the initial budget estimates. The Committee notes that the Revised Estimates 
have consistently exceeded the Budget Estimates. The Committee therefore urges the Department 
to implement regular internal and external audits and to ensure transparent reporting of any 
mid-year adjustments, with clear justifications for deviations from the initial allocations. 
Furthermore, it is recommended that standard operating procedures for urgent procurement and 
maintenance should be established to pre-empt emergency expenditures, while also integrating 
anticipated costs for global collaborations and new technologies into the budgetary framework. 
(Para 2.5 of the 387th Report) 
Action Taken  
1.2 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.3 The Committee recommends that the Department continue to streamline fund disbursal 
processes to ensure optimal utilization of allocated resources, particularly for multi-year atomic 
energy projects. The Committee also recommends that a more robust financial strategy be 
adopted, incorporating contingency planning to mitigate the impact of unexpected budget cuts. 
Additionally, the Committee urges the Ministry of Finance to consider the critical nature of the 
Department’s commitments, particularly those related to nuclear fuel procurement and 
international obligations, and to ensure that adequate funding is provided in a timely manner. 
The Committee urges upon the Department to implement these measures with immediate effect to 
restore the expenditure trajectory to match both the budget estimates and the requirements of 
multi-year projects.                                                                                                     (para 2.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken 
1.4 The budget utilization for last 3 years is tabulated below:

1.5 It is seen from the above, that the Department has fully utilized the allocations during FY 
2024-25 and the actual expenditure would correspond with the figures for the last years. 
 
Recommendations/Observations  
 
1.6 The Committee observes with concern that the Research & Development (R&D) Sector is 
the most impacted amongst all, with the R&D sector suffering the largest reduction of 
Rs.3,289.60 crore, from a proposed BE of Rs.14,516.38 crore to the approved BE Rs.11,226.78 
crore. The Committee observes that the shortfall ofRs.3,289 crore would impact long-term 
research initiatives under BARC, IGCAR, and RRCAT, slowing down innovations in nuclear 
reactor safety, radioactive waste management, and new reactor technologies. The Mega Science 
projects, which include research on fusion energy and directed research, may also face delays.            
                                                                                                                                  (Para 2.11 ibid) 
1.7 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends immediate action to restore essential 
funding, support nuclear research, and ensure uninterrupted progress in India’s nuclear energy 
and medical applications. The Committee recommends urgent restoration of at least Rs.5,933.62 
crore, particularly for the R&D and I&M sectors, to ensure continued progress in nuclear 
technology development and fuel production.                                                         (para 2.13 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
1.8 As recommended by the Hon’ble Committee the additional funds for R&D and I&M 
Sector shall be sought at RE stage, to ensure continued progress in nuclear technology 
development and fuel production. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.9 The Committee supports DAE’s initiative to attract private investment. However, the 
Committee recommends that clear regulatory frameworks and risk mitigation strategies should 
be developed to ensure private sector participation in the critical and sensitive nuclear 
infrastructure projects. While the Committee acknowledges DAE’s efforts to optimize its 
expenditures, it recommends a detailed financial audit to ensure that budgetary constraints do 
not result in inefficient cost-cutting measures that could compromise long-term technological 
advancements.                                                                                                           (Para 2.14 ibid) 

4 
 
Action Taken  
1.10 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.11 The Committee recommends priority-based funding for R&D sector and the funding 
should be allocated strategically, with a focus on high-impact projects such as Fast Breeder 
Reactor (FBR) development, fusion research (ITER), and radio isotope production for medical 
applications. Considering the importance of fuel availability, the Committee recommends that 
additional resources should be allocated to AMD for increased uranium and rare metal 
exploration to secure a stable domestic supply of nuclear fuel.                              (Para 2.15 ibid)                                                
Action Taken  
1.12 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.13 The Committee observes from Chart 3 that the total budget allocation for the Department 
of Atomic Energy (DAE) in B.E. 2025-26 stands at Rs.37,482.93 crore, with Rs.22,668.29 crore 
earmarked for revenue expenditure and Rs.14,814.64 crore for capital expenditure. The 
Committee observes that while the proposed capital expenditure was Rs.16,468.59 crore, the 
approved allocation was Rs.1,653.95 crore lower, whereas the revenue allocation saw a steeper 
decline of Rs.4,279.67 crore from the proposed Rs.26,947.96 crore.                     (Para 2.18 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
1.14 As observed by the Hon’ble Committee there are budgetary cuts in the BE allocations. 
The current shortfall of Rs.5,933.62 crore alongwith any further additionality, based on the 
budgetary requirements, shall be sought at RE stage. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.15 The Committee notes a significant disparity in proposed budgetary allocations against 
the actual allocations for 2025-26, between capital and revenue expenditure across key sectors 
of the Department, particularly in I&M and R&D sectors. A comparative assessment of the 
proposed and approved allocations (Table-2) highlights that while capital expenditure across 
sectors has been significantly curtailed, revenue expenditure has remained relatively stable.       
         (Para 2.19 ibid) 
1.16 The Committee notes that the I&M sector saw a capital allocation reduction from the 
proposed Rs.6,386.07 crore, in BE 2025-26, to Rs.5,293.18 crore, reflecting a 17.1% shortfall, 
while the revenue allocation was curtailed by 22.9% from the proposed Rs.6,762.58 crore to 
Rs.5,217.27 crore. The Committee notes with concern that R&D sector experienced an even 

5 
 
substantial reduction in capital expenditure, reduced by Rs.560.89 crore, a reduction of over 
27.3%, while the revenue component saw a reduction of Rs.2,728.71 crore (21.9%), indicating a 
prioritisationof operational expenses over infrastructure investments. The Committee notes that 
the Power sector has faced only a marginal reduction in capital allocation, with the approved 
amount standing at Rs.8,028.84 crore against the proposed allocation of Rs.8,029.01 crore. 
Revenue allocation for the sector also remained largely unchanged at Rs.7,631.72 crore.             
                                                                                                                                  (Para 2.20 ibid) 
1.17 The Committee feels that capital expenditure disparity is expected to have a negative 
impact on several high-priority projects. The Committee observes that the reduced capital 
allocation to the R&D sector could affect long-term research initiatives under Bhabha Atomic 
Research Centre (BARC), Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic Research (IGCAR), and Raja 
Ramanna Centre for Advanced Technology (RRCAT), potentially delaying innovations in 
nuclear safety, reactor technology, and radioactive waste management. The Committee 
emphasizes that while operational (revenue) expenses are necessary for maintaining institutional 
stability, the underfunding of capital investments may hinder advancements in nuclear energy 
infrastructure and indigenous technology development. To address these concerns, the 
Committee recommends a reassessment of expenditure priorities within the DAE, advocating for 
a more equitable distribution of funds between revenue and capital components. (Para 2.21 ibid) 
Action Taken  
1.18 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.19 The Committee acknowledges that the predominance of revenue expenditure is partly due 
to salary commitments, facility maintenance, and recurring operational costs. However, it 
underscores the need for a balanced allocation to ensure continued infrastructure expansion and 
modernization of nuclear energy facilities.                                                       (Para 2.22 ibid) 
 
1.20 The Committee urges the Department to recalibrate its financial strategy by enhancing 
capital allocations and ensuring a robust implementation framework for major nuclear projects. 
The Committee notes that the underfunding of capital projects could result in execution delays 
and inefficiencies in scaling nuclear infrastructure, ultimately impacting India’s long-term 
energy security. The Committee understands that a sustained focus on capital investment will be 
crucial for maintaining India’s leadership in atomic energy, fostering self-reliance in nuclear 
technology, and ensuring long-term energy security.                                              (Para 2.24 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
1.21 Necessary steps shall be taken to evolve a framework as desired by the Hon’ble 
Committee to recalibrate its financial strategy by enhancing capital allocations and ensuring a 
robust implementation framework for major nuclear projects. 

6 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.22 The Committee observes that the budget utilization in capital expenditure across various 
organisations under the DAE for the financial year 2024-25 demonstrates a mixed performance. 
While several institutions have exceeded or closely met the 75% benchmark set by the Ministry 
of Finance (MoF), some have experienced significant underutilisation, primarily due to delays in 
capital expenditure, procurement, and regulatory clearances.                               (Para 2.25 ibid) 
 
1.23 The Committee notes that the Nuclear Fuel Complex (NFC) has achieved a utilization 
rate of 78.1%, having spent ₹539.06 crore out of its ₹690.00 crore RE allocation, with the 
remaining balance expected to be fully utilized by March 2025. Reactor Fuel Cycle Facility 
(FRFCF) recorded 85.9% utilization, spending ₹383.57 crore out of ₹446.50 crore, reflecting 
steady progress in nuclear fuel cycle advancements. Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC) 
reported 75.9% utilization, spending ₹587.97 crore out of ₹774.82 crore, with assurances from 
the Department that full utilization is expected within the financial year.              (Para 2.26 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
1.24 The budgetary allocations under the three heads ‘BARC’, ‘NFC and ‘FRFCF’ at BE, RE 
& FR stage under Capital Section in the Financial Year 2024-25 along with the actual 
expenditure as on 31.03.2025 is indicated below:

1.25 The Department submits that, ‘BARC’, ‘NFC and ‘FRFCF’ have utilised around 98%, 
95% and 100% respectively of their respective FR allocations. The Department as a whole has 
been able to utilize 99 % of the total allocations. 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.26 While revenue expenditures remain largely on track, the Committee emphasizes that 
delays in capital-intensive projects highlight the need for enhanced financial planning and 
project monitoring mechanisms. The Committee recommends that the Department prioritize fund 

7 
 
utilization through improved project execution timelines, inter-departmental coordination, and 
strengthened procurement systems to prevent further delays. The Committee recommends that 
the Department should adopt a more proactive approach in nuclear infrastructure development, 
streamline financial disbursements, and implement stricter project monitoring mechanisms. This 
will ensure efficient fund utilisation, strengthen India’s nuclear energy programme, and 
reinforce its position as a leader in nuclear research and power generation.        (Para 2.30 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.27 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee shall be complied with. 
SCHEME WISE ANALYSIS OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS MADE TO THE 
DEPARTMENT OF ATOMIC ENERGY 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.28 The Committee is concerned that the budgetary shortfall of Rs.633.62 crore for 2025-26 
may negatively impact the progress of key nuclear research and infrastructure projects. The 
shortfall is likely to delay advancements in isotope production, nuclear safety technologies, and 
research in fast breeder reactor technology. Moreover, the reduction in funds may slow down 
ongoing work in nuclear waste disposal, a critical area for India’s nuclear sustainability. The 
Committee recommends that the Government should reconsider BARC’s budgetary allocation in 
the Revised Estimates (RE) for 2025-26 to bridge the funding gap, particularly in areas of 
nuclear safety, waste management, and advanced reactor research.                       (Para 3.4 ibid) 
 
1.29 The Committee taking into note the under-utilisation of funds in 2024-25, recommends 
BARC to streamline its procurement and project execution mechanisms to ensure timely 
implementation and optimal fund utilisation. The Committee urges BARC to prioritise high-
impact projects in nuclear safety, isotope production, and advanced reactor technology, 
ensuring that critical research is not disrupted due to budgetary constraints. The Committee 
recommends the DAE to ensure quarterly monitoring of fund utilisation and project progress so 
as to prevent delays in key infrastructure and R&D initiatives.                                (Para 3.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
1.30 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee to reconsider BARC’s budgetary 
allocations in the Revised Estimates (RE) 2025-26 to bridge the funding gap, particularly in 
areas of nuclear safety, waste management and advanced reactor research are noted.  
1.31 Major challenge in R&D Project is procurement of high and imported instruments/ 
components. These items are not available in India and are essential for new technology 
development. These items are needed in very less quantities and require sophisticated 
technologies and know-how therefore, not economically viable to develop and produce in India. 
Hence, procurement of such items from the global market will be required which necessitates 

8 
 
raising global tender enquiry (GTE). To streamline the process, BARC has compiled a 
comprehensive list of such imported items required in near future for R&D Projects and their 
exemption from existing procedures of GTE is being pursued with Department for Promotion of 
Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT). To ensure timely execution of R&D projects, pre-project 
activities like designs, tender specifications, drawings, regulatory clearances etc. are completed 
to maximum possible extent before the financial sanction of the projects to expedite the project 
execution. Specifications are framed to have participations of multiple vendors for 
competitiveness and streamlined processing. Mechanisms for quarterly monitoring of on-going 
projects is already in place. The financial progress of Projects is being regularly monitored by 
project review committees to prevent delays in project execution.  
1.32 Further, as recommended by the Hon’ble Committee all the Heads of Accounting Units 
have been advised vide OM dated 18.06.2025 to ensure quarterly monitoring of fund utilization 
and realistic budget formation. 
Recommendations/Observations 
1.33 The Committee notes that IGCAR had sought Rs.1,035.94 crore, but only Rs.800.39 crore 
was allocated, resulting in a shortfall of Rs.235.55 crore. TheCommittee believes that the 
reduced allocation may hamper R&D in fast breeder reactor technology, fuel reprocessing, and 
safety enhancements. The Committee also observes that capital allocation has been reduced 
from Rs.373.55 crore to Rs.204.77 crore, affecting infrastructure and equipment upgrades.       
(Para 3.7 ibid) 
 
1.34 The Committee observes that insufficient funding may slow down accelerator research, 
high-brightness synchrotron radiation sources, and laser technology development.   (Para 3.9 
ibid) 
1.35 The Committee notes that during the years 2023-24 and 2024-25 AMD focused on 
exploration of uranium, thorium, and rare earth elements to strengthen India’s nuclear fuel cycle 
and Geophysical surveys and drilling in high-potential regions and expansion of isotope 
hydrology applications for groundwater resource management.                            (Para 3.10 ibid) 
1.36 The Committee notes with concern that the budget shortfall for 2025-26 could 
significantly impact these institutions’ ability to meet their research objectives. The reduced 
allocations may delay crucial reactor safety upgrades and fast breeder reactor development at 
IGCAR. The Committee notes that slowdown in critical laser and accelerator research at 
RRCAT will affect India’s capability inmedical, industrial, and defence applications. The 
Committee recommends that IGCAR, RRCAT and AMD should increase collaboration with 
industry partners to generate additional revenue streams and reduce reliance on government 
funding. The Committee recommends quarterly reviews of fund utilisation to ensure that 
available resources are effectively deployed and that additional funding is sought wherever 
necessary.                                                                                                                 (Para 3.13 ibid) 
 

9 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.37 As suggested by the Hon’ble Committee, the options to increase industrial collaboration 
to generate additional revenue streams would be explored. However, it is felt that still 
government funding would be relied upon for R&D activities. Also it is to be emphasized that 
internal unit committees reviews the fund utilization periodically and additional funding as 
necessary would be sought at RE 2025-26 stage.  
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.38 The Committee notes that budget constraints will slow down geophysical surveys, deep 
drilling operations, and resource assessment, delaying efforts to expand India's nuclear fuel 
reserves considering the fact that Uranium is essential for pressurised heavy water reactors 
(PHWRs), while thorium is key to India's Advanced Heavy Water Reactor (AHWR) programme.                
                                                                                                                                  (Para 3.14 ibid) 
 
1.39 The Committee recommends that AMD should focus resources on high- potential 
uranium and thorium reserves in Jharkhand, Meghalaya, Andhra Pradesh, and Rajasthan and 
special attention should be given to monazite-bearing coastal areas in Odisha, Kerala, Tamil 
Nadu, Andhra Pradesh for rare earth and thorium extraction. The Committee also expressed 
concerns over illegal mining of Atomic minerals and its impact on the cost of exchequer and 
national security. In parallel with exploration, the Committee recommends enhancing uranium 
ore processing plants at Jaduguda, Tummalapalle, and Narwapahar to improve the efficiency of 
domestic fuel production. The Committee recommends expedited approvals for the construction 
of AHWR and associated fuel reprocessing infrastructure. The Committee urges upon the DAE to 
have collaboration with international nuclear agencies for technological exchange on thorium 
reactor operations.                                                                                                  (Para 3.16 ibid) 
Action Taken  
 
1.40 In order to augment the uranium, thorium and associated critical mineral(s) resources, 
AMD is carrying out integrated, multi-disciplinary exploration (geological, radiometric, 
heliborne and ground geophysical, geochemical surveys coupled with drilling) in identified 
thrust areas of the country by utilizing the state-of-the-art technology.  
1.41 Surveys / prospecting operations to augment rare earths resources in hard rock terrain is 
mainly focused in parts of Rajasthan, Gujarat, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Jharkhand 
and Andhra Pradesh; and monazite resources in the beach sand deposits along coastal tracts in 
parts of Tamil Nadu, Odisha, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. 
1.42 To overcome the illegal mining of Atomic minerals, necessary amendments have been 
incorporated in AMCR, 2016. 
1.43 Other observation of the Hon’ble Committee shall be incorporated in future activities.  

10 
 
Recommendations/Observations 
 
1.44   The Committee understands that given China’s dominance on production of global Rare 
Earth Elements (REE), India's lack of investment in domestic exploration and processing will 
keep the country vulnerable to supply chain disruptions. The Committee recommends the DAE to 
fast scale the exploration to reduce dependence on China-dominated REE supply chains. Given 
the increasing demand for nuclear and REE-based technologies, the Committee recommends 
establishing a strategic reserve for uranium, thorium, and REEs. The Committee observes that 
this will ensure long-term security and prevent supply disruptions in India’s nuclear and high-
tech industries.                                                                                                        (Para 3.18 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
1.45 AMD has established uranium, monazite, Beach Sand Minerals (BSM) and Rare Earth 
Elements (REE) as follows: 
 AMD established first hard-rock hosted REE deposit of the Country in Ambadungar, 
Gujarat. Besides, AMD has also established HREE enriched REO deposits in 
Bhatikhera and Dantala in Siwana Ring Complex, Rajasthan. Total Rare Earth Oxide 
resource in hard rocks of the Country is 1.23 Mt.

1.119 Below are some of the research studies that have made an impact on routine treatment 
guidelines of the cancer patients and provided evidence of high quality affordable treatment 
1) Low-Dose Immunotherapy in Head and Neck Cancer: A Randomized Study 
Immunotherapy treatment for treatment of cancer has been one of the key 
developments with two nobel prizes. Due to cost there are only 3-4 % of patients in 
India who can use it. With the research project done at Tata memorial Hospital the 
cost for this treatment has come down by almost one tenth of original cost which 
has led to use by the majority of patients of head and neck cancer. This also has 
opened the avenue to explore the similar concept and develop low dose cost 
effective immunotherapy in other cancers. This is part of routine care in our country 
and developing world. This paper had an editorial in JCO and was covered by NIH-
NCI, MEDSCAPE etc.  
2) Gefitinib vs Gefitinib Plus Pemetrexed and Carboplatin Chemotherapy in EGFR-
Variant Lung Cancer-Long-Term Results of a Randomized Clinical Trial:  Modern 
targeted therapy has improved outcomes in lung cancer with EGFR mutation but 
only 4-5% of patients in India can use it due to cost. Tata Hospital used an 
innovative approach of combining two relatively cost effective drugs and showed in 
a randomised study that their efficacy is similar to modern targeted therapy and 
accessible to almost every patient in India with lung cancer with EGFR mutation. 
This is part of international and national guidelines for lung cancer management eg 
- PAN ASIA ESMO guidelines, UpToDate guidelines, NCG guidelines etc. 
3) Low-cost oral metronomic chemotherapy versus intravenous cisplatin in patients 
with recurrent, metastatic, inoperable head and neck carcinoma: an open-label, 
parallel-group, non-inferiority, randomised, phase 3 trial: Chemotherapy is an 
integral part of treatment of Head and Neck cancer but has toxicities and is also of 
limited benefit. Tata Hospital used an innovative approach of low dose, oral 
administration of chemotherapy in head and neck cancer. TMC was able to prove in 
our research work that in platinum sensitive and resistant patients they are effective 
and also cost effective and almost every patient can use it and this also eliminates 
the IV administration of drugs. This research has been published in various 
prestigious journals. This is part of various guidelines - UpToDate, NCG etc. 
4) Late Toxicity After Adjuvant Conventional Radiation Versus Image-Guided 
Intensity-Modulated Radiotherapy for Cervical Cancer (PARCER): A Randomized 
Controlled Trial: This study was conducted by Tata Memorial Centre in women 
with cervical cancer who needed post-operative radiotherapy. It compared, in a 
randomized controlled trial, two techniques of giving radiotherapy to these women 
- intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT) or conventional 3D conformal 
radiotherapy. The results showed that IGRT markedly reduced the radiotherapy 
related short-term and long term side effects on the bowel and bladder. Thus, 

26 
 
although it is more resource intensive, it is now accepted that IGRT is a better way 
of delivering radiotherapy to these patients. 
5) Evaluation of 1-Year vs Shorter Durations of Adjuvant Trastuzumab Among 
Patients With Early Breast Cancer: An Individual Participant Data and Trial-Level 
Meta-analysis:Targeted cancer therapies are effective but very expensive. Once 
such expensive targeted therapy for breast cancer patients is an antibody drug called 
trastuzumab. Ordinarily it is given for a duration of 1 year. An individual-patient 
data meta-analysis conducted by Tata Memorial Centre, involving about 12000 
patients from six randomized controlled trials which compared 3-6 months of 
Trastuzumab with 1 year of Trastuzumab showed conclusively that shorter 
durations of this drug resulted in similar long-term cure rates. Another study 
conducted in collaboration between researchers of Tata Memorial Centre and PGI 
Chandigarh showed that shorter durations of Trastuzumab were cost-effective but 1 
year of Trastuzumab was not cost-effevtive, at current prices of this drug, in India. 
As a result of this study the PMJAY has rolled out short duration Trastuzumab as 
the standard treatment regimen in this scheme. 
6) Effect of Peritumoral Infiltration of Local Anesthetic Before Surgery on Survival in 
Early Breast Cancer: Clinical researchers at Tata Memorial Centre conceptualized 
and led a study wherein they injected the inexpensive local anesthesia drug 
lidocaine all around the breast cancer tumor, just prior to surgical removal of this 
tumor. This was a randomized controlled trial in 1600 women with breast cancer, 
wherein half the patients received this injection prior to surgery and the other half 
underwent surgery without this injection. The results showed that the recurrence of 
cancer and death were substantially reduced by this simple intervention which costs 
less than Rs 100. The results of this recently published study have been 
implemented in TMC and many other centres in India and in some other parts of 
the world.

1.122 Accessibility to all sections of society- One of the problems of our country is accessibility 
of the treatment.  In order to overcome the problem TMC has offered hub and spoke model. This 
is a distributed model of cancer care to offer patients high quality cancer care at their doorsteps. 
Common and less complex cancer care should be provided close to patients’ homes (spokes) to 
create minimum disruption in their lives and that of their families. Treatment of uncommon 
cancers and those with complex treatment protocols require management in expert centres of 

27 
 
excellence (hubs). However, to avoid over-burdening the hubs, the spokes need to be reasonably 
capable of handling less complex and common cancer types in the region. With an aim to 
decentralize cancer care and to make it more affordable and accessible. TMC registered 1,28,000 
new cancer patients in 2024 (Calendar year) of which about 70% are in general and nominal 
charges category.

2.30 Right from its inception, Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) has paid considerable 
attention towards the induction and development of human resources for achieving excellence in 
the field of science and technology.  DAE has followed a comprehensive policy to develop 
competent scientists, engineers and technical personnel to support its programmes.  DAE has a 
detailed and streamlined procedure for Recruitment and Promotion of Scientific and Technical 
personnel and filling up vacancies arising due to their superannuation.   
2.31 Merit is the prime consideration for Recruitment and Promotion of candidates to 
Scientific and Technical posts who have to work in the advanced field of  
Science and Technology in DAE.  Hence, there is a possibility of posts remaining unfilled after a 
recruitment drive. Such vacancies are considered for filling in subsequent recruitment campaign.   
Sometimes, selected candidates are not willing to join due to remote places of posting/places far-
off from their home-town etc. 
2.32 Scientific personnel are recruited through flagship Programme Orientation Course for 
Engineering Graduates and Science Post Graduates (OCES) and DAE Graduate Fellowship 
Scheme (DGFS). The candidates selected for OCES Programme based on score of Graduate 
Aptitude Test in Engineering (GATE) or Computer Based Test (CBT) and technical interviews 
by Experts Panel undergo one-year training in nuclear science & technology at BARC training 
school. The DGFS candidates, who have already secured admissions in selected Indian Institute 
of Technology (IITs), pursue their M Tech. OCES and DGFS candidates are absorbed in various 
units of DAE viz., Bhabha Atomic Research Centre (BARC), Indira Gandhi Centre for Atomic 
Research (IGCAR), Variable Energy Cyclotron Centre (VECC), Atomic Minerals Directorate for 
Exploration and Research (AMD), Board of Radiation and Isotope Technology (BRIT), Heavy 
Water Board (HWB), Directorate of Construction Services and Estate Management (DCSEM), 
as scientific officer after successful completion of training and MTech respectively. 
2.33 Technical personnel are recruited through Computer Based Test and Skill Test/Interview 
and the selected candidates undergo two-year stipendiary training scheme in areas related to 
nuclear science and technology.  On successful completion of training, Graduates in science and 
diploma holders in engineering are absorbed as Scientific Assistants and candidates having 
qualification of HSC (science) or SSC followed by ITI certificate are absorbed as Technicians in 
the various Units of DAE.

Recommendations/Observations 
2.36 The high vacancy rates across DAE institutions raise serious concerns about workforce 
planning, recruitment efficiency, and the overall sustainability of nuclear and research projects 
in India. The Committee expresses its concerns over these vacancies, especially in key 
operational areas such as nuclear power generation, research, and mineral exploration. The 
shortage of skilled personnel could lead to delays in research and development, inefficiencies in 
plant operations, and constraints in nuclear fuel production, ultimately affecting the country's 
nuclear energy programme. To address this issue, the Committee strongly recommends an 
immediate recruitment drive to fill the existing vacancies. It is imperative that recruitment 
processes be streamlined to ensure timely hiring of personnel in technical, scientific, and 
operational roles. A review of existing workforce policies should be undertaken to identify areas 
where delays occur in the hiring process, and necessary reforms should be implemented. The 
DAE must adopt modern human resource management strategies to attract and retain talent, 
ensuring competitive salaries, career progression opportunities, and research grants for 
professionals in nuclear science, energy, and advanced research.                           (Para 8.6 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
2.37 Department of Atomic Energy follows Merit based Promotion Scheme for Scientific and 
Technical personnel which is delinked from availability of vacancies and rewards them with time 
bound promotions. This merit-based career progression scheme is implemented through a well-
established mechanism of minimum residency requirements, performance assessment, screening, 
review and evaluation. The Merit Promotion Scheme has so far been regulated through norms 
and practices based on decisions taken by the Trombay Council and further approved by the 
DAE. 
2.38 In addition, the modern human resource management strategies as adopted by DAE, is 
followed in the Units to attract and retain talent by way of following measures: 

43 
 
i. Advance increments are given to the Scientific and Technical Personnel on their initial 
appointment. 
ii. Scientists are encouraged to carry out further studies like M Tech, MSc. Engg., PhD. After 
PhD, opportunities are also given to carry out Post-Doctoral Research works at reputed 
International laboratories.  
iii. DAE also grants Performance incentives in the form of Performance Related Incentive 
Scheme (Organization) [PRIS-O], Performance Related Incentive Scheme (Group) [PRIS-
G] and Performance Related Incentive Scheme (Individual) [PRIS-I] for timely completion 
of major activities related to DAE programmes. 
iv. DAE also grants Professional Update Allowance to Scientific / Technical Officers in the 
grade of SO/C and above, every year. 
v. DAE has collaboration with International Agencies like ITER/CERN Projects where they 
get opportunity to work on these projects on deputation. 
vi. To promote research and capacity building in the field of nuclear science and energy, 
grants are provided to young talented scientists for research projects and scientific events 
aligned with the departmental mandate through Board of Research in Nuclear Sciences 
(BRNS) an extramural agency of DAE through various schemes such as Young Scientist 
Research Project (YSRP) scheme, research fellowship for (JRF/ SRF/ RA) and DAE 
Graduate Fellowship Scheme (DGFS-PhD).  
2.39 In Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd. (NPCIL), Policy changes have been proposed 
and approved for recruitment of Technicians on Fixed Term Appointment basis so that locals get 
the opportunity for employment on Fixed Term basis. 
2.40 Electronics Corporation of India Ltd (ECIL), is constantly reshaping policies such as 
Promotion Policy with better norms, Medical Insurance Policy with Cashless facility and 
Recruitment Policy with an aim to create a conducive work environment to employee group and 
in line with the market trends.  
2.41 Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), an Aided Institution,actively seeks out 
talented Indian nationals with proven high credentials in emerging areas of scientific research 
from around the world to apply for advertised positions through continuous engagement via 
visits, collaborations, and conferences. They are provided with competitive initial start-up grants 
based on the research program’s requirements and salaries consistent with other premier 
academic institutions in the country.   
2.42 Tata Memorial Centre (TMC) has robust Training & Developmentsystem. Medical & 
Scientific Staff are encouraged to attend conferences, workshops, research programmes in India 
and abroad.  They are also supported with extramural and intramural research grants for various 
projects. 

44 
 
2.43 In order to retain talented and experienced medical staff, TMC has taken up a proposal 
for increasing the age of superannuation in case of Medical Staff from 60 to 65 years. 
Recommendations/Observations 
2.44 The Committee observes with great concern contractual employment and temporary 
staffing, particularly in research institutions such as TIFR. The Committee urges a review of 
these employment practices and recommends converting long-term contractual positions into 
permanent roles wherever necessary. The Committee recommends that regularisation of 
employment will not only enhance job security for researchers and scientists but also ensure 
continuity in long-term research projects. Additionally, for institutions such as TMC, where 
medical professionals are in high demand, the Committee recommends expanding recruitment 
efforts and increasing budgetary support for healthcare staff and researchers.       (Para 8.7 ibid) 
 
Action Taken  
 
2.45 With regard to employment on a contractual or short-term basis, it is stated that 
contractual appointments are made only for support services, execution of Plan projects for 
research activities and creation of assets and not for core scientific or technical roles. 
 
2.46 In Tata Institute of Fundamental Research (TIFR), the contractual positions are primarily 
used for administrative tasks that are suitable for outsourcing. Short-term contractual positions 
for research-related tasks are only utilised for projects which have a specific time and scope 
delimitation. This is in keeping with standard practices being followed at all leading research 
institutions at the national and international levels. It is highlighted that temporary Research 
Associate / Research Fellow positions offer valuable training opportunities for fresh Ph.D. 
holders, enabling them to grow as independent researchers and thereafter take up tenured 
positions in academia/research institutions/industry while at the same contributing to advance 
scientific research in the Institute.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
GOVERNMENT 
 
COMPARATIVE BUDGET ANALYSIS 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Committee expresses deep concern over the sub-optimal utilization of funds by the 
Department, particularly in the context of the Central Sector Scheme, Bio-RIDE. This 
underutilization not only hampers the effective implementation of critical programs but also 
undermines the potential impact of the Department’s initiatives. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Department take immediate and appropriate measures to address this issue 
and ensure the optimal utilization of funds allocated to it in the Budget Estimates (B.E.) for 2025-
26. The Department should conduct regular reviews and take corrective actions to prevent delays 
and inefficiencies, thereby maximizing the impact of its programs and achieving the desired 
outcomes in a timely and effective manner.  
(Para 2.11 of the 388th Report) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.2  The Department acknowledges the concern of the Committee.  In background, as per 
extant instructions of DOE, Ministry of Finance vide its O. M. F. No. 3/(06)/PFMS/2023 dated 
21st May, 2024, Department has closed its earlier revised funds flow system of CNA-02 
operations in December 2024 for its two Central Sector (CS) Schemes. In compliance to DOE 
O.M., following the merger of earlier two CS schemes along with a new component into newly 
Cabinet approved Scheme-Bio-RIDE, Department transitioned from earlier fund flow system 
(CNA-02) to new revised funds flow system of TSA-Hybrid (1A) in January, 2025. Department 
rolled out the fund utilization of Bio-Ride scheme through TSA-Hybrid system w.e.f. 29th 
January, 2025.   
1.3 Though overall RE budget utilization by the Department has been sub-optimal, the 
percentage (%) of assignments vs utilization in the new revised funds flow system was 84.8%. 
Department could not assign the full RE allocation to child agencies within such a short period of 
time (2 months) as several hundred implementing agencies could not onboard to new TSA-Hybrid 
system due to various reasons.  
1.4 The department has taken cognizance of the new funds flow system, and accordingly, 
necessary actions for the utilization of funds are being undertaken for maximal utilization of the 
budget for achieving the desired outcomes in the programs in a timely and effective manner in FY 
2025-26 and it will be ensured that 50% of the expenditure target is met by 30th September, 2025. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

3 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.5         Given the substantial allocation to Bio-RIDE, the Committee recommends that the 
Department must ensure optimal utilization of funds. Regular monitoring, timely implementation, 
and transparent reporting mechanisms should be established to avoid sub-optimal utilization and 
maximize outcomes. 
(Para 2.15 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.6 The Department has been taking all possible steps to ensure the optimal utilization of 
allocated funds in FY 2025-26 and the outcomes are being monitored regularly.  
 
BIO-RIDE: A UNIFIED FRAMEWORK FOR ADVANCING BIOTECHNOLOGY 
RESEARCH, ENTREPRENEURSHIP, AND BIOMANUFACTURING IN INDIA 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.7         The Committee appreciates the Department for integration of research, industrial 
development, and biomanufacturing under a unified framework. This will significantly enhance 
India's biotechnology capabilities and position the country as a global hub for innovation, 
sustainability, and bio-based industrialization.  
(Para 3.8 ibid) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.8 The Department is thankful to the Committee for the appreciation. The integration of 
earlier schemes, Biotechnology Research & Development and Biotechnology Industrial & 
Entrepreneurship Development, and the inclusion of a new component, i.e., Biomanufacturing & 
Biofoundry, will certainly enhance the efficacy of the implementation of programs and 
strengthen the Biotechnology Sector in the country. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.9         The Committee places its confidence in the Department’s ability to effectively implement 
the Bio-RIDE scheme and achieve its ambitious targets. The various initiatives under this scheme 
have the potential to drive transformative changes in healthcare, agriculture, environment, and 
industry. Most importantly, the Committee hopes that the advancements in biotechnology under 
this scheme will ultimately benefit the common man by providing affordable and accessible 
healthcare solutions, enhancing agricultural productivity, promoting environmental sustainability 
through carbon capture technologies and bio-based solutions and creating employment 
opportunities through bio-industrialization and entrepreneurship development. 
 (Para 3.9 ibid) 
  

4 
 
Action Taken: 
 
 1.10 The Department is thankful to the Committee for expressing confidence in the 
Department’s ability to effectively implement the BioRIDE scheme. The Department will ensure 
that the envisaged targets are achieved. The implementation of the scheme will certainly provide 
an impetus to research, development, and innovation in the biotechnology sector, which in turn 
generates biobased products and technologies to provide solutions for the unmet needs of society. 
  
1.11 The potential of emerging biotechnology will be leveraged to get more sustainable, 
economic, and environmentally friendly tools& technologies. 
 
AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.12   The Committee feels that the establishment of BRIC and its integration of research 
institutions under the iBRIC+ framework has significantly enhanced the governance, 
collaboration, and impact of biotechnology research in India. The data provided reflects 
commendable progress in interdisciplinary research, education, biomanufacturing, and industrial 
partnerships. However, to amplify the outcomes, BRIC should scale interdisciplinary research 
into a nationwide innovation network with industry-aligned translational centres, broaden the i3c 
BRIC-RCB PhD Programme via global academic- industry partnerships and merit-based 
fellowships, and develop regional Biomanufacturing Hubs for sector-specific bio-solutions. 
Prioritizing commercialization through streamlined regulatory approvals, incentives for startups, 
and centralized data-sharing platforms will expedite market readiness for innovations in 
diagnostics, biotherapeutics, and disease management. Strengthening mentorship programs, 
industry internships, and entrepreneurial fellowships will cultivate skilled talent, while leveraging 
breakthroughs. By scaling research initiatives, refining governance mechanisms, and deepening 
academia-industry synergies, BRIC can position India as a global leader in biotechnology and 
biomanufacturing, fostering equitable and sustainable advancements in healthcare, agriculture, 
and environmental resilience. 
(Para 4.6 ibid) 
Action Taken: 
 
1.13 In an endeavor to position India as a global leader in biotechnology and biomanufacturing, 
the Department is taking following steps:  
 (i) For scaling up i3C BRIC-RCB Ph.D. programme, the Department of Biotechnology 
(DBT) is in discussion with Wellcome Trust (WT) Alliance for seeking support of WT for the i3C 
PhD program. 
 (ii) Strategic group discussion meetings are being conducted for establishment of BRIC 
BioE3 Innovation Parks to strengthen industry-academia synergies. 
 (iii) Entrepreneur-in Residence (EIR) program is being launched in partnership with 
BIRAC and Venture Capitalists for taking forward academic research leads from iBRIC+ towards 
commercialization by supporting young post-docs with fellowships. 

5 
 
KEY INITIAVES AND ACHIEVEMENTS IN HEALTHCARE AND BIOTECHNOLOGY 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.14    The Committee applauds the Department for its strategic foresight and decisive action in 
confronting AMR. Initiatives such as pioneering homegrown therapies, cataloguing priority 
pathogens, establishing AMR bio-repositories, and advancing rapid diagnostics underscore 
India’s resolve to mitigate this global health crisis. The Committee recognizes the breakthroughs 
like Nafithromycin — India’s inaugural indigenous antibiotic targeting drug- resistant 
Community-Acquired Bacterial Pneumonia. This innovation exemplifies scientific excellence and 
addresses critical vulnerabilities among high-risk groups. The Committee emphasizes the need to 
expedite the deployment of such solutions through streamlined regulatory processes, scalable 
production, and inclusive partnerships. Strengthening AMR monitoring frameworks, broadening 
investigations into pathogen prioritization and integrating diagnostics into primary healthcare 
are vital next steps.  
(Para 5.5 ibid) 
Action Taken: 
 
1.15 Department is thankful to the Committee for encouraging observations. It is submitted that 
Nafithromycin has been developed by Wockhardt Group and the Phase III clinical study of 
Nafithromycin in India was partially supported by BIRAC, a PSU of DBT.  
1.16 As per the CDSCO guidelines, the Company has received the Manufacturing License from 
CDSCO and intends to launch the drug by mid-2025 
1.17 Further, the Department is continuing its support and coordination for various AMR 
related research activities focusing on advancing diagnostics, novel therapeutics and creating new 
knowledge related to mechanisms of emergence of drug resistance. The Department is also 
committed to contributing to the NAP AMR 2.0 being developed by the Ministry of Health & 
Family Welfare.  
1.18 The Department will continue facilitating the regulatory approval of innovations for their 
deployment by the concerned Ministries. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.19 The Committee commends the Department for its laudable efforts under the National 
Biopharma Mission (NBM) in advancing indigenous vaccine development against critical 
diseases such as Dengue, Chikungunya, Malaria, and cervical cancer. The noteworthy progress 
in pre-clinical studies, clinical trials, and translational research, alongside strategic international 
collaborations, underscores India’s growing capacity to address global health challenges through 
innovation. 
(Para 5.7 ibid) 
 
1.20 The Committee urges the Department to expedite regulatory clearances, ensure robust 
post-trial protocols, and prioritize cost-effective manufacturing to facilitate the swift market entry 

6 
 
of these vaccines. Emphasis must be placed on equitable access and affordability for all citizens, 
particularly vulnerable populations. The Committee expresses confidence that the timely 
deployment of these vaccines will significantly reduce disease burden, align with national health 
objectives, and reinforce India’s leadership in global vaccine equity. 
(Para 5.8 ibid) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.21  The Department is grateful to the committee for the appreciation of the NBM program 
and also for the guidance.  
1.22  It is submitted that the NBM team is working in close coordination with the grantees to 
understand the bottlenecks in the road to regulatory approvals, as well as other development 
issues. 
1.23 In addition, NBM is also helping the grantees with access to the Clinical Trial Networks 
(CTNs) and other shared facilities set up under the National Biopharma Mission and by BIRAC 
to accelerate the development process. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.24 The Committee extends its profound appreciation to the Department for the visionary 
launch and strategic implementation of the UMMID Initiative, a critical intervention to address 
the burden of genetic disorders in India. The initiative’s three-pronged approach — establishing 
NIDAN Kendras for genetic diagnosis, enhancing the capacity of healthcare professionals, and 
expanding outreach in aspirational districts — has demonstrated remarkable success in its pilot 
phase. The screening of over 2,73,000 pregnant women and newborns, identification of 37,000 
positive cases, prevention of 34 hemoglobinopathy-affected births, and timely diagnosis of 350 
newborns with congenital metabolic disorders underscore the programme’s transformative 
impact on maternal and neonatal health. Furthermore, the integration of mass awareness 
campaigns, skill-building workshops, and collaborations with educational institutions reflects a 
holistic model for tackling inherited disorders through prevention, early diagnosis, and 
community engagement. 
(Para 5.13 ibid) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.25 The Department is grateful to the committee for appreciation for the visionary launch and 
strategic implementation of the UMMID Initiative.   
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.26 The Committee commends the Department for its exemplary commitment to advancing 
multi-disciplinary research and innovation in the domain of biomedical science and engineering. 

7 
 
The development of pioneering technologies such as InoHeal, Hip Pro, Urovib, and Preztic 
reflects a laudable effort to address pressing healthcare challenges through indigenous solutions. 
However, the Committee notes with concern that a major chunk of India’s medical device 
requirements continue to be met through imports, exposing vulnerabilities in healthcare security 
and economic sustainability. To address this critical gap, the Committee strongly urges the 
Department to intensify its focus on cutting-edge research and development in high-priority 
domains where import dependency remains acute. Priority areas could include the indigenous 
design and manufacturing of advanced imaging systems, such as CT scan machines and MRI 
systems, which are indispensable for modern diagnostics yet predominantly sourced from foreign 
markets. Similarly, the development of ophthalmic devices, including intraocular lenses for 
cataract surgery and retinal imaging equipment, must be prioritized to address the growing 
burden of vision-related ailments and reduce reliance on external suppliers. 
(Para 5.16 ibid) 
 
1.27 Furthermore, the Committee emphasizes the need for innovation in critical care 
equipment, such as ventilators, dialysis machines, and radiation therapy systems, which are vital 
for tertiary healthcare but remain largely imported despite rising domestic demand. Integrating 
emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and machine learning with medical diagnostics 
could further enhance precision, efficiency, and scalability, positioning India as a global leader 
in next-generation healthcare solutions. 
(Para 5.17 ibid) 
 
 
Action Taken: 
 
1.28 The Department acknowledges the concern expressed by the committee on the import of a 
major chunk of medical devices.

solutions, portable real time high frequency ECG device, SAANS: a multipowered

Recommendation/ Observation 
1.33 The Committee appreciates the mission program launched by the Department. It is a 
remarkable effort to address rare genetic disorders in children, combining research, diagnosis, 
and care. The program’s focus on identifying novel genes, improving diagnosis, enabling prenatal 
counselling, and developing targeted therapies reflects a transformative approach to addressing 
unmet medical needs. The creation of apan-Indian database of genetic variants promises to 
empower clinicians and researchers globally while advancing precision medicine tailored to 
India’s diverse population. The Committee expresses confidence that PRaGeD will catalyze 
breakthroughs in understanding and managing rare diseases, reducing suffering through early 
intervention and innovative therapies. Sustained funding, capacity-building, and integration of 
research into clinical practice are critical to its success. The Department is urged to strengthen 
global partnerships, ensure ethical data- sharing frameworks, and prioritize accessibility of 
outcomes for vulnerable families. 
(Para 5.19 ibid) 
Action Taken: 
 
1.34 A dedicated web portal is developed by the Project Coordinating organization, Centre for 
DNA Finger Printing and Diagnostics (CDFD), Hyderabad for capturing the data of patients and

1.35 The Department will further strengthen the global partnerships and ensure ethical data

HUMAN RESOURCE CHALLENGES 
Recommendation/ Observation 
1.36 The Committee expresses its deep concern over the acute staffing gaps plaguing the 
Department and autonomous institutions under it, condemning the systemic over-reliance on 
temporary contractual hiring to mask chronic manpower deficits. It underscores that such short-
term stopgap measures erode institutional capacity, stressing that a robust, permanent workforce 
with specialized expertise is indispensable for driving scientific advancement and maintaining 
global competitiveness. To rectify this, the Committee urgently calls for the Department to 
prioritize filling all critical positions—scientific, technical and administrative through a mission-
driven recruitment strategy. 
(Para 6.7 ibid)

CHAPTER – II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES 
 
AUTONOMOUS INSTITUTIONS 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1         The Committee expresses deep concern over the current state of BIBCOL and IVCOL 
and urges the Department to take immediate and decisive action for their revival. Recognizing 
their immense potential, the Committee strongly believes that both PSUs can play a pivotal role in 
strengthening and transforming India’s vaccine manufacturing ecosystem. The Committee 
recommends that the Department proactively engage with the Department of Public Enterprises 
(DPE) and persuade them to secure a revival package for both BIBCOL and IVCOL. The 
Department could explore the possibility of merger of both the units to achieve efficiency. If the 
Department succeeds in securing the revival package from DPE, the Committee recommends that 
the Department should expand BIBCOL’s current product portfolio by initiating the production of 
critical vaccines. Additionally, the Department should actively seek technical collaborations with 
reputed international organizations to enhance manufacturing capabilities and technological 
expertise. The Committee acknowledges the Department’s ongoing efforts in developing vaccines 
for Dengue, Malaria, and Chikungunya and suggests that, upon receiving necessary regulatory 
approvals, these vaccines may be manufactured at BIBCOL and IVCOL. Reviving these PSUs 
would not only contribute to ensuring affordable vaccine availability for citizens but also position 
them as key players in the global vaccine market. Once operational, these PSUs can leverage 
their infrastructure to support vaccine exports, further strengthening India’s presence in the 
international biopharmaceutical industry. 
(Para 4.8 of 388th Report) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
2.2 A revival proposal for the BIBCOL was submitted to the Department of Expenditure 
(DoE) for seeking extra funds. The Department of Expenditure (DoE), advised DBT to approach 
the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) for a review under para 2.1 of DPE’s guidelines dated 
13.12.2021 related to the New Public Sector Enterprises (PSE) Policy for CPSEs in non-strategic 
sectors.  Accordingly, the proposal was forwarded DPE for further consideration by the 
Committee of Group of Officers (CGO) headed by the CEO of NITI Aayog including Secretary of 
the concerned Ministry for closure or privatization under the PSE Policy.  
IVCOL: At present, in line with the Government’s commitment to green growth, the Finance 
Minister announced a new scheme on Biomanufacturing and Bio-foundry in the Interim Budget 
2024–25 (Para 69), aimed at promoting environment friendly alternatives like biodegradable 
polymers, bio-plastics, biopharmaceuticals, and bio-agri-inputs. Under this scheme, the 
Department of Biotechnology (DBT), in collaboration with BIRAC, plans to establish 
Biomanufacturing Hubs across the country. IVCOL’s existing facilities may be repurposed for 
this national initiative. 

12 
 
KEY INITIAVES AND ACHIEVEMENTS IN HEALTHCARE AND BIOTECHNOLOGY 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2.3 The Committee acknowledges the Department’s progress in scaling the UMMID Initiative, 
including its expansion to 30 aspirational districts, establishment of30 NIDAN Kendras and 9 
training centres, and the inclusion of private healthcare institutions such as SVIMS Tirupati and 
Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences, Sevagram, in Phase-II. These efforts signify a 
commendable stride toward decentralizing access to advanced genetic screening and care. 
However, given the persistent challenges posed by genetic disorders - particularly in rural and 
underserved regions - the Committee urges the Department to expedite the pan-India expansion of 
the UMMID Initiative with a renewed focus on universal, time-bound screening coverage. This 
must include100% screening of all pregnant women and newborns, irrespective of their access to 
private or Government healthcare facilities. The Committee also recommends that following the 
100% screening, the Department should work upon creating a vulnerability index which would be 
helpful in assessing the susceptibility of specific demographic groups to various genetic disorders. 
(Para 5.14 ibid) 
Action Taken: 
 
2.4 The Department is grateful to the committee for appreciation. It is envisioned that  Phase-
II of the UMMID programme  will cover more than 20 States/ UTs all over India with nearly 70 
UMMID components (outreach centres in aspirational districts, NIDAN Kendras and training 
centres) being supported, which may be beneficial to more than 6 Lakhs pregnant women and 
newborns. The UMMID programme is for development of trained manpower, resources and to 
establish network in government setup within the R&D mandates as per its AoB rules of the 
Department.  After completion of the projects funded under Phase-II of the UMMID programme, 
capacity development in terms of the trained manpower and the minimal required infrastructure in 
the major hospitals will be ready in the country. Also, through this project mode implementation 
of the UMMID programme, a primary ecosystem will be in place to take it up further in the mode 
of a National Screening Program by the concerned agency in the Government. Thus, though 100% 
screening may not be possible, given the limited budget for UMMID initiative; this programme 
can pave the way for  setting up of a ‘National Screening Programme’ for genetic disorders to be 
taken up by health agencies like MoHFW or ICMR. Further, through implementation of UMMID 
initiative, sufficient R&D resources will be generated like samples of positive cases, data 
generation on approximation of percentage of genetic disorders in the areas wherein limited 
screening programs are being implemented, that will help our researchers in advancing country 
specific R&D studies on diagnostics and treatment in genetics disorders.  However, the statistical 
data on vulnerability of the population to genetic disorders and creation of vulnerability index can 
be taken up only when the Government initiatives like ‘National Screening Programme’ for 
genetic disorders to cover 100% screening is carried out. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.5     The Committee appreciates the commendable efforts made by the Department in advancing 
research on neurological disorders, particularly through cohort-based studies and investigator 

13 
 
driven projects. These initiatives are crucial in deepening our understanding of disease 
mechanisms and developing innovative diagnostic and therapeutic solutions. 
(Para 5.22 ibid) 
2.6 Keeping in view the rising prevalence of neurological disorders, particularly among the 
aging population, the Committee recommends that the Department should launch a dedicated 
mission to comprehensively research the most prevalent neurological diseases. This mission 
should be supported by substantial funding, targeted research programs, and strategic 
collaborations with leading healthcare institutions, academic centres, and industry partners to 
ensure a holistic approach to prevention, early diagnosis, and treatment. 
(Para 5.23 ibid) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
2.7 The Department will intensify its ongoing efforts in the area of Neurological diseases. The 
Department will support targeted interdisciplinary network projects to advance research towards 
prevention, early diagnosis and treatment of neurological diseases like Alzheimers/ Parkinson’s/ 
Acute encephalitis.

GOVERNMENT 
 
BUDGET ANALYSIS  
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1         The Committee notes with concern the sub-optimal utilization of funds under the Central 
Sector Scheme - 'Industrial Research & Development', as over half of the allocated funds remain 
unutilized as the current financial year enters its final quarter. In light of this, the Committee 
emphasizes the critical need for the Department to expedite expenditure and ensure the optimal 
deployment of resources within the remaining timeframe of the financial year. To preempt such 
inefficiencies in subsequent years, the Committee strongly advocates for the institutionalization of 
robust quarterly monitoring mechanisms.                                               (Para 2.3 of 389th Report) 
  
Action Taken: 
 
1.2 Department duly acknowledges and agrees with the Committee's observations regarding 
expenditure. It is humbly submitted that 99% of the Revised Estimates (RE) for FY 2024-25 have 
been utilized for department CRTDH, PACE & A2K+ schemes. Furthermore, the Program 
Division has planned for 100% utilization of the allocated funds for FY 2025-26 and intends to 
seek additional funds at the RE stage through supplementary provisions. It is submitted that under 
PRISM scheme, more than 99% of the budget is utilised in past five years except for FY 2023-24 
wherein nearly 80% of the budget was utilised in view of the challenges faced due to 
implementation of CNA mechanism.  Also, for FY 2023-24 Rs. 2.32 Crores was utilised against 
RE of Rs 3.0 Crores and Rs.  67.71 lakhs was booked/utilised against unspent balance available

Recommendation/ Observation

underutilization of allocated funds. Such underutilization may hinder the intended impact of these 
schemes and delay the realization of their objectives. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Department take proactive measures to ensure effective fund utilization by addressing 
administrative bottlenecks, streamlining project approvals, and enhancing monitoring 
mechanisms. 
(Para 3.4 ibid)

instituting stricter timelines for implementation. Additionally, robust monitoring mechanisms have 
also been put in place, including monthly and quarterly progress/ expenditure reviews at various

efficiency, accountability, and the timely realization of its programmes/projects objectives.

1.14 Two recent progressive initiatives of CSIR along these lines for the kind information of the

1. Proposal for pilot plant installation is submitted at Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB)/

solid waste management practices for bulk waste generators. The said proposal is motivated by 
the fact that bulk generators contribute to nearly 30-40% of the daily waste stream in the city, 
New Delhi. Using scientific methods to process MSW is crucial to turning it into value-added 
products. There are several technologies developed by CSIR that could be incorporated into a 
solution for MSW disposal. This would involve following CSIR Technologies: 
  
I. Sorting of MSW using CSIR-CMERI’s sorter technology 
II. Plastic Waste Sorting System for recycling of Polyethylene Terephthalate (PET) Materials 
III. Plastic Waste Sorting System for five types of plastics 
IV. Conversion of waste plastics to diesel unit using CSIR-IIP’s plant 
V. High rate bio methanation technology called “Anaerobic Gas Lift Reactor (AGR)” for the 
generation of biogas and bio-manure from organic solid waste 
VI. Waste plastics to tiles unit 
VII. Waste Plastic with Red Mud Composite for prefabricated Plastic Panel for Road Construction 
VIII. A process of using Thermocol (expanded polystyrene) waste in hot bituminous mixes for road

COUNCIL OF SCIENTIFIC & INDUSTRIAL RESEARCH (CSIR) 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
2.7 The Committee recognizes the pivotal role played by CSIR in driving research, innovation, 
and technological advancements across diverse domains. As one of the premier research 
organizations in the country, CSIR has contributed significantly to scientific breakthroughs, 
industrial applications, and the development of indigenous technologies that have strengthened 
national self-reliance. Its extensive research network, spanning multiple disciplines, has facilitated 
advancements in healthcare, engineering sciences, environmental sustainability, agriculture, and 
emerging technologies, thereby supporting India's economic and strategic objectives. 
(Para 4.4 ibid) 
 
Action Taken: 
 

 
11 
 
2.8 The Department along with CSIR sincerely acknowledges the Committee’s appreciation 
and recognition. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
 
2.9 However, the Committee notes with concern that CSIR has substantial overlaps in research 
activities with other scientific institutions, including the Ministry of Earth Sciences, the 
Department of Biotechnology, the Department of Science and Technology, the Ministry of 
Electronics and Information Technology, the Indian Agricultural Research Institute, etc. This 
duplication of research efforts leads to fragmentation of resources, inefficiencies in execution, and 
a lack of cohesive direction in national scientific pursuits. The Committee strongly recommends 
that CSIR undertake a comprehensive restructuring to optimize its research priorities, ensuring a 
sharper focus on projects that are highly critical, have a substantial impact, and align with the 
country's strategic interests. The Committee urges CSIR to realign its research portfolio by 
concentrating on areas of national importance where it can deliver unparalleled expertise and 
breakthrough innovations. Rather than engaging in research that overlaps with other institutions, 
CSIR should collaborate with relevant Ministries and research organizations to ensure synergy 
rather than redundancy. By leveraging its strengths in cutting-edge technologies, translational 
research and industrial applications, CSIR can maximize its contribution to India's scientific and 
economic development. The Committee also recommends that CSIR establish a clear roadmap to 
prioritize high-impact research, streamline its organizational structure, and enhance its role as a 
leader in addressing national challenges. A well-defined and strategic approach will not only 
enhance CSIR's efficiency but also position it as a key driver of India's scientific and technological 
advancement in critical sectors. 
(Para 4.5 ibid) 
 
Action Taken: 
 
2.10 CSIR acknowledges the Committee’s concerns regarding perceived overlaps in research 
activities with other scientific institutions. However, it is important to clarify that what may appear 
as duplication is, in many instances, a reflection of necessary convergence in addressing complex, 
multidisciplinary national challenges. Scientific research today, by its very nature, involves 
intersecting domains where coordinated efforts are essential to generate comprehensive and 
impactful outcomes. 
CSIR’s research programs are designed with a focus on translational and industrial applications, 
aiming to deliver end-to-end solutions, develop indigenous technologies, and enhance national 
self-reliance. Thus, CSIR’s mandate centers on converting knowledge into deployable 
technologies, prototypes, and processes that serve India's industry, strategic sectors, and societal 
needs. This translational emphasis distinguishes CSIR’s contributions from those of other 
organizations working in similar areas. A part of CSIR’s activities that seemingly overlap with 
other agencies (such as genome sequencing initiatives with DBT, etc.) are specifically meant to 
generate redundancy, aiming towards improving the quality and robustness of data. 
CSIR actively collaborates with other scientific ministries and agencies, including MoES, DBT, 
DST, MeitY, and ICAR, through joint initiatives, co-funded programs, and shared platforms. 
These partnerships ensure synergy and resource optimization as well as effective exchange of 
scientific knowledge among sister ministries/departments. Few of the examples about inter 
departmental/ ministerial collaboration are as below: 
 

 
12 
 
1. CSIR has been undertaking a nationally important project entitled “Indian Breast Cancer 
Genome Atlas’ in collaboration with Dept. of Biotechnology Institute -National Institute of 
Biomedical Genomics (NIBMG) Kolkata. 
  
2.  CSIR is also partnering with All India Institute of Medical Science (AIIMS), New Delhi, 
Ministry of Health & Family Welfare to work jointly for identified healthcare related research 
projects. 
  
3. CSIR has initiated a new Scheme titled Aerospace Projects of National Importance to undertake 
much needed R&D in National aerodynamic testing facilities, Civil and Military aircraft including 
electric aircraft. 
  
4. CSIR is also partnering with the Ministry of Civil Aviation to develop a National Drone 
Mission. 
  
5. CSIR is in collaboration with the Department of Space, Department of Defence (MoD) for 
various High Technology research and development for national programs. 
  
6. CSIR has entered into Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with Ministry of Micro, Small 
and Medium Enterprises (MoMSME) on June 27, 2025. Both the organizations will work jointly to 
meet the needs and demands of MSMEs under the diversified areas of Science & Technology.  
  
7. CSIR is implementing mission mode projects CSIR Aroma mission and CSIR Floriculture 
Mission. The activities being undertaken under these projects are implemented in collaboration 
with Indian Council of Agricultural Research (Krishi Vigyan Kendra), Directorate of Floriculture, 
Pune and Department of Horticulture, ICAR-IARI, New Delhi across the country.  
  
8.  Under CSIR Floriculture Missions, apiculture has been integrated in collaboration with KVIC, 
wherein the Bee boxes and colonies are provided by KVIC to the clusters established by CSIR 
under these missions. Besides, CSIR is also partnering with agencies like APEDA, TRIFED, State 
Horticulture Departments, FFDC (MSME), Central and State Agriculture Universities etc. 
  
9. Under another mission mode project, which aimed at the development of genetically modified 
cotton resistant to insect pests especially Pink bollworm, CSIR collaborated with ICAR institutes 
and Punjab Agricultural University for validation of the technology in containment. 
  
10. In line with direction of the NITI Aayog, CSIR is pursuing a project under mission mode 
aimed at identification of potential sites for commercial cultivation of seaweeds across the coastal 
states and union territories of the country and their valorisation through downstream processing to 
several value added products. Earlier CSIR had worked with the Department of Fisheries, GoI and 
several state Fisheries departments for this purpose under PMMSY and other schemes. 
 
2.11 Further, in line with the Committee’s recommendations, CSIR has already been conducting

check. Projects are chosen and evaluated through a cross-disciplinary committee of experts drawn 
from peer institutions. CSIR remains committed to continuously evolving its strategy to stay 
aligned with India’s scientific and economic goals, while reinforcing its active role in addressing
