11.The Committee was informed that during the discussions, in respect of Annual Plan 1997-98, the Planning Commission had
 agreed for a minimum net Plan Outlay of Rs. 1200 crores. However, in view of severe budgetary limitations, the Planning
 Commission could allot only a net Plant Outlay of Rs. 990 crores (Gros8-'-Rs. 992.55 crores). While communicating this, the
 Planning Commission had also mentioned that depending on the progress of expenditure on approved schemes and the over all
 resource situation, the position regarding additional allocation of funds to the Department of Space might be reviewed during the
 course of the year.
11.1 The Committee finds that against the allocation of Rs. 761.77 crores (RE) for the year 1994-95 stage the actual
 expenditure was Rs. 759.08 crores. Likewise in 1995·96 against the allocation of Rs. 918.56 crores (RE stage) the actual
 expenditure was Rs. 917.88 crores. In terms of percentage the utilisation works out to 99.65% for 1994·95 and 99.93% for 1995-96.
 Details in respect of 1996·97 are not yet available. In view of satisfactory utilisation of the expenditure the Committee recommends
 that the additional requirements of funds of the department of Space be met in full so that Spare Programmes do not suffer for want
 of funds.
12. The original financial outlay approved by the Planning Commission in respect of the Eighth Five Year Plan (1992-97) was
 Rs. 1804 crores as against the projection of Rs. 3500 crores. By virtue of annual allocations made so far, the Eighth Plan allocation
 comes to Rs; 3170 crores including the additional allocation of Rs. 150 crores for 1996-97. Non-Plan allocation totalled Rs. 773
 crores which includes additional provision of Rs. 7 crores at RE stage in 1996-97.
13. The Committee has been informed that the Eighth Plan accomplishments of the Department of Space in different fields
 were as follows:-
Satellite Communications:
INSAT-2A and 2B launched in July 1992 and July 1993 respectively have enhanced the INSAT Space Segment Capacity,
 facilitating introduction of Metro Channel, rural network, search and rescue service and additional regional channels. INSAT-2C
 launched in December, 1995 provides additional capability vis Ku band transponders for business communication, mobile satellite
 services and extended coverage of C-Band transponders for reception of TV Programme beyond Indian boundaries thus catering
 population from South­ East Asia to the Middle-East. the transponders in the INSA T system have increased from 14 to 70 and
 will further increase to 93 with the launch of INSAT-2D by the end of May/early June, 1997. The cumulative monthly utilisation of
 INSAT transponders for TV and radio networking has increased to 6860 and 13000 hours respectively. The INSAT derived
 services such as telecommunication and television, radio-networking, development and communication, weather forecast disaster
 warning, search and rescue, etc. have also recorded phenomenal growth. The INSA T \based meteorology data collection continues,
 to be an important element of country's meteorological  system. It has also been stated that the Disaster Warning System (DWS) too
 continues to provide timely and invaluable cyclone alert services using 200 DWS receivers installed in eight States. A satellite
 based interactive communication system (I-way video and 2-way audio) has been successfully used to create awareness and provide
 training to adult education functionaries, rural development functionaries, teachers, students, industrial workers, banking staff, etc.
Earth Observation Systems
13.1 IRS-IB, launched in August, 1991 was pressed into operational service combined with IRS-I, launched in March, 1988,
 they provide vital remote sensing data for the National Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS). Utilising the launch
 opportunities from the developmental flights of PSL V, application specific low cost, quick turn-around time satellite missions
 called IRS-P series of satellite were identified. Accordingly, IRS-P2 and IRS-P3 satellites were launched and operationalised in
 1994 and 1996. These satellite complement the data requirements of the user community which was not hitherto available.
IRS-IC, most sophisticated civilian satellite all over the world today, was launched in December, 1995. It has unique
 capabilities being harnessed for a wide range of new applications in the areas of agriculture, cartographic mapping and terrain
 modelling. One up in the series IRS-ID is scheduled to be launched in the current year from Sriharikota. IRS Satellite Constellation
 has become an international system recently', Data from these satellites is being received already by ground stations in USA and
 Germany; some more stations are expected to start' reception in the near future. Commercial agreements are underway for reception
 and marketing of the data worldwide.
SPACE  SCIENCES
14. The National MST Radar facility has been fully commissioned and is being used by the scientific community for advanced
 research in the area of atmospheric sciences. Sounding rocket experiments have been conducted with pay loads development by
 Indian and foreign scientists. The SROSS-CI and SROSS-C2 satellites launched by ASLV in May, 1992 and May, 1994
 respectively are providing useful data in the area of aeronomy and astronomy.
LAUNCH VEHICLE SYSTEMS
15. Successful completion of ASL V programme, development of PSL V and successful flights of PSL V, progress in
 development of GSL V and implementation of agreement with Russia for cryogenic stage and starting of indigenous; cryogenic
 upper stage project were some of the highlights of the Eighth Plan.
15.1 During the Plan period three flights of ASLV were scheduled. However, ASLV-D3 mission 'of May, 1992 proved a
 turning point in the programme. Subsequently, after detailed studies the Department has decided to concentrate its efforts in the
 development of PSL V and, GSL V and to discontinue ASL V which have served immensely as a low cost flying test bed for
 evaluating complex technology. The maiden flight of PSL V took place on September 20, 1993. However, an error in
 implementation of on-board software resulted in a sub-­orbital flight. After the corrective actions second flight took place on 15th
 October, 1994 which successfully placed the IRS-2 satellite weighing 804 kg. in 817 Kms. polar sub- synchronous ·orbit (SSPO).
 With further improvements and higher pay load of 922 kg. the PSLV-D3 was flown on March 21, 1996 with IRS-P3. PSLV has
 now been declared operational. Under the PSL V continuation programme three more flights of PSL V are planned.

15.2 Geosynchronous Satellite Lauch Vehicle (GSLV) is a three stage vehicle, configured with maximum utilisation of PSL V
 modules and infrastructure created for its development. It uses a cryogenic upper stage which was planned to be procured along
 with technology from Russia. However, due to geopolitical reasons, the technology transfer agreement had to be modified into a
 supply contract under which the first cryo stage was revised and consequently the first developmental flight was rescheduled for
 1997-98. It has entered the hardware realisation and qualification phase.
Cryogenic Upper Stage
15.3 After the modification of the agreement with Russia, a separate cryogenic upper stage project for indigenous development
 was initiated. Significant progress. has been achieved in the project, approved in 1994, which was not· envisaged in the Plan.
 Designs have been completed and fabrication activities have commenced. Establishment of test facilities is in an advanced stage.
16. After the completion of the -Eight Five Year Plan the Department of Space has come to conclusion that barring some minor
 slippages or deliberate postponements most of the programmatic targets and missions planned have been accomplished and, in
 some cases, even exceeded. Establishment of UN centre for Space Science and Technology Education in Asia-Pacific were
 additional accomplishments not envisaged under the Plan. Indigenous development of cryogenic upper stage for GSL V was
 initiated though not originally envisaged under the Plan.
17. As already stated in the foregoing paragraphs the expenditure utilisation by the Department has been nearly cent percent.
 An outlay of Rs. 12,200 crores is envisaged for the Ninth Five Year Plan period, the non-Plan component of Rs. 1200 crores and
 plan component of Rs. 11,000 crores. With the confidence achieved by the Department in meeting the set targets during the eighth
 Plan period, the space missions for the Ninth Five Year Plan have been worked out during the year through a series of interactive
 process of interactions with experts and end beneficiaries. Accordingly, the Ninth Plan envisages continuation of development and
 applications of space technology for the social economic benefit of the country adopting an application driven approach while
 efforts would also be made towards developing and harnessing advanced technology in a self-reliant manner.
17.1 The Ninth Plan targets envisage providing services in newer and renovative areas of space applications using state of art
 remote sensing and communication satellites. Scientific investigation in the areas of astronomy including the study of earth and its
 environment would be further pursued. The Department hopes to continue its efforts towards commercialisation of India's
 technological capabilities through marketing space hardware and services in the global market. The Department seeks to achieve
 the space programme objectives by strengthening its partnership with Indian industry, academia and the user community.
17.2 The Department of Space has planned the 16 satellite missions and 11 indigenous launch . vehicle missions during the
 Ninth Five Year Plan.
18. The Committee feels satisfied with the achievements during the Eighth Plan period.
The Committee is also satisfied with the utilisation of expenditure during 1994-95 and 1995­96. While the details of utilisation of
 expenditure for 1996-97 are not yet available, the Committee hopes that the utilisation of expenditure during 1996-97 would also
 be cent- ­percent. Keeping in view the immense importance of the programmes proposed to be undertaken by the Department of
 Space during the Ninth Plan period, the Committee recommends that the adequate funds should be made available to the
 Department so that the space programmes do not suffer.
19. The major missions/projects proposed to be undertaken/continued during 1997-98 include INSAT-2D, INSAT-2E, G.SAT-
l. IRS-1D, IRS-P4, PSLV continuation, GSLV (MK-1) development and cryogenic upper stage development. These projects would
 require Rs. 452.64 crores during 1997-98. Considering the lead time for development and realisation of the missions as envisaged
 in the Ninth Five Year Plan period, the Department considers it imperative to initiate immediately IRS-P5 (Cartosat), IRS-P6
 (Resourcesat) G.SAT-2, G.SAT-3, INSAT-3 DTH, Second Launch Pad, development of advanced technology for IRS programme
 as well as developmental efforts for S-250 booster stage and C-20 cryo upper stage. These projects would require cash flow of Rs.
 313.01 crores.
20. A provision of Rs. 26.62 crores has been sought in Budget Estimates for 1997-98 for the major space application
 programmes essentially for NNRMS/NRIS programme, remote sensing applications development, disaster management system,
 integrated mission for sustainable development, Gramsat, Pilot Project (Jhabua), G.SAT-1 Utilisation and other Satellite
 Communication application programmes as well as space science activities.
20.1 An allocation of Rs. 15.18 crores has been sought towards technology development, indigenisation efforts, advanced
 R&D, etc. which are essential and need to be taken up immediately.
20.2 A provision of Rs. 40.75 crores has been sought for replacement and augmentation of critical facilities. This would cater to
 facilities at VSSC, LPSC & SHAR for supporting launch vehicle programme, facilities at ISAC, LEOS & SAC for supporting the
 satellite programme and facilities at ISTRAC / MCF for providing telemetry / tracking / telecommand support for the multiple
 launch vehicle/ satellite missions.
20.3 A sum of Rs. 287.99 crores including the non-plan component of Rs. 178.55 crores for organisation and infrastructure
 maintenance (including salary and administrative expenses) grant-in-aid to NRSA/PRL/NMRF, international co-operation and
 joint international projects (including the Centre for Space Science & Technology Education in Asia and the Pacific, etc.)
20.4 General Civil Works & Housing have been provided a sum of Rs. 33.96 crores. Housing alone would require 15.26 crores
 for the employees at Bangalore, Ahmedabad, Thiruvananthapuram and Sriharikota and for construction of building for technical
 facilities (Rs. 18.70 crores). The total allocation amount to Rs. 1169.55 crores.
21. The Committee takes note of the assurance given by Planning Commission to the Department of Space for a review of the
 expenditure during the course of the year and for providing additional funds if necessary, and depending on the progress of various
 projects and overall situation with regard to availability of resources. The committee feels that in view of the assurance held out by
 the Planning Commission, its intervention is not necessary at this stage. Nevertheless, the Committee sincerely hopes that in view
 of the national importance of the programmes / mission proposed to be undertaken by the Department of Space during 1997-98, the

REPORT 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to submit the report on its behalf, present 
this Fifty-first Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the Demands for Grants 
pertaining to Department of Biotechnology (Ministry of Science & Technology) for the year 
1997-98 (Demand No. 76). 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the 15th April, 1997, the representatives of 
the Department of Biotechnology gave an overview of the. various activities of the 
Department and the Committee sought clarification on the various aspects of the functioning 
of the Department of Biotechnology. 
3. The Committee considered and adopted the draft report at its meeting held on 8th 
May, 1997. 
4. The world has witnessed spectacular advances in the fields of biotechnology during 
the last 44 years after the discovery of the structure and DNA by Watson and Crick, in 
1953, for which they were awarded Nobel Prize in Medicines and Physiology. The field was 
regarded as the greatest individual enterprise of the humankind. It has revolutionised the 
industrial scenario, especially, the pharmaceutical industry all over the world, particularly in 
technologically advanced countries. Biotechnology is a science which uses the living 
organisms to make or modify a product-to improve plants or animals and microorganisms for 
specific uses. It aims at harnessing the genetic diversity in the living organisms for 
manufacture of useful products and production of strains of microbes, plants and animals 
with improved qualities. 
5. The Department of Biotechnology, estabished in 1986, is expected to give a greater 
impetus to the development of biotechnology in the country. The objectives of the 
Department include development of products and processes and technologies whose large­
scale applications would result in societal and economic benefits. 
The Mandate of the Department of Biotechnology includes:-
• Support R&D and Manufacturing in Biologicals 
• Identify and set up Centres of Excellence for R&D 
• Promote large-scale use of Biotechnology 
• Integrated Programme for Manpower Development 
• Establishment of infrastructural Facilities to support R&D and Production 
• Evolve Biosafety Guidelines 
• Promote University-Industry intemr.tion 
• To serve as Nodal Point for specific International Collaborations 
• Manufacture and application of cell-based vaccines 
• Responsibility of National Institute of Immunology (Nil), National Centre for Cell 
Science (NCCS), Centre for DNA Finger ~rioting and Diagnostics, (CDFPD) and 
International Centre for Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology (ICGEB)

9. The Department has been doing well with the generation of Expert manpower, 
establishment of Infrastructure and R&D projects in Modern Biology and thus could achieve 
an expotential growth within the budget allocation during the last decade. The Department 
would further support programmes aimed capacity building, conservation of biodiversity and 
germplasms, and Research & Development in ide~tified areas during the year 1997-98. The

10. The ongoing activities, . many of which were started under the auspices of the 
erstwhile National Biotechnology Board and were included in the Seventh Plan and Eighth

Technology and Manufacturing activities and International Collaboration. The biotechnology

feed unit with a capacity of 250 Kgs. pellets per hour has also been established. In order to 
cater to the requirement in respect of feed, indigenous feed with a protein level of 35-45% 
(35 to 40% as mentioned in the Annual Report for 1996-97 p.94) has been developed using 
locally available ingredients. Personnel of the institute had been provided intensive training

in prawn aquaculture with a view to disseminate the hatchery and grow-out technology.

17. The objectives of the Department includes, development of products and processes 
and technologies whose large-scale applications would result in societal and economic 
benefits. The DBT has provided a systematic support for: research and development, 
demonstration and new technology transfer for the manufacture of biological and bio­
technological products development, industrial biotechnology support for infrastructure 
facilities, vaccine research and production, international collaboration, biosafety guidelines 
and support to autonomous institutions. The Department has supported major programmes 
in the area of agriculture, health care, biochemical engineering, industry and environment. 
These efforts have made their impact on the weaker sections of the society and also in rural 
areas especially on the farming community. 
18. The Committee was apprised that the major efforts have been initiated to apply 
biotechnological tools for efficient and sustainable utilisation of natural resources bringing 
together experts for interfacing of disciplines and evolving new inter-disciplinary approaches 
for obtaining end products. A special drive was made to consolidate the R&D information, 
based on which further activities were undertaken. Agriculture and allied fields have made 
tremendous progress. Technology transfer activities have been geared up as also filing of 
patents. Development of transgenic crops, diagnostics and vaccines,· human genetics and 
genome analysis, biodiversity conservation, bio-prospecting, biosafety and the like were 
approached with added vigour. 
19. The Committee is happy to note that a biosensor has been developed for the 
detection of organophosphate pesticide residues in water. This is being evaluated by field 
trials. Reclamation of degraded ecosystem at Bhatti Mines (near Delhi), coal and manganese 
mines (near Nagpur) is in progress. Under this project HCN producing microbe has been 
isolated from grasses that are resistant to termites. A kit for detection of biological toxins is 
under development. Studies for removal of heavy metals by bacteria and algae are in 
progress. Attempts are underway for conservation of endangered plant species of Himalyan 
ranges (includ{ng North-Eastern), desert plant species and mangrove species as part of 
biodiversity conservation. 
20. The Committee appreciates the work done by the Department. It, however, 
observes that it is necessary to carry the programmes to the door-steps of the weaker 
sections and the department should concentrate more on programmes meant for the welfare 
of the weaker sections. 
The Committee also recommends that suitable steps be taken to develop the biological 
toxins detection kit without any further loss of time. 
21. The Department of Biotechnology has initiated the project on Technology 
Development and Demonstration of Biofertilizers (Blue Green Algae and Rhizobium) in 
September, 1990. Considering the importance of biofertilizers in the improvement of soil 
productivity and making environment less polluted, in the biofertilizer mission several strains 
of Blue Green Algae and Rhizobium are isolated and screened for their nitrogen fixing 
ability. The performance of the project in terms of technology development, quality control, 
training and demonstration have been encouraging. Keeping in view the importance of 
biofertilizers from the environmental angle for catering to the requirements of poor farmers 
it was decided to enlarge the project in Mission Mode during 1994-97. 30 Research and 
Development Projects have been supported to generate information in gap areas. The 
programme is under implementation in the states of Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Jammu & 
Kashmir, Maharashtra, Punjab, Delhi and West Bengal. 

22. Improved new technologies have been developed for the production of biofertilizers .. 
which include live algal cultures in polybags and in carriers like pulverized straws of wheat , 
rice and maize. An efficient suitable medium for the culture of BGA under polyhouse .· 
conditions has been standardized. Technologies for the production of soil based BGA and 
packets of fresh algal suspension have also been developed. Algal biofertilizer parks have 
been set up in Tamilnadu and Maharashtra. The data shows increase in paddy yield ranging · 
from 3.09 to 27 per cent when BGA was used alongwith chemical fertilizers. 
23. One hundred fifty tonnes of quality assured algal biomass including Anabane a 
Azolla was produced. 7900 demonstrations and experimental trials were conducted in the 
rice growing States. 9827 farmers were trained in these States. 192 training programmes and 
farmers' rallies were organised. Booklets and handouts have been brought otlt in local ' 
languages and adequate media coverage arranged. 
24. The Department of Bio-technology has developed technologies for the production of 
strains specific for chickpea, rajmash, mungbean and soyabean in fermentors upto 1000 Its. 
capacity. Incubation period has been reduced considerably resulting in faster commercial 
production of Rhizobium cultures. About 47 tonnes quality assured carrier based Rhizobia! 
biofertilizer inoculum have been produced so far. 1126 experimental trials and field 
demonstrations were conducted through out the country. In order to build up awareness 
amongst the farming community about 74 training courses farmers' meals were organised. 
5785 farmers were trained . 
25. A farmer can save Rs. 200/- per ha. by using biofertilizers for rice as well as 
leguminous crops. An yield increase of 3 to 27% for rice crop has also been recorded in 
different states. The residual effect of biofertilizers have also been recorded on the 
subsequent crops where yield increase of 9.29% has been observed in the states of 
Maharashtra. 
26. Efforts were made to produce and transfer the eight candidate biopesticides for 
large scale application . Unde( the mission mode programme, 10,500 hectares have been 
covered in different States. Farmers had expressed satisfaction about the performance of 
biopesticides technology in IPM. Economic benefits have been realised in terms of yield 
increase, monitoring benefits per hectare and reduction in pesticide consumption. An~ 
estimated area of 55,000 hectares would be covered under various crops by the end o.f 
Eighth Five Year Plan. 
27. A Biocontrol Network Programme (BNP) was established in 1989 by the departmen t 
of Biotechnology. The main object of BNP is to lay greater emphasis on developing better 
formulation and to develop cost effective, commercial viable production technologies for the 
biocontrol agents and biopesticides. Various extension activities were organised for 
popularisation and large scale adaptation of the Biocontrol based IPM Technology. These 
activities included training programmes, travel Workshop-cum-farmers melaslfield days/ 
Krishi Melas, radio and television talks etc. In some states lab visits were also arranged for 
the farmers. 
28. The Committee observes that the National Centre for Cell Science, Pune has been 
able to standardise the technique of skin culture and grafting of the same in Vitiligo and 
bum cases during the year. The technique has been utilised successfully and effectively in 
clinical applications. The technology is being taken up in a number of hospitals of Bombay , 
and Pune in the bum units for mass uses with the help of NCCS, Pune. 
29. The Committee was informed that there have been major achievements in the field 
of Agriculture and allied areas such as production of transgenic tobacco plants, rice and 
mustard, isolation of gene for enhancing nutritional qualities under Tissue Culture of cereals , 

regeneration of protocols developed for important trees and plantation corps such as Coffee, , 
Pepper, Cocoa, Populous and Soapnut. 
30. A demonstration project on evaluation of the performance of elite tissue culture 
plantlets of large cardamom in planters field over an area of 70 ha. in the States of Sikkim 
and West Bengal has been launched jointed with the Spices Board. 
31. The Hepatitis C kits and Rotaviral diarrhoea strain for vaccine have been very 
significant achievements. Efforts were made to commercialize through Indian industry the .. 
two diagnostic kits for Hepatitis C. Evaluation of VI polysaccharide typhoid vaccine is 
progressing well at two centres namely urban at AIIMS, New Delhi and rural at Tirunal , 
Valley under TRC, Madras. 
32. A mission mode project on semi-intensive prawn aquaculture was launched at seven 
sites in March, 1994. The emphasis has been on non-traditional species like fresh water 
prawn and P. merguiensis. The demonstration on fresh water prawn farming is fully 
underway. Hatcheries have been set up for freshwater prawns and the marine prawn P. 
merguiensis. The programme attemps a diversification of aquaculture through development 
of culture technologies in non-traditional species. 
33. The Department has supported programmes on indigenous feed development. This 
involved basic studies on various feed ingredients and also development of feeds for semi­
intensive prawn farming and carp culture. A feed developed at CETRI, Mysore was field 
tested. Results indicated a production level of 5 t/croplha. The selling price of 1 kg of 
shrimp feed developed works out to be about Rs. 30 per kg. This compares favorably with 
imported feeds which may cost around Rs. 55 per kg and more with an integrated package. 
Attempts are also underway to develop low cost indigenous feeds. This is expected to 
strengthen the efforts towards reducing dependence on imported shrimp feeds. 
34. The Committee commends the work done by the Department to support Phase-III 
clinical trials of the Anti-leprosy vaccine in conjunction with the standard Multi-Drug 
Therapeutic (MDT) regimen. Trials have been conducted in two urban leprosy centres in 
Delhi and at Kanpur Dehat. In Kanpur Dehat, 820 patients received the full dose of vaccine 
and 23950 contacts -have been immunized. The trials indicated quick recovery of the patients 
when vaccine was given alongwith the MDT. The technology for manufacture of the vaccine 
has already been transferred to ~adila. The approval of the Drugs Controller of India is 
waited before marketing the product. 
The Committee recommends that the matter may be pursued for expediting the approval 
of the Drugs Controller of India. 
35. The Committee is happy to note that as a national facility, a brain bank, the first of 
its kind has been established at NIMHANS, Bangalore to promote research in neurobiology 
using precious human material. The facility established a good collection of fresh human 
brains, as tissue fluids and DNA Bank and in supplying the material to various research 
centres all over the country. 
36. Biotechnology based Programmes have been started for SO'ST population to

aromatic plants and extraction/distillation of active principles in crude form are being 
demonstrated for the benefit of SO'ST population. Around 15,000 persons/families have 
benefited under the various programmes. 
37. Eight special projects have been implemented for the benefit of earthquake victims 

in Latur and Osmanabad districts. In the earthquake affected areas nearly 1400 families have 
benefited; 18,800 animals have received vaccination and feed supplemented with mineral 
mixtures so far. Apart from this health-care of sick animals and artificial insemination was 
also taken up. 
38. The Committee was informed that in addition to six genetic clinics established for 
molecular diagnosis and counseling for common genetic disorders -prevalent in the country, 5 
more centres would be set up, out of that two centres are likely to come up in the North­
Eastern Region. A comprehensive document on Genomic Diversity and people of India has 
been finalised with a view to studying the genetic variation among specific groups. In order 
to initiate programmes on Gene Therapy and Bioethics, guidelines have been finalised for 
Gene Therapy research. 
39. The Committee notes with satisfaction the work being done for the rehabilitation of 
earthquake victims in Latur. The Commiteee recommends that the rehabilitation programmes 
be completed expeditiously. 
40. Three assay systems were developed for the detection of the HIV I and II infections 
with the support of the Department. All systems i.e. Western blot, ELISA using synthetic 
peptides and recombinant reagents for testing with the drop of blood showed encouraging 
results during in-house labo~~tory testing. The validation of the test systems has been 
initiated with the help of five clinical centres covering different geographical regions of the 
country. 
The Committee observes that this needs to be taken up on priority basis with the ultimate 
aim of the welfare of the mankind 
41. The Department of Biotechnology is not lagging behind in the field of Human 
Resource Development. The Department has stated that the programme covering post­
graduate and post-doctoral training, short term training, associateship, visiting scientists and 
various popularisation measures has been very successful and useful. Thirty-five Post­
graduate and Post-doctoral courses in selected universities and other institutions located in 
17 States/Union territories include 29 PG courses in Basic Biotechnology, Agricultural, 
Marine, Medical, Veterinary Biotechnology, Biochemical Engineering and Bioprocess 
Technology, four Post-doctoral research and training programmes and 2 post-MD/MS one 
year certificate training courses in Medical Biotechnology. 
42. India is the overall co-ordinator for the G-15 project on establishment of gene bank 
for the medicinal and aromatic plants and also the coordinator for the Asian Region. Other 
regional coordinators being Brazil for South America and Egypt for Mrica. The Department 
interacted with other member countries to pursue the activities. Programme of co-operation 
among the G-15 countries for setting up of Gene Banks for aromatic and medicinal plants 
has expanded. The setting up of a Trust Fund has been agreed to. In the area of animal 
biotechnology and plant bio~echnology co-operation with ASEAN countries is being firmed 
up. 
POPULARISATION OF BIOTECHNOLOGY 
43. Considering the enormous biological wealth of the country and the biodiversity 
which exists, the application of biotechnological tools as well as enhancing the knowledge on 
the fundamentals of modern biology would be the thrust for the new Plan period to prepare 
the country for a major bio-industrial development as we move into the 21st century. 
43.1 The programme of popularisation of Biotechnology is being implemented through 
CSIR National Institute of Science Communication (NISCOM), New Delhi. The programme 
was initiated during 1991 under which 10 popular monographs and many popular articles on 

various aspects of Biotechnology are being published. These publications bring awareness 
among the students, teachers and general public of the development and potential 
application of Biotechnology in various sectors. Also posters showing· Biotechnology 
processes and concepts as visual learning aid specially for school children, besides bringing· 
out biotechnology columns in popular science magazines. 
43.2 The scheme of popular lectures by experts was started in institutions and 
universities, which are engaged in Biotechnology Research activities, in order to bring 
general awareness of basic concepts, recent advances and potential application of 
biotechnology among the students of schools, colleges and universities as well as the 
members of the general public. 
43.3 The Department of Biotechnology also participated in exhibition like International 
Crop Science Congress, "Agrotech Exhibition", "lndi-2010" and "Science & Culture Expo" 
to demonstrate various immunodignostic kits, plant raised through tissue culture techniques, 
bio-fertilisers, bio-pesticides. 
43.4 Apart from this, partially/fully supported seminar&lsymposia are conducted by the 
department to bring together young scientists to interact with each other. 
44. While the Committee is satisfied with the work done so far by the department of 
Biotechnology, but feels that little is known about the activities of the Department. There is 
therefore a need to disseminate the work being done by the Department particularly among 
the targeted sections of the society so that they can make use of its activities and benefit 
from its programmes. The Committee, therefore, observes that there is need to focus in that 
area and the Department should devise ways to communicate its activities in a layman's 
language. 
45. After Considering the Demands for Grants of the department of Biotechnology and 
assessing the progress of various programmes and projects admiriistered by it, the Committee 
recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 113.87 crores as sought by the Department 
of Biotechnology for the year 1997-98, under demand No. 76 may be approved.

REPORT
I, the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Science and Technology, Environment & Forests, having been
 authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present the Fifty-Second Report, on the Demands for
 OJ-ants pertaining to the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research for the year 1997-98 (Demand No. 75).
2. In its meeting held on 1st April, 1997, the Committee discussed in details the Demands for Grants of the
 Department of Scientific and Industrial Research on the basis of documents made available to it and the submissions'
 made before it by the Secretary of Scientific and Industrial Research and other officers of the Department.
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications sought by
 the Members and. placing before it the requisite material to enable the Committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants
 of the Department.
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 8th May, 1997.
5. Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, (DSIR) forms part of the Ministry
of Science & Technology and is entrusted with the matters concerning the following:-
(i) Council of Scientific and Industrial Research
(ii) National Research Development Corporation
(iii) Central Electronics Ltd.
(iv) National Information System on Science & Technology (NISSAT) (v) Registration and
 Recognition of R&D units
(vi) United Nations Conference on Trade & Development and WIPO (vii) National register for
 foreign collaborations
(viii) Creation of a pool for temporary placement   Indian Scientists and Technologists (ix) National register of
 scientific manpower.
6. The thrust of the programmes and activities at the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) is on
 the activities of Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) - a premier Science & Technology (S&T) agency
 with a network of 40 national laboratories, two complexes and 81 Extension and Regional Centres spread all over the
 country that undertake R&D in various disciplines.
7. Other major programmes of the Department include Research and Development by Industry (RDI) consisting of
 in-house R&D in Industry, Scientific and Industrial Research Organisations (SIROs) and Fiscal Incentives for

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA RAJYA SABHA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/52nd%20Report.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:06]
 Scientific Research; Programme Aimed at Technological Self Reliance (P A TSER) consisting of development of new
 or improved technologies, and to promote indigenous development of capital goods, absorption and adaptation of
 improved technology, studies and interactions concerning Technology Evalua ­tion and pre-feasibility ,reports of
 major sectors/products; Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT), National Register of
 Foreign Collaborations (NRFC), Industrial Technology, Transfer and Trading in Technology (TA TI), Linkages with
 International organisations including Asian and Pacific Centres for Transfer of Technology (APCTI) and Promotion
 and Support to Consultancy Services (PSCS) including the Consultancy Development Centre (CDC) and two Public
 Enterprises viz. National Research Development Corporation (NRDC) and Central Electronics Limited (CEL) engaged
 in the commercialisation of indigenously developed technologies.
8. Budgetary Estimates of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) for the year 1997-98
 provide Rs. 513.49 crores (Plan as well as non-Plan). The plan compr)nent amounts to Rs. 230 crores while the non--
plan component amounts to Rs. 283.49 crores. The big chunk of allocation has gone to the Council of Scientific and
 Industrial Research which has got Rs. 486 crores ( Plan as well as non-Plan) against Rs. 444 crores at RE stage of 1996-
97 and Rs. 412.68 crores at BE stage of 1996-97. There has thus been an increase of Rs. 74.68 crores in the overall
 allocation approved for CSIR. The Plan expenditure which remained at the level of Rs. 161 crores at BE as well as RE
 stage of 1996-97 has gone up to Rs. 204 crores whereas non-plan component has risen from Rs. 251.68 crores (BE of
 1996-97) to Rs. 283 crores at BE stage of 1996-97 and has slightly declined to Rs. 282 crores in the BE of 1997-98. A
 large part of non-Plan expenditure amounting to Rs. 130 crores has been allocated to national laboratories whereas a
 sum of Rs. 50 crores has been earmarked for modernisation. Even in the case of administration, the non-Plan
 expenditure amounting to Rs. 46 crores provided in the BE for 1997-98 is higher by Rs. 3 crores over the expenditure
 of 1996-97 and Rs. 1 crore over the RE of 1996-97. It has been stated that the activities and programmes in respect of
 national laboratories will be guided by the white paper, CSIR 2001, vision and strategy drawn up recently with a
 mission statement as "to provide scientific industrial research and development that maximises the economic,
 environmental and societal benefits for the people of India."
9. Major scientific and technological achievements of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research during the
 Eighth Five Year Plan were in the areas of aerospace, biology and biotechnology, chemicals, drugs and
 pharmaceuticals, earth resources and natural hazards mitigation, ecology and environment, electronics and
 instrumentation, energy, food and food processing, housing and construction, leather, rural development and exports of
 R&D and services.
10. In the field of chemicals, the country today is in a position to offer among others internationally competitive
 teshnologies for aromatic extraction, food grade hexane pyroly­sis, gasoline hydrogenation. In the area of organic
 chemicals cost effective novel process for NMB (a solvent used in refinery processes) was developed. In the area of
 polymers about 35 industrial adhesive formulations were developed.
11. In the area of drugs and pharmaceuticals a new molecule centchroman discovered earlier was developed by
 Central Drug Research Institute, first as a new non-steroidal as a female oral contraceptive. Besides, piperine isolated
 from an indigenous plant has been developed by Regional Research Laboratory (Jammu) as a novel bio-enhancer that
 enables the dosages of the common anti-TB drugs, particularly, Rifampicin to be reduced by at least 50% resulting not
 only in the reduction of cost of medication but more importantly in the reduced side effects such as hepatotoxicity and
 neurotoxicity. The know-how has been transferred to industry. Its use with other modem drugs is being pursued.

12. Another memory enhancer Brahmi has been standardised and validated by CDR!.
Besides, CSIR has developed novel and drug intermediates which have been licensed and most of them have been
 commercialised. These are anti-Aids, anti-Viral, anti-Cancer, anti­Bacterials, anti-Malarial, Cardiovascular, analgesics
 and anti-inflammatory, anti-allergic, anti-ulcer, anti-glaucoma and anti-hypertensive. In the field of ecology and
 environment CSIR's achievements have been in the field of environmental monitoring, environmental biotechnology,
 toxic waste management, environmental system design and optimisation.
13. In the field of food and food processing CSIR was designated as the nodal agency for the Mini Mission on post-
harvest technology  of the Technology Mission on oilseeds and pulses. It is participating in the mission through its
 laboratories namely CFTRI, IICT & RRLS (Thiruvananthapuram and Jammu). Besides, in-house activities have
 resulted in development and transferring of several processes to the industry and for their commercial utilisation.      
14. In the area of housing and construction, CSIR has contributed to the development of newer housing designs,
 construction techniques, building material to substitute wood and utilised wastes and dwelling units for disaster hit
 populace, .etc.
15. In the area of leather, the significant achievements of CSIR/CLRI include establishment of the model carcass
 recovery centre at Bakshi Ka Talaab in V.P. for training and demonstration techniques of better collection, and
 recovery of products from fallen carcasses, modernisation of two tanneries through improvement of implant ecology,
 partial automation and process control for product consistency, cleaner leather processing, technology, packages ..
 Besides, a Modem Footwear Design, Development, fabrication and Testing Centre was set up with a pilot facility for
 stuck-on and stitch-down type computer aided design and laser cutting of pattern for footwear and conveyer fabrication
 facility,
16. The major programmes proposed to be undertaken, during the Ninth Plan including the first year of the Plan
 i.e., 1997-98 fall into the following schemes-(i) national laboratories, (ii) National S&T Human Resource
 Development, (iii) R&D Management Support (Central Administration), (iv) "Residential Building and other
 Amenities, (vi) modernisation, and (vii) intellecutal property and technology management.
           17. The first five schemes are continuing in nature with additional new components built in as per the national
 requirement and priorities. A new scheme on intellectual property and technical management has been proposed with a
 view to attain mastery over management and intellectual property and technology in the global context in the years to
 come. Besides, 40 national laboratories would pursue programmes categorised for convenience under various socio-
economic structures and covering areas of aerospace, biology and biotechnol ­ogy, chemicals, drugs and
 pharmaceuticals, earth resources and hazards mitigation, ecology and environment, electronics and instrumentation,
 energy, food and food processing, housing and construction, non-products, leather machinery and equipment minerals,
 metals and materials, rural development exports and R&D and services, national S&T human resource resource
development.
18.In the case of plan expenditure although, there is an apparent sizeable increase of Rs. 43 crores, this is not really
 so significant as it apprises there was no plan increase in 1996-97 over 1995-96. Besides, during 1997-98, the
 committed liability of salary and pension expenditure is expected to go up ,by Rs. 41.35 crores as compared to 1996-
97. The expected increase of Rs. 41.35 crores does not include any element of increase on account of implementation of
 the recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission. In the event of the implementation of the recommendations of the

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA RAJYA SABHA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/52nd%20Report.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:06]
 Fifty Pay Commission during 1997-98 a gap between the Budget allocation and the committed liability will get further
 widened.
19. DSIR has stated that in the Eighth Five Year Plane part of salary expenditure was met out of the plan allocation
 right from the beginning of the plan. In the year 1996-97, out of the total expenditure of Rs. 221.75 crores on pay and
 allowances about Rs. 50 crore had
to be met out of plan funds. It has. been stated that the problem may continue even in the Ninth Plan peiod. Out of the
 total estimated expenditure of Rs. 247.80 crore on pay and allowances for the year 1997-98, a sum of Rs. 25 crore is
 proposed to be met from the plan funds at the Budget EstimateJstage. The Committee has been informed that during
 the annual plan discussions for 1997-98, the Planning Commission has taken a stand that no expenditure on pay and
 allowances should be met out of plan allocation and the same should be made from the non-plan Budget only. The
 Planing commission further advised CSIR that it should approach the Ministry of Finance for additional allocation
 under non-Plan to meet this liability. This diversion from plan to non-Plan of funds has placed CSIR in serious
 difficulty as the deficit under .. non-Plan Budget on account of pay and allowances and pension alone has gone up
 toRs. 91.35 crores (Rs. 41.35 crores + Td. 50 crores).
20. It has been stated that in addition to the above, the expenditure on contigencies and maintenance has been
 gradually increasing due to general rise in price level. They have. not been provided with any increase under non-plan
 to neutralise this additional liability which is estimated to be Rs. 10 to 15 crores. There would thus be a deficit of Rs.
 100 to 107 crores under non-plan for the year 1997-98.
21. The Committee observes that the CSIR has a work force of 25,233 employees comprising of 19,095 scientific
 and technical and 6,138 administrative employees. The ratio of scientific and technical employees to administrative
 employees works out to 3:1. The Committee feels that the entiresfaffing pattern of CSIR should be reviewed with a
 view to bringing down the ratio of scientific and technical personnel to administrative personnel to a level where the
 productivity is optimum. As regards the diversion of plan expenditure to non­plan expenditure, the Committee
 reiterates its earlier recommendation that the Ministry of Finance should give one time additional allocation to regula
 rise the diversion. At the same time, the DSIR should sincerely endeavour to review its non-plan expenditure so that the
 necessity of diversion in future does not arise.
22. Out of the total allocation of Rs. 486 crores (Plan as well as non-Plan) for the year 1997-98, a total of Rs.
 335.65 crores has been provided for 40 national laboratories with 80 field extension centres which. CSIR has built up
 over the years and which have expertise and knowledge and diverse scientific disciplines and serve practically the
 entire gamut of socio­economic sectors. Programmeslprojects of the national laboratories that would be pursued by
 them have been categorised under various socio-economic sectors such as aerospace; biology and biotechnology;
 chemicals; drugs and pharmaceuticals; food and food processing; housing and construction; information products;
 leather; machinery and equipment, miner­als; metals and materials and rural development. Another sum of Rs. 50
 crores (Plan) has been provided for modernisation of these laboratories. Justifying the allocation, it has been stated that
 a most significant factor in realising the goals set for CSIR is the immediate upgradational replacement of the obsolete
 equipment and communication and networking system in CSIR. The mo/dernisation of the ageing equipment and
 facilities has been of concern at different levels and a vexing issue in the CSIR for the past decade. This is stated to
 have adversely affected the productivity and competitiveness of CSIR labs. It, therefore, need hardly be stressed that

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA RAJYA SABHA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/52nd%20Report.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:06]
 phenomenal advances in equipment and instruments have come about as a result of developments in micro-electronics
 and information technology. It has been further stated that if the CSIR is to have some semblance of global
 competitiveness, upgradation and modernisation of facilities is called for besides creating new facilities which have
 since become essential CSIR's endeavour, it is stated, would be to modernise and upgrade facilities in these
 laboratories.
23. The Committee fully shares the concern expressed with regard to the functioning and modernisation of
 laboratories. It feels that at present the laboratories give a look of some department-run officis with not much takers
 of its facilities.
The Committee agrees that of course there is a need to modernise these laboratories. The point which the
 Committee seeks to stress is that the test facilities given by these laboratories should be charged on commercial basis
 except where they facilitate a national effort. Even i,n the process of modernisation apart from the equipment the
 laboratories should have faster communication facilities and give a business like appearance which attracts the
 customers and provides business to the laboratories. At the same time, the Committee recommends that the CSIR
 should endeavour to cut down, as far as possible, the non-plan expenditure which they may fund from their
 commercial activities so that the burden on the national exchequer is reduced.
24. It was pointed out to the Secretary that the technology innovation of excellence mainly depends on discovery
 in the field of science and technology. Therefore, stress should be laid on fundamental research and basic sciences.

 examined expeditiously.
25. It was pointed out to the Secretary, DSIR that the country has a rich heritage in respect of herbal medicines.
 He was asked whether any attempt was being made to gather these secrets and commercially exploit them as the
 allopathic medicines were costlier which the common people could not afford to buy. Besides, herbal medicines
 were being commonly usede in countries like China where every hospital had a branch of herbal medicines with

The Committee is not satisified with the reply given by the Secretary, DSIR and feels that no sincere attempts

4. The Department of Ocean Development was established ia 1981 as a part of Cabinet

S. The major programmes of this Department, which are being implemented at present

Development; Internatio.1al Law including Treaty and Programmes relating to international 
co-opernti<Jn. The Programmes of the Department are based on Ocean Policy Statement of 
the Government besides the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS). The 
Programmes are directed to explore and exploit vast potential of marine resources, hitherto 
hidden undet the mysterious ocean nnd sons, for the socio-economic benefit of the society 
and to protect and preserve \he marine environment.

programmes like Antarctic Research Programme, Polymetallic Nodules Programme, 
Oceanographic Research Vessel, Fishery and Oceanographic Research Vessel (FORV) and 
Marine Satellite Research· Information and Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction System 
(COMAfS). 
22. It has been stated by the Department that it had projected its demand originally for 
Rs. 63.80 crores but the Planning Commission agreed for a sum of Rs. 57.75 crores. 
Subsequently, however, the Department was informed that the outlay finally approved by 
the _Planning Commission stood at Rs. 52 crores. With the reduction in the outlay, the 
Department has been compelled to shift some of its activities to the next financial year. The 
Department has proposed to manage with the existing allocation by rescheduling some other 
activities. 
23. The Committee feels that the Department should make out a strong case for 
enhancement in its allocation in the revised estimates for the current year. 
24. As regards the Antarctica Research Programme, the Department has originally 
sought Rs. 23 crores . The Planning Commission had first agreed to provide Rs. 20.20 crores 
but it finally approved an outlay of Rs. 20 crores. India's foray in the Antarctica commenced 
with the launching of the first expedition in 1981. Thereafter a number of multi-disciplinary 
and multi-institutional scientific expenditions have beeri sent to the Antarctica regularly on 
annual basis. The first research station in the Antarctica, "Dakshin Gangotri" was 
commissioned in 1983 and was functional until 1987. In 1988 the settting of Indian permanent 
station "Maitri", with modern infrastructural facilities for conducting temporary scientific 
research was established in the Schirmachar Oasis. Dakshin Gangotri Station is being 
maintained as a supply base. Sdentists from diverse fields drawn from national laboratories, 
institutions and universities are P.rovided with adequate opportunities to carry out experi­
ments in all major branches of polar science. The ·logistic support is extended by various 
wings of the Defence Services and Laboratories of the Defence Research and Development 
Organisation. The programme has thus become one of international Prestige and is therefore 
necessary that the programme is allowed to continue with adequate budgetary support. 
25. The Committee therefore recommends that the Department should get what it had 
originally projected i.e. a sum of Rs. 23 crores. Besides, the Department should endeavour for 
commercial exploitation of the Krill ftshery and other such resources in the Antarctic waters 
because of its demand in the overseas markets. 
26. The Polymetallic Nodules (PMN) Programme is another national programme with 
international commitments. It consists of three components "Survey and exploration of 
polymetallic nodules in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB)", "Development of 
Technologies for mining of nodules " and "extraction of metals from sea bed". The 
programme is reviewed and guided by the PMN Board of Management. Considering the 
potential of the benefits that could accrue for future industrial programmes, the Committee 
feels that in view of the need for India to be among the developed nations in the high 
technology in the Ocean sector and from the long-term strategy and geo-political considera-

tions, it is essential to continue technology development efforts for exploration and exploitation 
of the polymetallic nodules so that we do not lag behind other pioneer investors and enable 
' the country to begin commercial exploitation when economic feasibility is established. Here 
also the Committee is of the view that the Department's original demand of Rs. 11 crores 
should be met in full whereas the Planning Commission has sanctioned only a sum of Rs. 9 
crores. 
27. The Committee had recommended in its 11th and again in 19th Report on Demands 
for Grants (1994-95 and 1995-96) that the Department should make vigorous efforts to acquire 
a multi-purpose vessel/ice-breaker ship expeditiously to obviate the possibility of escalation in 
its cost in case the matter is delayed any further. Such a project would call for increased 
financial allocations for the Department during this plan period. The Committee was apprised 
that an Expert Group constituted for the purpose recommended in September 1993 that the 
new ship may cost Rs. 100 crores keeping in view our requirements in respect of the design of 
construction and it may take 3 to 4 years to time to get the same. Therefore, the ready 
availability of the suitable second-hand ship may be explored for the purpose. The Committee 
has now been given to understand that the offers made by South Africa, Germany, Ukraine, 
Finland, Norway and Denmark in response to the global enquiry did not conform to our 
detailed specifications, the Department has evaluated in the meantime, the option of 
chartering a vessel for a period of 3 years instead of annual charter which could result in 
reduction of charter cost. Accordingly, Department has entered ;-into a contract with M/s. 
Reiber Shipping Company, Norway for a three year charter. They have stated that an official 
delegation which visited Russia for a on-the-spot market survey in January, 1995 could not 
identify a suitable second-hand vessel meeting our requirements. 
28. The Committee feels that the Department should work out the economics for all the 
alternatives to acquire including the purchase of a new vessel and plan its strategy 
accordingly. The Committee should be apprised of economic of all the proposals. 
29. The marine instrumentation has received an allocation of Rs. 2 crores· in the budget 
estimates for 1996-97 against the budgetary support of Rs. 1 crore last year. The allocation 
covers shore to fishing vessel communication which is a reliable means of passing messages. 
SOS signals and data with the help of a fixed shore station and a hand held VHF radio 
telephone on board the fishing craft. The system would help the traditional and small-scale 
fishermen who are venturing for fishing for a range of about 40 kms. from the shore and had 
no means to communication from the fishing craft and vice-a-versa. With the advancement in 
the communication technology it has become possible to provide such facilities to the 
fishermen for ensuring their safety at sea. 
30. The Committee therefore recommends that expeditious steps be taken to select a 
suitable model of walkie-talkie set and the other technology to cover maximum number of 
fishermen within a short span of time across the country. 
31. The Committee is of the view that the extraction of drugs from the ~ea has immense 
potential. By now more than 100 pure compounds have been isolated and characterised 
some of which posses interesting biological activities while others even though biologically 
not promising possess interesting structures. The Department has taken up standardisation 
and introduction of new bioassay methods for violating anti-viral activity both IN VITRO 
and IN VIVO, casting hepatoprotective agents, anti-diabetic agents, anti-filarial agents, anti­
fungal agents using multi-fungal infection models. 
32. The Committee recommends that the Department should put in sustained effort in 
tapping this potential by involving universities/institutes. The Committee is happy to note that 

the number of active/modern organisms have been screened. The Committee hopes that in the 
near future it will be possible to commercially exploit the area for development of drugs from 
medical substances obtained from sea.

REPORT
 
The Ministry of Science and Technology is mainly responsible for formulation of policy and guide­lines on Science and Technology,
 promotion of new areas of S&T in which a number of Institutes Departments have interest and capabilities, scientific and technological surveys,
 R&D activities, inter­national scientific and technological cooperation, promotion of S&T and its application to the develop ­ment of the nation.
2. The Department of Science and Technology (DST) was established with the primary objective o( promoting new areas of Science and
 Technology (S&T) and to play the role of a nodal department for organising, co-ordinating and promoting S&T activities in the country. This
 Department is the nodal agency in regard to the formulation of policy statements and guidelines in the areas of science and technology. It also
 deals with the apex level science policy structures.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
3. The Secretary, Department of Science and Technology (DST) informed the Committee that the Department had asked for an allocation of Rs.
 1800 crores for the Ninth Plan period to meet the require­ment of the Department but the allocation was restricted to Rs. 1576 crores and this is
 also subject to review and restriction on yearly basis. This allocation is about 50 per cent more than the expenditure incurred during the Eighth
 Plan Period.
4. The Committee observes that this enhancement is practically at the Eighth Plan level as inflation cost has not been taken into account. The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the Planning Commission may consider raising this outlay at the time of conducting mid-term ap­praisal
 of the Plan so that the projects and programmes administered by DST do not suffer due to paucity of funds.
5. The total outlay for DST for 1998-99 is Rs. 628.12 crores as against Rs. 562.86 crores in 1997-98 which was later revised to Rs. 617.43
 primarily for implementation of the recommendations of the Fifth Pay Commission and for implementation of the Swarnajayanti Fellowship
 Scheme under which a one­time grant of Rs. 50.00 crores was placed at the disposal of the Ministry for creation of a corpus (Annexure I). The
 Planning Commission made an allocation of Rs. 305.00 crores for the year 1998-99 out of which Rs. 12.00 crores are proposed to be transferred
 to the Ministry of Urban Development for incorporation in the Budget document of that Ministry for Capital Works to be executed during 1998-
99. The increase in Plan provision of 1998-99 as compared to RE 1997-98 is mainly due to the "Fund for Improvement of Science and Technology
 (FIST) Infrastructure in Universities & Related Institutions" for achieving India's quest for competitive advantage in the emerging new world for
 which an amount of Rs. 25.00 crores has been allocated.
6. Similarly, under Non-Plan, there are increases largely under the Survey of India (SOl); India Meteorological Department (IMD); Autonomous
 Institutes and Professional Bodies; Secretariat and Na­tional Atlas and Thematic Mapping Organisation (NATMO) mainly to cater to the
 enhanced level of expenditure under salaries, travelling expenses and other expenditures.
 
7. The budgetary allocation for Survey of India has been increased from Rs. 137.00 crores (R.E.) in 1997-98 to Rs. 148.57 crores in 1998-99 and
 and for the National Atlas and Thematic Mapping, Organisation, the total allocation is Rs. 7.20 crore which is Rs. 1.44 crores more than the Budget
 esti­mates of 1997-98. The quantum of assistance to scientific bodies has been placed at Rs. 105.17 crore which is at the previous level of Budget
 Estimates of 1997-98, and Rs. 1.56 crores more than the revised estimates of last year. In the current year, the payment to Technology
 Development Board against cess receipts, the non-Plan expenditure is being reduced from Rs. 70 crore to Rs. 50 crore. There is a quantum jump in
 the allocation made for Observatories and Weather Stations and is proposed to be kept at Rs. 50.09 crores against Rs. 39.58 crores in the Budget
 Estimates of last year. The allocation for other Meteorological Services has also been increased from Rs. 18.43 crore in BE of 1997-98 to Rs. 22.74
 crores in 1998-99, whereas the allocation for other programmes is being reduced from Rs. 9.78 crore in BE of 1997-98 to Rs. 6.33 crore in the
 1998-99 which is equivalent to the level of RE of last year.
SUPER CONDUCTIVITY PROGRAMME
8. The Committee while going through the various documents supplied to it to facilitate the exami ­nation of the demands found that there is no
 allocation indicated for the super conductivity programme and also there was no allocation for it in 1997-98 and this made the Committee to
 enquire from the Secretary of the Department if this Programme has been abandoned in view of making no allocations for it. The Committee was
 told that the programmes in the area of super conductivity have not been abandoned. The Department has reorganized support to R&D programmes
 and activities in this area are now funded and monitored under the Science and Engineering Research Council (SERC) scheme. This was done as
 necessary infrastructure facilities and capabilities to conduct R&D activities in the area of super conductivity have been developed and such
 activities can now be implemented through project mode like other areas in science and engineering.
TRANSFER OF TECHNOLOGY TO INDUSTRIES AND COMMERCIALISATION OF INDIGENOUS TECHNOLOGY
 
9. In reply to a question about the steps being taken by the Department for revenue generation by way of transferring technology to industries and
 the breakthrough technologies which have been devel ­oped with the assistance of the Department during the last two or three years, the
 Committee was in­formed that the Department attaches a lot of importance to return on investment made for generating technologies. In order to
 encourage transfer of technology to industries, the Department attempts to associate industries with the researc9 programmes right from the
 beginning. In the area of Drugs and Pharmaceuticals industries like Dabur, SPIC, Zandu, Bharat Biotech, Ranbaxy have been associated. Two
 patents have been filed-one, "An antiangiogenic drug" was filed in India as well as in USA and the other on "Novel peptides for the treatment of
 cancer" was filed in India. Some instruments have also been developed and know how transferred to industries for commercial production.
10. The Committee recommends that more efforts need be made to transfer greater number of know how developed indigenously to industries.
11. In this regard, the Committee wanted to know about the role which the Technology Board is playing to accelerate the commercialisation of
 indigenous technologies and drafting/the imported technologies for wider application. The Committee was informed that during 1997-98 the
 Technology Development Board signed 20 agreements with 18 commercial enterprises for development and commercialization of indigenous
 technology. These 20 projects covered areas such as medical and health, engineering and electronics, chemicals and lubricants, agriculture and
 biotechnology, power cable, trans­port, environment and communication. The total cost of these projects was Rs. 143.84 crores including the loan
 assistance of Rs. 51.46 crores by the Board. The disbursement during the year amounted to
Rs. 30.14 crores, as the loan assistance is released in installments on the basis of assessment of the progress of the project by Project Monitoring
 Committees. The technology provided for these projects included National Laboratories, Academic Institutions and In-house R&D Units in the
 industry recognized by the Government. In addition, the Board/Project Evaluation Committees for evaluating the project applications had
 recommended financial assistance of Rs. 97.67 crores for 9 more projects. Further, 11 applications with the projected Board funding of Rs. 38.40
 crores had been referred to Project Evalua ­tion Committees for their evaluation. M/s Shantha Biotechnics Private Limited, Hyderabad, the first
 industrial enterprise to be provided with the Board's loan assistance, has launched India's first geneti ­cally engineered Hepatitis- B vaccine in
 August 1997 and the vaccine is available in the market.
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY COUNCILS
12. The State S&T Councils have been set up in all States and Union Territories. The Department provides financial support for the scientific

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA RAJYA SABHA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/55th%20Report.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:07]
 posts and equipment like computers and communication systems. The Department regularly conducts regional meetings and annual review
 meetings with partici ­pation of the Planning Commission, Central Scientific Departments, State S&T Councils, Central Research Agencies like
 CSIR, ICAR and State Institutions in order to have better understanding regard­ing the functioning of various State S&T Councils and to review
 their programmes. The last regional meeting took place on the 5th and 6th June, 1998 at Gandhinagar, Gujarat.
SCIENCE AND TECHNOLOGY POLICY MECHANISM
13. On a question on the revision of the Scientific Policy Resolution of 1958, in view of the New Economic Policy announced in 1991, the
 Committee was informed that the Scientific Policy Resolution does not require any major changes and is still valid. The Technology Policy
 Statement, however, re­quires some modifications keeping in view the changed scenario both at global and national level and the modifications
 required are under consideration.
14. The Committee is of the view that there is no need to have two different policies-one for science" and the other for technology. There can be
 no technology without science. Both these areas are clearly linked.
15. The Committee, therefore, recommends that attempts be made by the Department to pre­pare an update on the Science and Technology
 Policy.
16. As regards scientific structures which exist at the apex level to guide the Science and Technol ­ogy Policy, the Committee was informed that
 three tier mechanism to advise the Government on S&T policy matters has been set up consisting of a Cabinet Committee on Science and
 Technology under the Chairmanship of the Prime Minister; Scientific Advisory Committee to the Cabinet (SAC-C); and Com­mittee of
 Secretaries on Science and Technology. On a specific question about how many times these Committees have met during the past three years, the
 Committee was told that the Cabinet Committee on Science and Technology has not met so far, as the need for this was not felt. The Scientific
 Advisory Committee to the Cabinet (SAC-C) was constituted in June 1997. This Committee has met seven times and had held discussions on
 issues like improvement of working conditions of research fellows, fund for infrastructure in S&T in the academic sector, guidelines for
 implementation of Swamajayanti Fellow­ships, creation of National Botanical Gardens, programme to develop expertise in the area of taxonomy
 and modernisation of the patents, etc.
DRUGS AND PHARMACEUTICAL RESEARCH
17. The scheme on Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Research was initiated by DST in 1994-95 for promoting R&D in drugs and pharmaceuticals
 sector. Under this scheme the financial support is provided to national laboratories and academic institutions for the research programmes which
 are conceived jointly by the industry and public funded R&D institutions. The programme aims at development of new mol-eculs leading to
 commercialisable technology towards new drug development, giving special thrust to the development of drugs for treatment of diseases prevalent
 in the Indian climatic zone, promoting R&D in all, systems. of medicines, bringing together the scientific expertise existing in the country in
 research institutions and industry on a joining platform in a project mode, establishment of mechanisms and linkages so as to facilitate the
 development of new drugs by the Indian Industry and the Research Institutes, creating state-of-the art infrastructure facilities on par with
 international standards for the benefit of the Indian Industry and other users on payment basis and any other activity which is incidental to the
 above objectives. During the year 1997-98,5 projects have been sanctioned for financial support involving an amount of Rs. 113.00 lakhs towards
 the first release of grants. Three of the projects are related to, the development of novel anti-mycotic agents, anti-cancer agents and new cardio-
vascular drugs. Two of the sanctioned projects involve synthesis of NCEs as potential antifungal agents and development of Tran mucosal drug
 delivery systems for anti ulcer-drug.
18. The Committee was informed that in the current year, the Department plans to continue efforts to support joint research projects for the drug
 development for diseases like Tuberculosis, Leprosy, Malaria, Filaria, Gastrointestinal disorders, Diabetes, Hypertension, Cardio-vascular
 disorders and other prevalent infectious diseases in particular acute respiratory infections, Encephalitis, Dengue Virus and food borne diseases,
 etc. Special emphasis is planned to be given towards development of novel drug delivery systems. Efforts towards" drugs development" based on
 traditional system of medicines will also be made. This will be carried out by development of new formulations and standardization testing of
 traditional formulations.
19. The Committee brought to the notice of the Secretary of the Department the vast biodiversity which exist in the country and particularly
 wanted to know whether the Department intends to develop drugs on the basis of traditional system of medicine and herbal medicine. The
 Committee was told that under the 'Drugs ~d Pharmaceuticals Research Programma' of the Department two research projects and a national
 facility have been commissioned. The research programme, jointly undertaken by the Dabur Research Foundation and the Delhi University
 envisages standardisation of the various Ayurvedic formu­lations such as Asawas and Arishthas. The research project of the Zandu
 pharmaceuticals and RRL, Jammu envisages validation of efficacy of some of the herbal formulations including Asvagandha, Satavari, etc. The
 objective of the national facility that has been set up at the Indian Institute  of Chemical Biology, Calcutta is to' screen the herbal extracts for their
 immuno-modulating potential. Apart from these research programmes and national facility, the Department has also initiated a survey on the
 medicinal plants in the State of Sikkim.
20. While the Committee appreciates that the Department has engaged itself in the development of drugs for the diseases which are peculiar to our
 country, the Committee would like the Department to consider development of drugs on the basis of traditional system of medicines and herbal
 medicines because . traditional medicines derived from plants and herbs are gaining popularity in other parts of the world, including the developed
 countries because of these drugs being safe and having no or little side-effects.
METEOROLOGY
21. India Meteorological Department (1M D) has been set up to provide forecasts and climatologically statistics for optimum operation and
 planning of weather-sensitive activities, such as agriculture and aviation; and to establish and maintain a large number of observatories and to
 provide instrumental and technical support to the acquisition of observational data. Apart from this, the Department is also working in the field of
 providing warning against severe weather phenomena such as tropical cyclones, heavy rain, snow, heat and cold waves, etc. and also monitor and
 locate earthquake and monitor seismic events risks. IMD is also responsible to carry out and promote research and development and impart
 training in various aspects of meteorology and allied disciplines. During the year 1996-97 eight Automatic Visual I Assessor (AVRA) were
 commissioned at national airports and the balance AVRA were received {or deployment at other airports. Ten X-band weather radars with digital
 processing facilities were commissioned. AMSS at Guwahati and Chennai were Commissioned. The Committee was informed that IMD had
 made efforts to receive and instal ten HFRT sets and seven RTT sets. The CWDS system under phase III was further extended to cover more
 vulnerable coastal districts. One new RMC at Guwahati was created for NE region. The network of Seismological Observatories was strengthened
 by establishing more observatories. The Seismological Telemetry Network in the National Capital Region is under progress. Modernisation of
 weather forecasting system at major forecasting offices at IMD (WAN System) is likely to be established. The Department proposes to upgrade
 the quality of the service and explore the new areas of development. As a part of modernisation, sophisticated Doppler Radars will be introduced
 in the cyclone detection network to enable more purposeful study of the devastating cyclones. IMD proposes to undertake a number of new
 projects/programmes during 1998-99 in the areas of Weather Forecasting Services, Instrumentation, Telecommunications, Agrimet, Space
 Meteorology and Hydrology. The programmes involves modernization augmentation of existing facilities i.e., procurement of S-Band Doppler
 Radars. BREWER Ozone Spectrophotometer, High Speed Wind Recorders, etc. with a view to enhancing the quality of forecast.
22. In the current year's budget, a sum of Rs. 131.35 crores has been allocated to the Meteorology sector as against Rs. 111.84 crores allocated
 last year at the RE state under this head. The Committee hopes that the new initiative which would be taken up by the Department in the area of
 meteorol ­ogy in view of the significant enhancement in the budgetary support under the head 'Meteorology' would enable the Department to
 upgrade and modernise its existing facilities and initiate new projects and programmes which would ensure more accuracy in the weather
