 forecasting work done by the Department.
FUND FOR IMPROVEMENT OF S&T INFRASTRUCTURE IN UNIVERSITIES AND RELATED INSTITUTIONS (FIST)
23. In recent years great concern has been expressed about the lack of infrastructural facilities for imparting good quality higher education and
 conducting advanced research. As a result of the ongoing efforts, departments in the universities and related institutions have made some impact on
 the develop ­ment of teaching and research. These university departments are now in a stage to be identified for selective strengthening of their
 infrastI1lcture for post-graduate education and research. It is also neces­sary to extend such infrastructural support to other higher technical
 education institutions and medical education institutions. Considering all these factors, a major new programme named Fund for Improve­ment of
 S&T infrastructure in universities and related institutions (FIST) has been envisaged. The De­partment has made a provision of Rs. 25.00 crores
 for the year 1998-99 under the Fund for Improvement of Science and Technology (FIST) infrastructure in Universities and related Institutions. The
 purpose of the FIST scheme would be to provide basic infrastructure and the enabling facilities and environment for promoting R&D in new and
 emerging areas and attracting fresh talent. The basic infrastructure would cover modem instrumentation facilities, access to information system and
 netw6rking and other infrastructural facilities like space, electricity, water and library facilities. The Committee was informed that the Department
 pleaded its case for allocation of Rs. 100 crore; before the Planning Commission for the FIST programme but it was restricted to Rs. 25 crores
 which C0.JiStitute only the one-fourth of the allocation demanded.
24. The Committee is convinced of the usefulness of the programme and, therefore, recommends that keeping in view the large number of
 universities and other institutions engaged in research and development work in frontier areas of science, the Planning Commission may consider
 providing higher allocation to the Department under this head at the RE stge. The Committee would also like that the Institutions! Universities for
 support under the FIST programme be selected through a transparent mechanism.
 
 
SWARNAJAYANTIFELLOWSHIPSSCHEME
25. 'The Committee found that an allocation of Rs. 50.00 crores under the Swarnajayanti Fellowships Scheme was made at the revised estimates
 during 1997-98 plan outlay and no allocation has been made for the current year. The Department explained that the amount is being kept in an
 interest bearing deposit account in PL Account. The rate of interest to be allowed on the deposit is at the rate of 13 per cent per annum which is
 expected to ensure an interest receipt of -Rs. 6.50 crores for the year 1998-99. The Fellowships will be awarded every year out of the interest
 earned. No provision was, therefore, made in the 1998-99 plan outlay. The Committee was informed that in response to the advertisement for short
 listing of the fellowship 765 applications were received and after the first screening only 65 were left in the fray, and in the second screening the
 number was reduced to 24, which ultimately resulted in final selection of 11 fellowships.
26. Looking at the response to the advertisement inviting applications under the Swaranajayanti Fel­lowship Scheme, the Committee is of the
 view that in future the Department should provide adequate publicity to the scheme through newspapers, radio and television so that more
 applications are received for the Fellowship.
SELF-EMPLOYMENT PROGRAMME FOR WOMEN
27. The Department has started a number of projects for generating self-employment of women.  During the year 1997-98, 26 projects were
 supported by the Department. These projects include produc­tion and marketing of mushroom, training in modem sericulture activities, orchid
 farming for rural women, etc. A list of projects is given at Annexure-II. The Department has also started coordinated projects on horticulture in
 Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Orissa, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Delhi and Tripura also for the benefit of women, wherein they are trained in
 processing and preservation technology. The detail of coordinated projects is placed at Annexure-III,
28. The Committee would like the Department to generate more such programmes which should lead to development, self-employment and income
 generation of women and other weaker section of society.
29. Outlining the broad strategy for S&T development, the Committee was given an account of the activities which the Department proposes to
 undertake during the Ninth Plan period. The Proposed Programme include: i) Promotion of advanced research in frontier areas, ii) Improvement of
 infrastructure facilities for R&D, iii) Encourclgemant to young outstanding scientists, iv) Improvement of S&T educa­tion and training, v)
 interaction of ST in all development activities, vi) use of S&T in mission mode projects, vii) Joint R&D projects with industry, viii) Fiscal
 incentives for conducting research, ix) Commercialisation of research results, x) support to information technology, and xi) priority in society
 related programmes.
R & D EXPENDITURE
30. The Committee noted with concern that while R&D expenditure per capita and as percentage of Gross National Product has been growing
 over the years in the developed countries, national expenditure on research and development in relation to Gross National Product in India, was
 declining. The Committee was told that according to the latest official statistics, the expenditure on R&D in India as percentage of Gross National
 Product has been around 8 per cent during the past few years. However, in absolute terms, India's R&D expenditure has increased from Rs.
 3974.17 crores in 1990-91 to Rs. 6821.02 crores in 1994-95.
31. The Committee observed that there is not only a need for higher allocation in the field of R&D work, but also the Government should think in
 tenns of giving fiscal incentives to private companies and industrial units, like income-tax rebate, who spend a part of their earnings towards R&D
 work.
PATENTING OF SCIENTIFIC INVENTIONS, PRODUcrs AND PROCESSES
32. The Committee wanted to know about the linkage between the Department of Science and Tech ­nology and the Council of Scientific and
 Industrial Research in regard to the patenting of scientific inventions, products and processes and the steps taken by the Department to strengthen
 the area of patenting.
33. The Committee was informed that a patent facilitating Cell (PFC) has set up to provide a single window facility for facilitating protection of
 inventions of Indian scientists, particularly from the univer­sity sector. Scientific agencies like the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research,
 Department of Atomic Energy, Defence Research and Development Organisation, Department of Space, ICAR, etc. have their outfits to protect
 inventions emanating from their laboratories and institutions. However, university scientists do not have any mechanism to protect their inventions.
 PFC extends full technical and financial support for protecting inventions emanating from universities either through Government support or their
 own funds. PFC is also open to extend the facilities to State level institutions supported by patent information centres at State levels by involving
 the State S&T Councils to make necessary facilities within the easy reach of scientists spread over the whole country.
34. PFC has developed necessary expertise and a small infrastructure as essential ingredients needed for providing services like patent search
 facilities, development of databases on Indian patent applications, patents granted in India and elsewhere and setting up of a panel of patent
 attorneys. A major imitative has been under-taken to orate awareness about intellectual property rights, especially patents among Indian scientists,
 R&D managers and policy makers. 35 such workshops have been held so far in different parts of the country. In all, academicians from about 80
 universities- have attended these work­shops. PFC has also filed 36 patent applications including 6 in foreign countries. Most of these
 applica ­tions are from the University sector. The CSIR has its full fledged set up for protecting the inventions. The experts from CSIR and
 scientists from other organisations along with patent attorneys are faculty members for the workshops of the DST. Many projects which may lead to
 patentable inventions are provided support through Patent searches, etc.
35. Patent Information Cell has been receiving requests from State Governments and universities for setting up Patent Information Centres. Each
 agency receiving support under the scheme will have to sign a Memorandum of Understanding with TIFAC. One such centre has been set up at

 West Bengal State Council for Science and Technology, Calcutta and second at the MP State Council of Science and Technology, Bhopal. Other
 such centres have been planned in Chandigarh, Jaipur and Imphal.
36. The Committee recommends that Patent Information Centres be set up a Chandigarh , Jaipur and Imphal at the earliest possible. The
 Department sould also explore the possibility of setting up one such centre in any of the Southern States.
COOPERATION IN S&T BETWEEN INDIA AND CIS COUNTRIES
37. In response to a question about utilization of the services of the scientists belonging to Common­wealth of Independent States (CIS), the
 Committee was informed that scientists from Russia and other CIS countries are visiting India for joint work on the identified projects as well as for
 discussions and work related to technology transfer. While in all cases, local hospitality of such visiting scientists is met by the Indian side, in select
 cases, the international airfare is also being provided. Five Russian scientists were awarded the ILTP Fellowships, a scheme instituted this year, to
 work in Indian institutions. Three research fellows from Kazakhstan were provided with international fare and full hospitality during their stay at
 the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research at Bangalore . More than 30 spe­cialists from CIS countries were invited to ARC-I,
 (International Advanced Research Centre for Powder Metallurgy and New Materials), Hyderabad on contract basis with international fare and
 attractive re­muneration to work on specific technology development programmes. Two lectures, one each by emi ­nent Indian and Russian
 scientists, were organised under Bose-Lomonosov Lecture Series, a scheme introduced this year. The Joint Council for ILTP (Integrated Long
 Term Programme of Cooperation in Science and Technology between India and Russia) in its eighth meeting held in Moscow on May 14-15, 1998
 recommended the establishment of a Technology Clearing House supported by Technology Plat­forms to facilitate industrial realisation of results
 of ILTP projects as well as available accomplishments of the two countries. A bi-monthly publication 'Technology Route', which is aimed at
 disseminating information about relevant Russian technologies to Indian industries, was also instituted.
38. After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Science and Technology and assessing the progress of various important
 programmes and projects administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 628.12 crores, as sought by the
 De­partment of Science and Technology, for the year 1998-99 under Demand No. 75, may be ap­proved.

REPORT
Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR) forms part of the Ministry of Science and Technology.  The Department
 deals with the schemes in specific areas of Scientific and Industrial Research including recognition of in-house R&D units of industry and
 Scientific and Industrial Research Organisations (SIROs). DSIR is also concerned with the activities of the Council of Scientific and
 Industrial Research (CSIR), an autonomous body. The National Research Development Corporation and the Central Electronics Ltd. are two
 public sector enterprises of the Department. Apart from supporting the activities of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research, the
 Department administers an autonomous scheme like Research and Development by Industry (RDI), Programme Aimed at Technological Self
 Reliance (PATSER), Scheme to Enhance the Efficacy of Transfer of Technology (SEETOT), National Information System for Science and
 Technology (NISSAT). The Department also provides support to international scientific institutions such as Asian and Pacific Centre for
 Transfer of Technology, New Delhi.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2. The Secretary, DSIR gave a brief account of the activities of the Department and informed the Committee about the new projects which the
 Department proposes to undertake during the. year 1998-99. Some of the ongoing projects which are proposed to be accelerated are the
 design and development of a Light Transport Aircraft (LTA) which would help build domestic civilian aircraft industry, development and
 commercialisation of bioactive molecules from plant and other sources, exploration of new resources for hydrocarbons, setting up of a pilot
 plant for making nickle  from chrome overburden which would result in creating wealth from waste, extending shelf life of food products,
 development of microwave tubes for strategic application and generation of R&D on information products.
3. The Department had made a demand of Rs. 2075.97 crores under Plan component comprising Rs. 1834.80 crores·for CSIR and Rs. 241.17
 crores for DSIR including its undertakings and against this the Planning Commission had allocated a plan outlay of Rs. 1448.60 crores for
 the Department, comprising Rs. 1321 crores for CSIR and Rs. 127.60 crores for DSIR. During the Eighth Plan period the Department was
 given a plan allocation of Rs. 774.94 crores (Annexure-I). For 1998-99 the total demand made by the Department was Rs. 755.62 crores
 comprising Rs. 312.55 crores under plan and Rs. 443.07 crores under non­plan. As against this, the Department has been allocated a sum of
 Rs. 638.00 crores consisting of Rs. 230.00 crores as plan and Rs. 408.00 crores under non-plan (Annexure-II).
4. The plan component of the budget of the DSIR for 1998-99 has been retained at the Budget Estimates level of 1997-98 which is Rs. 230
 crores, while the non-Plan component has been increased to Rs. 408 crores from Rs. 283.49 crores (B.E.) for the last year. The big chunk of
 allocation has gone to the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research which has got Rs. 610 crores out of which Rs. 204.00 crores is under
 Plan sector and Rs. 406.00 crates is under non-Plan sector against the actual expenditure of Rs. 444 crores in 1996-97 and Rs. 564.13 crores
 at RE stage of 1997-98. There has, thus, been an increase of Rs. 124 crores in the overall budgetary allocation approved for CSIR for 1998-
99 compared with the budget estimates of last year. The plan expenditure of the CSIR was Rs. 161 crores in 1996-97 which was increased to
 Rs. 204 crores in the B.E. of 1997-98 whereas non-plan component has risen from Rs. 251.68 crorres (approved) in 1996-97 to Rs. 282
 crores at B.E. stage in 1997-98. This was increased to Rs. 360.13 crores at the R.E. stage in 1997-98. In the budget estimates of 1998-99, the
 non-Plan. outlay for CSIR has been further raised to Rs. 406 crores. A large part of the Plan expenditure amounting to Rs. 130 crores as
 against the R.E. of Rs. 135.10 crores in 1997-98 has been allocated to national laboratories whereas a sum of Rs. 50 crores has been
 earmarked for modernisation  which is equivalent to the B.E. level of last year. In the case of administrative expenditure, the non-Plan
 provision for 1998-99 is Rs. 65.10 crores, which is higher by Rs. 19.70 crores over the expenditure of 1996-97 and Rs. 19.10 crores over the
 B.E. of 1997-98 and Rs. 4.60 crores over the Revised Estimates of last year.
5. The Committee, during the course of its deliberations was informed that even though for CSIR there is an increase in the non-Plan
 allocation in 1998-99 amounting to Rs. 45.87 crores, yet it is not adequate to cover even the actual committed expenditure arising due to the
 revision in emoluments at all levels. DSIR, therefore, requires for the CSIR additional budgetary support of Rs. ] 04.98 crores for the
 purpose of neutralising this commitment, the details of which are as follows:
 
 
I. Salaries Rs. 29.76 crores
II. Pensions Rs. 30.27 crores
III. Extra Mural HRD  
 (Research Fellowship/ Associateship) Rs. 33.95crores
IV. R&D support expenditure  
 (Library, Chemicals, etc.) Rs. 11.00 crores
 TOTAL: . Rs. 104.98 crores
 
 
Under the Central Management Head which includes, inter alia, salaries, pensionary expenses, etc. during the last year the Department had
 spent a sum of Rs. 88.44 crores against the allocation of        Rs 67 .15crores. For this purpose the Department diverted its internal receipts,
 which otherwise could have been used for the R&D work.
6. The Committee observes that it is not a happy situation. Funds which could have been utilised  for R&D work were used for meeting
 inescapable commitment towards payment of salaries. pensions and other related administrative expenditure. Something need urgently be
 done to remedy the situation. The DSIR should pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance for higher allocation at the Revised Estimates
 stage to enable it to meet its liability under the Central Management Head. As regards the diversion of Plan funds to non-Plan sector. the
 Committee would like to reiterate its earlier views. as contained in its Thirteenth, Twenty-fourth, Thirty-sixth and Fifty-second Reports in
 which this Committee had recommended in unambiguous terms that sufficient provision be made in the non-Plan outlay of DSIR to meet its
 committed liability. Despite a clear recommendation of the Committee, in the budget estimates of 1998-99, there is stili  a wide gap between
 the allocations made and expected liability of the Department. The plan funds should be utilised  for plan activities only as per the accepted
 budgetary norms.
 
MODERNISATION OF CSIR LABORATORIES
7. An allocation of Rs. 436.47 crores has been made under the Head 'National Laboratories' which comprise Rs. 130.00 crores as plan
 component and Rs. 306.47 as non-plan component as against Rs. 400.55 crores (R.E.) for the year 1997-98 consisting of Rs. 135.10 crores as
 plan outlay and              Rs. 265.45 crores as non-plan outlay.
 
8. The Committee observes that most of the laboratories functioning under the administrative control of DSIR are equipped either with the

 ageing equipments. and facilities or with the obsolete equipment and communication and networking system. Most of the laboratories
 require urgent upgradation and replacement to make them globally competitive. The Secretary, DSIR informed that the Government, keeping
 in view the recommendations of this Committee in Its Thirty-sixth and Fifty-second reports has committed to provide a modernisation grant
 of Rs 250 crores to DSIR during the Ninth Plan period. But the Committee would like the Department to generate internal resources also for
 modernising the CSIR laboratories. DSIR should also make concerted efforts to bring down the Non-plan expenditure of the laboratories

FINANCIAL SELF-RELIANCE AND INTERACTION OF CSIR LABORATORIES WITH INDUSTRY
9. The Committee was informed that as far as the issue of self-financing is concerned, CSIR has been able to achieve target with great
 difficulty and by the year 2001 it is going to be only 50 per cent self-financing. A lot is depending on industry's response. The year before
 last DSIR have an earning of Rs. 203 crores as against the budgetary allocation of around Rs. 400 crores. AH laboratories are not equal.
 They are located in different regions. Some of the laboratories do not have access to industries and many of these laboratories do something
 which goes beyond industrial research. They work for the nation. They do projects where they do not expect returns. It is equally important
 to keep the science in CSIR alive and also in view of the fact that there is no high technology without high science and no industry will pay
 for the science, DSIR has to make investment in keeping that science alive. The industry today is not willing to pay for it because of the
 shortsightedness.
 
10. The Committee was informed that CSIR has set up a system of periodic performance appraisal of all the laboratories wherein the level of
 self-financing is a major assessment parameter. The level of financial self-reliance of a laboratory depends on its specific area of activities,
 the local potential client base and competition and it differs from laboratory to laboratory. However, higher growth targets for financial self-
reliance are set every year commensurate with the resource endowments of the laboratories.
 
11. DSIR has created the Customer Satisfaction Evaluation Cell which operates as an independent unit. It takes the feedback from customers.
 There are standard ways of evaluating customer satisfaction. First of all DSIR has taken a group of chemical laboratories as a model for
 intensive discussions for which a procedure for evaluating the customer satisfaction has been devised. In order to put pressure on the
 performance of the laboratories indicators have been set up, which determine their budgets and each laboratory is judged in terms of
 customer satisfaction. DSIR has established Research Councils having around 50 per cent participation by industry. In fact, in many
 laboratories which arc strongly industry-related, even the Chairmen of the Research Councils are from industry, so that they are in a position
 to guide in terms of where the laboratories should be moving. DSIR has also created incentives for laboratories doing industrial research.
 Department of Scientific and Industrial Research also undertakes technology forecasting exercise.
 
12. The Committee is of the view that the industry-related laboratories of the CSIR should aim at having better interface with the industry so
 that the technologies developed by them are eventually commercialised. This would bring self-reliance and confidence within the CSIR
 system providing further impetus to R&D activities of these laboratories.
 
PROVISION OF HOUSING AND OTHER AMENITIES FOR SCIENTISTS
13. The Committee noticed that in the budgetary allocation of the current year an outlay of Rs. 16.30 crores has been earmarked for the
 residential buildings, staff quarters and other amenities while allocation under this Head last year was Rs. 15.70 crores (R.E). There is,
 therefore, an increase of Rs. 67 lakhs only. The Committee wanted to know as to what steps the Department is taking to provide housing
 facility to the scientists so as to attract talented and dedicated scientists.
 
14. The Committee was told that housing for scientists, particularly, in metropolitan cities is an acute problem being faced by the Department.
 Attracting talent to take up S&T as a career, and more so R&D is a major national problem.  CSIR is seeking to ameliorate this problem to
 some extent by providing to young scientists housing and other amenities in the campus. The financial allocations thus earmarked are
 inadequate to realise the objectives of providing dwelling units to house a significant percentage of employees. However, it is hoped that the
 enhancement of HRA as well as HBA arising from the adoption of the Fifth Pay Commission recommendations would ease to some extent
 pressure on the CSIR to provide campus housing. The CSIR has also drawn up a long term strategy to provide housing to its staff to tackle
 this problem. The Committee was further informed that a Committee was set up to look into the housing needs of CSIR and a report has been
 submitted with regard to individual laboratories.
 
15. Tile Committee is of the view that in order to attract talent to take up S&T as a career, and retain them, housing and other amenities be
 provided to the scientists. Possibilities may also be explored for providing campus housing facilities to the scientists working in CSIR
 laboratories.
 
RESEARCH SCHEME, SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS
16. The Committee found that in the budgetary allocation under the programme  'Research Scheme, Scholarships and Fellowships' there is a
 meagre increase of Rs. 70 lakhs in this year's budget. The Committee wanted to know as to how successful this programme  of the
 Department ii. It was informed that the CSIR has been a primary source for nurturing budding scientific talent in the country through the
 award of Junior and Senior Research Fellowships and Research Associateships. Its munificence has helped create a band of researchers in
 the country. the Committee was given to understand that the total amount spent on Research Scheme Fellowships was around Rs. 19 crores
 in 1997-98 which now has been raised to Rs. 28.70 crores and 4070 persons were supported comprising around 970 Junior Research
 Fellows, 2080 Senior Research fellows and 1020 Research Associates. The Junior Research fellowships are awarded on the basis of a
 national competitive examination and only the most talented are able to secure these fellowships. DSIR has devised a built-in procedure
 whereby the periodic progress of a Fellow/ Associate is evaluated by a Committee for the continuation or otherwise of the fellowships.
 Considering the high quality of the Fellows, there is negligible rate of dropouts or discontinuance.
 
ECO-FRIENDLY AND COST EFFECTIVE LEATHER TECHNOLOGIES
17. Leather industry in India is presently undergoing a rapid transition form manual techniques to mechanised  production. It faces stringent
 'environmental regulations both within and outside the country. Also cost advantage no longer remains a winning tool in a demanding global
 market. The Committee, therefore, wanted to know about the steps proposed to be taken by the Department during the Ninth Plan period to
 help modernise the leather processing technique by making it more eco-friendly and cost effective.

18. The Committee was informed that the Department has been alerting and assisting the leather industry to the challenges of quality, costs,
 fashion and environment. The programmes in this area are drawn up in close association and consultation with the leather industry. The
 Committee was assured that the DSIR would endeavour  to enlarge the scope of its programme  and would see to it that the gains realised
 from the Technology Mission mounted by it to modernise  the leather sector through introduction of eco-friendly and cost effective
 processing techniques and technologies reach the target groups. It is a matter of concern to the Committee that in spite of having the highest
 population of animals in the world, the share of India in the world leather market is very small. According to one estimate it is less than 4 per
 cent. In order to enhance  this share substantially it is necessary to use high technology. The Department is also trying to incorporate
 environmentally clean and benign technologies in the tanneries.
 
19. The Committee is of the view that since we have got the highest cattle population in  the country and, therefore, raw material is available
 in abundance, if the eco-friendly and cost effective technologies and techniques are utilised for leather processing, it would be possible for us
 to compete at the international level and increase our exports. For this there has to be greater interaction between tanneries and the concerned
 laboratories of the CSIR.
 
20. On a specific question on the Calcutta Leather Complex, the Secretary, DSIR informed that the Central Leather Research Institute (CLRI)
 has been given the task of looking at the feasibility of location as well as the design of the Calcutta Leather Complex. CLRI is likely to
 submit its report shortly.
 
DEVELOPMENT OF DRUGS
21. In view of the enormous biodiversity that exist in India, the Committee wanted to know what the Department is doing for the
 development of drugs from plant species and herbs. The Committee was told that CSIR laboratories have a vast potential to create newer
 drug molecules and therapeutics. The laboratories which are doing pioneering work in chemistry and biology' have the capacity from
 identifying a plant source to its isolation and active molecular formulations to its identification to create formulations and testing under the
 regulatory toxicology. The Committee was further informed that the DSIR is trying to bring in all these laboratories together to launch Bio-
active Molecular Programme, which will not only be beneficial in adding value to the natural resources but also create products which are
 globally competitive. The Committee was given to understand that a large number of skills are required in order to have improvement in the
 herbal medicines. It is not only identifying a plant or isolation of a compound or elucidation of a compound, creating lead molecules by using
 inflow in organic chemistry, protein engineering, process development and so on. All these skills are required to be improved particularly, in
 developing new drugs. Therefore, DSIR is trying to link the 19 laboratories which are also being linked with other institutions such as the
 Arya Vaidyashala in Kottakal district in Kerala. DSIR and the Arya Vaidyashala have now formed a memorandum of understanding (MoU).
 
22. The Committee is of the view that plant-based drugs and herbal drugs are becoming popular all over the world. This can become our area
 of strength and the traditional knowledge about plants and herbs which exists in this country is required to be probed scientifically for Its
 medicinal use and further validation. The Committee would like the CSIR to work in this area with appropriate thrust.
 
FOOD PROCESSING TECHNOLOGIES AND COLD CHAIN
23. In regard to development of an indigenous version of the Food Processing Industries rather than making an attempt to push through costly
 imported technology which is beyond the reach of the entrepreneurs of our country, the end products coming from such technology being
 beyond the reach of average consumer, the Committee was informed that NRDC has been at the forefront of commercialising  indigenously
 developed food processing technologies such as Invert Sugar and Spirulina  algae. DSIR is making efforts to implement Technology Mission
 on Oilseeds, Pulses and Maize and for this purpose is involved in development of technologies relating to post harvest and processing
 technologies for Oilseeds, Pulses and Maize. The shelf life of food products especially fruits and vegetables is critically dependent upon
 temperature. India being a tropical country, fruits and vegetables deteriorate fast. If a cold chain could be established from the farm to the
 consumer i(would greatly help to reduce wastage. The Committee was told that there are 3200 existing cold storages with a capacity of
 around 26 million CuM, but nearly 90 per cent of these store only potatoes. Adequate domestic cold storage capacity around 5 ml. tonnes
 also exists and is being enhanced by 2.5 ml. Refrigeration/year. Thus the gaps/shortfalls in the cold chain are to be made up. Firstly, the
 movement from the farm to the local mandi which is non-refrigerated needs to be brought into the cold chain. Thereafter, for most of the
 produce cold storage also is not available. Both these factors together contribute to 40 per cent of the damage. Thereafter, the cold transport
 and distributor storage and retailer cold outlet have to be provided.
 
24. The Committee would like the CSIR to devise appropriate and economically viable solutions for bridging the gap at diverse stages of the
 cold chain for which it is seeking to set up a Technology Mission. The Committee is of the considered opinion that the Food Processing
 sector In our country offers tremendous scope for application of techniques and technologies for reducing post harvest losses and for
 generating wealth and employment in the rural sector. The Committee would like that cheap and simple processing technologies for value
 addition, minimizing post-harvest losses and employment generation be developed which could be easily learnt by the people living in rural
 areas.
 
TECHNOLOGY FOR RURAL ROADS
25. The Committee was informed that the Central Road Research Institute (CRRI) has developed new techniques for planning. design.
 construction and maintenance of rural roads. using local soil, soft aggregates and waste materials. The specific techniques are: (a) use of
 treated soil in place of stone or brick in the lower layers of road pavement; (b) use of naturally occurring gravel mixtures; (c) construction of
 water bound. macadam road in black cotton soil using a sub-base of local expansive soil stabilizer with lime; (d) construction of water bound
 macadam road using a sub-base and the base course of non-expansive soil (moorum, alluvial soils). stabilised  with lime; (e) stabilisation  of
 soil with soft aggregates for the construction of all weather roads in dry areas; and (f) stabilisation  of road with soft aggregates for all
 weather roads in wet areas. These techniques can enable a saving of up to 25 per cent in the cost of road construction as compared to
 conventional techniques. Small lengths of road using these techniques were successfully demonstrated in Punjab. Jammu & Kashmir,
 Rajasthan, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu and Kerala . Rural roads being a State subject further propagation and i-
nplementation of technologies development by CRRI lies with the State Governments/agencies. The services of CRRI are always available
 for any S&T inputs that may be needed.
 
26. The Committee recommends that innovative work of generating new technologies for rural roads should continue and the State and

INTELLECTUAL'PROPERTY RIGHTS AND PATENTS LITERACY
27. With regard to the intellectual property issue the Committee was informed that DSIR has set consistent targets for our laboratories for
 patenting. Patenting is done not only in India but also abroad. DSIR has world-class laboratories and at least half a dozen of them can run
 shoulder to shoulder with the rest of the world in the fields of chemicals, biology, aerospace, catalysts, etc.
 
28. The CSIR leads in patents movement in India. Out of 1,200 to 1,300 patents coming from India, one-fourth of them belong to CSIR. Last
 year CSIR had 90 patents. That number has gone up substantially now. DSIR has launched a massive programme  on creating intellectual
 property awareness not only within the CSIR but even outside. At the laboratory level, right from proper documentation to writing and filing
 patents, DSIR runs a large number of courses. DSIR is having Intellectual Property Management Division. On the question of promoting
 patent literacy among our scientists, the Committee was assured that DSIR, under the Scheme on Intellectual Property and Technology
 Management, would continue its efforts to spearhead patent literacy and national IPR issues so as to retain its identity as the largest Indian
 patent holder and the first to launch an IPR management programme. For this purpose the Department will keep on providing value added
 patent information services and put its efforts to develop skills to manage IPR for strategic alliances.
 
29. The Committee is happy over the fact that in 1997 DSIR and NRDC had organised over fifteen patents and IPR-related workshops for the
 scientific community with expert resource persons drawn from India and abroad and these Initiatives are being further enlarged. The
 Committee would like the Department to provide wide publicity to its scheme being administered by NRDC under which assistance is
 provided to Indian scientists and inventors to secure patents for their products and processes through engaging of patent attorneys.
 
NATIONAL DRINKING WATER MISSION
30. The Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission was launched in 1986 with the objective to provide drinking water to all the villages
 of the country in a time bound manner. While the Department of Rural Development has been the nodal agency for the implementation of
 the Mission, CSIR as technology provider, has been given the responsibility to provide Science & Technology inputs and undertake R&D
 activities under the Mission. The CSIR has been made responsible to provide S&T inputs for programme !! related to water source finding,
 conservation/augmentation of water, water treatment technologies and for standardization of geophY8lc~1 techniques. The success rate of
 water source location improved from existing 40 per cent to more than 90 per cent. In order to undertake field surveys for water finding and
 water quality assessment technologies for bacteriological testing kit for early detection of faecal pollution, rapid aqua tester and mobile water
 testing laboratory have been developed and released for commercialisation . 21 mobile testing laboratories have been supplied to various
 States. In a bid to remove arsenic from drinking water over 250 excess iron removal plants, 9 defluoridation , 3 fill and draw type of
 defluoridation, 5 stationary reverse osmosis and 3 mobile plants for desalination of water were installed by CSIR laboratories and for
 conservation and augmentation of water improved shallow wells and hand pumps, water economy taps and rain water harvesting structures
 have been designed and developed. Seventy-five shadow structures have also been installed.
31. Around 3000 personnel of PHE Departments of various State Governments were trained for application of geophysical techniques for
 source finding, rain water harvesting, water quality analysis and water treatment technologies; desalination, defluoridation, excess iron
 removal and slow sand filtration, respectively in various blocks of rural areas. During the Ninth Plan, CSIR has intensified its participation in
 the Rajiv Gandhi National Drinking Water Mission by giving special emphasis on programmes  for: Arsenic removal in ground water, West
 Bengal; Iron/fh.1oride removal in water: Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan and West Bengal; in diverse states large scale prolilferation  of water
 economy taps, solar operated desalination plants installation; electrochemical defluoridation; hydraulically operated medium-head hand
 pump; water quality assessment and impact assessment meaasures to check bacteriological and chemical contamination of rural water
 resources in problem areas; water prospecting in difficult areas (hard rock, drought prone areas, lateritic rocks,\ etc.), and percolation tanks to
 harvest surplus rainwater.
32. The Committee is of the view that on the front of providing drinking water to all the villages In the country not much work has been done.
 The dream of Rajiv Gandhi, the former
Prime Minister of India, who launched the National Drinking Water Mission, still remain. to be fulnlled. Despite the technical inputs
 provided by CSIR Laboratories to the Mission by way of quality testing of water, removal of arsenic from drinking water, etc. what is
 needed today Is to develop technologies for water conservation and water harvesting. The water table everywhere Is going down. Traditional
 sources of water are drying up. Water is the necessity of life. The Committee would like the Department to coordinate its activities with the
 Ministries of Water Resources, Rural Development and the State Governments for transferring technologies In the area of purifying water to
 make it potable. At the same time scientists working in the area may also think of devising new and cheaper methods of water harvesting and
 water conservation.
33. After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research and assessing the progress of various
 important programmes and projects administered by It, the Committee recommends that the Demand for Grants of Rs. 638.00 crores, as
 sought by the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, for the year 1998-99, under Demand No. 76, may be approved.

July, 1998 Chairman
 Committee on Science &: Technology, Environment &: Forests.
 
REPORT
The Department of Ocean Development since it started functioning in July, 1981 has directed its programmes  towards
 development and use of Science and Technology for the sustainable and environment friendly exploration and exploitation of
 marine resources for the socio-economic benefit of the country. The Department of Ocean Development is a nodal Department for
 organizing, coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country. The National level R & 0 Laboratories,
 Educational Institutions and Industries assist the Department in carrying out its plans and programmes of National importance.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
2. The Committee was informed that the Planning Commission constituted a working group comprising eminent scientists in
 the field of Ocean Development to formulate plan proposals for the Ninth Five Year Plan. The working group kept in mind the
 views of six expert groups which had been set up by the Department to draw up a 10 year perspecti ve plan keeping in view the
 vital role oceans could play. The annual plan for 1998-99 is based on t~ese reports and recommendations.
3. The Secretary, Department of Ocean Development (000), in his presentation before the Committee informed that the
 Department of Ocean Development proposed an outlay of Rs. 656 crores for the Eighth Five Year Plan period. The Planning
 Commission allocated Rs. 130 crores only as indicative outlay. However, based on the requirements of various programmes , a sum
 of Rs. 224 crores was provided agai,nst which the expenditure was about Rs. 200 crores. During the Eighth Five Year Plan period
 the strategic areas such as Antarctic Research, Polymetallic  Nodules Programmes and International Cooperation and Programmes
 received higher priority in terms of fund allocation amounting to a total of 66 per cent, followed by societal Programmes 21 per
 cent, Scientific and Technological Development Programmes 8 per cent and Basic Research 5 per cent. The Planning Commission
 has also indicated an outlay of Rs. 557.69 crores for the plan schemes of the Department for the Ninth Five Year Plan period.
4. The plan outlay for the Department for 1998-99 is Rs. 88.00 crores. Besides, it has also been provided with a Non-Plan
 outlay of Rs. 19.50 crores. The Department would thus have a total outlay of Rs. 107.50 crores as against the revised estimates of
 Rs. 102.11 crores (Plan as well as Non-Plan) for 1997-98 whereas the actual expenditure of the Department for that year was Rs.
 100.79 crores. The financial outlay for 1998-99 shows an increase ofRs. 6.71 crores as compared to the actual expenditure for
 1997-98. In the current financial year, as informed by the Secretary, 000, emphasis is more on Technology Development
 Programmes which is around 30 per cent of the total financial outlay for 1998-99. The comparative figures in terms of actual
 expenditures for various programmes  of the Department for 1995­96,1996-97 and 1997-98 are given in Annexure-I and the
 financial allocations earmarked for 1998-99 are set out in Annexure-II.
5. Th~ Committee was informed that the reduced plan outlay for 1998-99 of Rs. 88.00 crores than the allocations made in the
 B.E. for 1997-98 would require the Department to shift some of its activities to the next financial year. The Department would thus
 manage by rescheduling its activities. During 1997-98, on account of the plan outlay being reduced at the level ofRs. 85 crores in
 the revised estimates as against the projected budget of Rs. 88.10 crores compelled the Department to shift some of its activities and
 some of the projected expenditure to the current financial year.
6. The Non-Plan expenditure of the Department has been broadly under four heads, namely (i) ORV Sagar Kanya; (ii) FORV
 Sagar Sampada; (iii) Secretariat and Economic Services; and (iv) Administrative Infrastructure. The major increase in the Non-Plan
 expenditure is against FORV Sagar Sampada, which was acquired in November 1984. It is a sophisticated multi-purpose research
 vessel which; has been carrying out survey of Indian Exclusive Economic Zone (EEZ) on Living Resources and the Oceanographic
 factors influencing their distribution. It provides a common platform to the National Institutes/Laboratories in the field of
 Oceanographic research. Last year this vessel conducted 14 cruises covering a total track length of 22578 nautical miles both in the
 Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. The Major scientific investigations/ research carried out by FORV Sagar Sampada  during 1997-98
 include evaluation of performance of specially designed trawl gears, assessment of fishery resources and location of new grounds,
 post harvest technology and bio-fouling accumulation of biofoulers on copper, brass, aluminium , stainless steel and galvanised iron
 panels, screening of free amino acids, fatty acids composition, trimethylamine oxide degradation, etc. from the muscles of various
 fish species and collection of the sea truth data for validation of modular opto­electronic scanner onboard the Indian Remote
 Sensing Satellite, IRS-P5.
ANTARCI1C RESEARCH PROGRAMME
7. The Indian Antarctic Programme and its scientific expeditions are held on annual basis with the launching of the first
 expedition to Antarctic in 1981. The first Indian research station, Dakshin Gangotri was commissioned in 1983 and replaced by the
 indigenously designed second Indian permanent station 'Maitri' in the Schirmacher Oasis in 1988. The Station 'Maitri ' has adequate
 infrastructural facilities for conducting multi-faceted scientific research in Polar (Antarctic) Science. While using Antarctica as a
 platform for conducting scientific experiments, India has always recognised the importance of preserving the pristine nature of this
 remote and unique continent. In order to uphold this commitment, India, an original votary of the Protocol on Environmental
 Protection to the Antarctic Treaty, has ratified the Protocol in April 1996. The Committee was informed that so far 19 scientific
 expeditions had been launched on a regular basis which have carried out research work in the thrust areas of polar science,
 including two expeditions to the Southern Oceans for assessment of Antarctic Krill. During the period 1998-99, the Eighteenth
 Indian Antarctic Expedition would be launched to continue research in polar science with special emphasis on International

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA RAJYA SABHA

 collaboration. The Scientific Expedition to Antractica will be launched with the participation of the neighbouring countries. The
 Committee was informed that application and utilisation of clean energy sources like wind and sun in Antarctica  will be attempted.
 Upgradation of communication facilities with special emphasis on real time picture transmissjon will be undertaken, studies on
 adoption :techniques  ofhuman beings in adverse conditions would continue and waste handling and discharge facilities are
 proposed to be modified in accordance with the Environmental Protocol.
8. The Antarctic Study Centre (ASC) at Goa is a state-of-the-art national facility for conducting front ranking research in the
 field of polar sciences and launching all expeditions to Antarctic. It will have a unique facility for low temperature research on ice
 cores retrieved from Antarctic and the Himalayas . It will also have an Antarctic  Museum and a data base repository on polar
 sciences. For the entire programme a budgetary provision of Rs. 18.50 crores has been made in the current financial year.
9. The Committee expresses its support to the Antarctic Science Programme though the achievements of this programme
 cannot be significant at the present stage. The programme  has enabled the Department to generate valuable data which would be
 useful at a future date. The programme has provided an opportunity to Indian scientists to interact with scientific community of the
 developed nations. The entire Antarctic Research Programme can prove to be an area of strength of tile Department.
POLYMEI'ALLIC NODULES PROGRAMME (PNP)
10. In 19h7, India was accorded the status of Registered Pioneer Investor and started the Polymetallic Nodules Programme
 (PNP). Accordingly, the International Seabed Authority (ISBA) allotted 150,000 sq.km. mine site for exploitation of nodules in the
 Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB). After prolonged negotiations India became member of the Council of ISBA under Investors'
 category in March 1990.
1O.1 The Committee was infonned that Polymetallic  Nodules Programme (PNP) was a national programme with international
 commitments. The major activities proposed to be undertaken in the curtent  financial year are survey and exploitation for
 revalidation of relative concentration and quality charatteristjc of nodules in different pre-determined blocks, environmental impact
 assessment to assess the environmental impact of large scale deep seabed mining activity, technology development for nodule
 mining at greater depths and technology development (extractive metallurgy). The Department proposes to spend Rs. 18.95 crores
 in the current financial year as against Rs. 15.50 crdres spent last year.
10.2 The Committee was further infonned that the R.E. outlay for 1997-98, for Polymetallic  Nodules Programme (PNP) was
 Rs. 15.60 crores of which Rs. 5.50 crores was towards mining technology development. In this year's budget the Department
 proposes to spend an amount of Rs. 15.45 crores towards mining technology development. The Committee was told that the major
 element in this development are the ongoing joint project between University of Siegen (IKS), Germany an<l NIOT and
 establishing facilities in India and operational requirement for system trial. The hardware realisation is in progress and· the system
 is now scheduled for sea trial before the end of 1998.
1.0.3 The Committee was apprised that PN Programme  is still in experimental stage. Therefore, commercial exploitation of
 polymetallic nodules may not be feasible for some more time. However, the technology for exploration and exploitation has been
 demonstrated. Thus development of technologies for nodule mining purposes for the deep sea may be viewed as contribution to a
 long term objective.
10.4 Under the Polymetallic Nodules Programme, it is proposed to set up a continuously operating pilot demonstration plant for
 extraction of copper, nickel, cobalt and manganese from the polymetallic nodules, as a joint programme with MIs. HindustaIt Zinc
 Limited. The estimated cost of this pilot plant is about Rs. 25.00 crores and the project duration will be about 2 years. The
 Committee was informed that in the current financiill year, an additional outlay of Rs. 5.00 crores will be required for implementing
 this programme.
11. The Committee observes that the Polymetallic  Nodules Programme  has a long gestation period and woUld become
 economically viable by the year 2010. Considering the potential benefits that could arise in future from this programme, there is a
 need for India to be among the top ranking nations in the field of generating high technology required for commercial exploitation
 of Polymetallic Nodules. The Committee, therefore, recommends that this Programme should not starve of funds. The Committee is
 of the view that 'at the time of considering revised estimates of the Department, an extra budgetary support for the Department for
 this programme during the current financial year may be considered.
DRUGS FROM THE SEA
12. The National Project on "Drugs from the Sea" initiated during 1990-91 is a multi-institutional project on development of
 potential drugs and chemicals from marine organisms. This project was funded under R & D programme till the end of Phase-II
 (1995-96). The approved allocation for Phase III of the Project for 1996-97 to 1998-99 is "'Rs. 8.16 crores. Out of this, Rs. 4.50
 crores has been spent in the first two years of Phase III, leaving a balance of Rs. 3.66 crores to be released in 1998-99. However,
 keeping in view the resource crunch, the Budget provision for 1998-99 has been restricted to Rs. 2.50 crores.
12.1 The Committee was informed that over 450 species of marine biota were collected and over 500 voucher specimens were
 identified possessing biological properties for treatment of human diseases. The biological screening have led to identification of 17
 organisms possessing promising activities. From these organisms over 100 pure compounds were isolated and characterised . Out of
 these 17 organisms, 5 organisms possessing anti-viral, anti-amoebic, anti-diabelic, anti-anxiolytic and larvicidal activities have been
 taken up for further evaluation and drug development during the current year.
12.2 The Committee was informed that three promising leads have been identified for immediate development which are COR
 134 (Mangrove: Anti-diabetic) which is to be developed as a marine herbal drug using traditional approach, NI0-450 (Mangrove:

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA RAJYA SABHA

 Anti-anxiety) and CU-OO1/OO4 (Fish: Anti-cholesterol) which has a strong lipid lowering activity and a patent has been filed.
13. The Committee reiterates its view expressed in its Forty-seventh Report that the National Project on from Sea a
 comiderable potential, but the exploitation so for been negligible with practically no commercial exploitation. The Department
 should take necessary steps to transfer the technology for commercialisation in regard to the anti-cholesterol drug. The anti-diabetic
 drug derived from marine herbal source needs further probing and if its efficacy is proved in human subjects, it would prove to be a
 significant achievement of the Department.
OCEAN OBSERVATION AND INFORMATION SERVICES (0018)
14. The research programmes viz., Marine Satellite Information Services (MARSIS), National Ocean Information System
 (NOIS), Sea Level Monitoring and Modelling  (SELMAM) and Data Buoy Programme implemented during the Eighth Five Year
 Plan period have now been integrated into Ocean Observation and Information Services (OmS) with a view to synergising and
 generating reliable coastal and ocean data and data products for supporting coastal and of shore developmental activities and
 oceanographic research. The Programme consists of four major projects viz. , Ocean Observing Systems, Ocean Information
 Services, Satellite and Coastal Oceanographic Research and Ocean Modelling and Dynamics.
15. The Committee was informed that under the OOIS, even though the actual expenditure during 1997-98 was Rs. 20.93
 crores, the outaly for 1998-99 has been restricted to Rs. 13.75 crores. Out of this, Rs. 7.00 crores is meant for completing the
 ongoing project on moored data buoys under the National Data Buoy Programme  with NORAD (Norwegian Agency for
 Development Co-operation) assistance, procurement and deployment of drifting buoys, data acquisition and processing, quality
 90ntrol and archival, and other related programmes. A sum of Rs. 4.00 crores is provided for Ocean Information Services which is
 essential to integrate the activities of the Marine Data Centres to generate user driven application-oriented data products and
 interact with user agencies. To support the Ocean Information Services, R & 0 programmes in Satellite Oceanography and Ocean
 Modelling and Dynamics have been evolved and initiated during 1997-98. Due to the overall ceiling the outlay for these R & 0
 efforts is kept at a reduced level or Rs. 1.25 crores for Satellite Oceanography and Rs. 1.50 cror~s for Ocean Modelling and
 Dynamics. To Support these R & 0 efforts, to meet targets as planned, an additional outlay of Rs. 3.00 crores is required. 'The
 Committee feels that the Department should make out a strong case for enhancement of its allocations under this head at the revised
 estimates stage of the current financial year.
COASTAL OCEAN MONITORING AND PREDICTION SYSTEM (COMAPS)
16. The Department is implementing a programme  namely Coastal Ocean Monitoring and Prediction Systems (COMAPS)
 since 1990. The outlay for the programme for 1998-99 has been kept at Rs. 1.5 crores. The COMAPS programme  at present deals
 with monitoring the pollution aspect of marine environment. The variety of pollutants (Chemical and biological) and untreated
 domestic waStes reach the oceans either directly through pipelines or indirectly through rivers and run offs from the land.
16.1 The other causes of pollution include disposal of untreated wastes from a large number of small and medium scale
 industries and few large industries situated along the coastal areas. Most of the small and medium scale industries discharge their
 effluents through domestic sewage channels and many of the large scale industries either in the channels or through pipelines in the
 sea. Oil pollution due to operation of ships and tankers is also a source of pollution. Generally the oil pollution is chronic in nature
 and only during the oil spill incidents mortality of marine organisms occur.
16.2 The Committee was informed that in order to achieve adequate coverage for monitoring of our coastal waters, DOD
 Centrel Units are established in many National laboratories situated in maritime States which are also included in the programme.
17. During 1998-99, in order to make the programme more comprehensive, microbiology programmes would be expanded
 incorporating therein physical oceanographic studies to understand the diffusion and dispersion characteristics of pollutants in the
 sea, which is location specific due to varied current and circulation patterns. Results obtained from this would be useful in setting
 up of disposal standards and locations for their disposal in the sea. Besides, pollutants would be monitored in ecologically sensitive
 areas like Gulf of Kutch wherein large-scale developmental activities are being planned. Levels of pollution would be monitored at
 77 locations along the coastal areas of the country. Data in respect of 25 parameters including nutrients, heavy metals, pesticides,
 pathogenic bacteria will be collected. The programme  was being monitored by a Steering Committee, reconstituted in 1995-96,
 headed by the Chairman of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) and all the Coastal State Pollution Control Boards (SPCBs)
 are represented on the Committee.
17.1 It has further been revealed that the pollution levels in Versova, Mahim, Thane and Ulhas creeks in Maharashtra, Veraval
 port in Gujarat, Veli in Kerala, Kakinada  Canal and Visakhapatnam  harbour in Andhra Pradesh and Puri in Orissa are areas of
 concern. The pollution in these areas have reached significant levels.
17.2 The data and information relating to the rising trends of pollution at the observed locations are periodically brought to the
 notice of the concerned State Pollution Control Boards who are empowered to take preventive and control action for mitigation of
 pollution.
17.3 The Committee was also informed that the Programme  was progressing as per the target set for the Ninth Five Year Plan,
 both in physical and financial terms. The Department plans to assess the pollution trends in the areas of high concentration of
 pollutants so as to document the increase or decrease in pollution-related problems.
COASTAL RESEARCH VESSELS (CRV)
18. The Coastal Research Vessels (CRVs) namely, Sagar Purvi and Sagar Paschimi were acquired during 1996-97 for enabling

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA RAJYA SABHA

 continuous collection of samples from the coastal areas for monitoring the pollution levels in different points. These CRVs have
 been deployed to facilitate systematic collection and analysis of water, sediment and biological samples from different locations
 under the guidance of Vessel Management Cell, National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai.
18.1 The Committee was informed that during 1998-99 about 48 cruises are proposed to be undertaken for collection of
 chemical and biological parameters. For the successful execution of the programme, suitable linkages with different National and
 State R & D institutions including Universities will be maintained.
19. The Committee is a1anned over the magnitude of marine pollution and the inadequate steps taken to prevent as well as
 control the same. It is stated in para 12 of the Ocean Policy Statement that "Surveillance and conservation of the marine
 environment and its resources call for an integrated legal framework and its concomitant enforcement. Several laws have already
 been promulgated regarding the maritime zone, fisheries, etc. The Coast Guard Organisation looks after the enforcement aspects of
 several of these legislative measures. The co-ordinating mechanisms of the overall structure to legislation will have to be suitably
 strengthened under the aegis of the Department of Ocean Development". The Committee, therefore, recommends that initiatives
 should be taken to develop a co-ordination mechanism between the DOD and various other Ministries with the Ministry of
 Environment and Forests as the key member to prevent and control marine pollution in the coastal areas.
SHORE TO FISHING VESSEL COMMUNICATION SYSTEM
20. The Department of Ocean Development has taken up the Programme "Shore to Fishing Vessel Communication System" in
 two phases. The first phase covers four States i.e., Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Karnataka and a part of Goa. The second
 phase covers the rest of the country except Gujarat  because the Government of Gujarat did not want to participate in the
 programme. In phase-II programme , 10 shore stations have been planned to be established i.e., two each in the States of
 Maharashtra, West Bengal and Orissa and one each in Pondicherry, Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicobar Island. Construction
 work for providing the infrastructure facilities is complete. Equipments are made available to the concerned coastal State
 Governments. This pregramme is being executed by the State Governments. However, the Government of Gujarat did not want to
 participate in this programme.
21. The Committee recommends that adequate steps should be taken to cover Gujarat and Daman & Diu under the Programme
 "Shore to Fishing Vessel Communication System".
ISLAND DEVEWPMENT PROGRAMME
22. The Committee was told that the Andaman & Nicobar Centre for Ocean Development (ANCOD) was set up for
 coordinating the efforts on the Marine Living Resources in the Island Groups. During the current year the ongoing programmes
 such as rejuvenation of coral reef, studies on the ecology and environmental aspects of the A & N waters will be continued.
 Besides, steps for introduction of the Mariculture programmes and a pilot demonstration project for lobster fattening will also be
 initiated. In order to strengthen the Centre, the Department got four posts approved recently and out of which one post has already
 been filled up.
23. According to a survey conducted by the Zoological Survey of India (ZSI), tremendous pressure has been put on coral reefs
 in the country due to human activities, like coral mining, sand mining in coastal areas, situation from soil runoff· mainly due to
 deforestation. The tourist influx in recent years, unplanned collection of shells and corals for ornamental trade and commercial
 exploitation offish have also contributed to reef damage. In addition, the white band disease has resulted in coral mortality and
 increased susceptibility. The Committee recommends that adequate steps should be taken to preserve the coral reef system of the
 country, particularly of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
24. The Committee has noted that a Senior Scientific Officer has been posted at ANCOD. The Committee would like that the
 vacant posts of Technical Officer, Technical Assistant and other supporting staff should also be fillip up on a regular basis. Posts of
 a Technical Officer and a Technical Assistant with supporting administrative staff have also been created. The Committee would
 like that the vacant posts existing in ANCOD be filled up expeditiously.
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF OCEAN TECHNOLOGY (NIOT)
25. National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) was established in 1993 with a view to developing technology to facilitate
 activities in Ocean Sector. Besides, NIOT is also rendering consultancy services to industry. The Budget allocation for NIOT has
 been substantially increased to Rs. 13.50 crores for 1998-99 as against Rs. 7.50 crores allocated at the revised estimates stage for
 1997-98.
26. The Committee was informed that the increased allocation of Rs. 13.50 crores to NIOT for 1998-99 is mainly due to the
 proposal to take up the pilot activity  on Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion (OTEC), consolidating the gains made in the wave
 energy programme, technology development for an integrated deep sea mining system, coastal and environmental engineering and
 marine instrumentation.
27. It is observed by the Committee that National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) is still functioning under the administrative
 control of the Ministry of Science & Technology (Department of Scientific & Industrial Research).
28. The Committee reiterates its view that multiplicity of the institutions working in the same field needs to be avoided. The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) should be brought within the administrative
 control of the Department of Ocean Development for better co-ordination and result oriented activities in the marine related fields.
29. After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean Development and the progress of various important
