July 9, 1998 Committee on Science & Technology,Environment & forests
 
 
REPORT
The Department of Electronics (DOE) has been entrusted with the responsibility of formulation, implementation and review of various
 schemes/programmes in the field of electronics. The objectives of the Department are to provide a focal point of Government's
 attention to electronics sector and act as a coordinator within and outside the Government, to bring the benefit of electronics to every
 walk of life in India and to make the Indian Electronics Industry a global player.
2. The Secretary, DOE in his presentation gave an overview of the achievements of the Department during the Eighth Plan period, the
 areas which would be focused during the Ninth Plan period and the efforts intended to be made to pursue the set targets. The
 Committee was informed that the Department pursued policies leading to a commendable progress in the fields of electronics
 production and export, which achieved a cumulative annual growth of 20 per cent in production and 40 per cent in export. An export
 target of Rs. 48,930 crores has been set for the terminal year of the Ninth Plan with a growth rate of about 52 per cent. The policies of
 the Department have led to a tremendous progress in the field of software export. The software industry has emerged as one of the
 fastest growing sectors in the economy with a CAGR exceeding 50 per cent.
3. The Committee was informed that the Department has implemented a number of programmes/missions in specialised areas, such as
 Massive Parallel Processing (C-DAC); Future Air Navigations System (FANS); National HVDC Programme; Industrial Electronics
 Promotion Programme; Centre for Liquid Crystal Research:
Microprocessor Applications Engineering Programme; and Appropriate Automation Promotion Programme.
4. In order to promote international S&T Cooperation and evolve joint R&D projects in the area of Electronics and Information
 Technology with various countries. the Department of Electronics is also interacting with Department of Science & Technology
 (DST). The Programme of Cooperation includes exchange of scientists! experts, participation in conferences/workshops, training and
 evolving joint R&D projects in the areas of mutual interest.
5. The Committee was informed that during the Ninth Plan period the thrust areas under focus shall be export, employment and
 productivity led growth of Electronics and Information Technology as this sector has the propensity to increase the overall growth
 rate to a higher level. In the liberalised economic scenario, the Department aims at bringing the benefits of electronics to every walk
 of life and playing a catalytic role to make the Indian electronics industry a global player. These objectives would be achieved
 through a three pronged strategy of supporting technology development, setting up of critical infrastructure and formulating policies
 conducive to industrial growth .•
6. In order to achieve the above goals, the strategic imperatives being followed are production level at international cost and prices;
 market promotion and export thrust; quality of products at internationally competitive levels; rationalisation of procedures to ensure
 growth; identifying niche areas in the world market; strengthening R&D efforts; strengthening manpower base; computing in Indian
 languages; develop new applications of electronics relevant to India. etc. The penetration of computers in India, at present, is at two
 per thousand of the population. It is targeted to grow to ten per thousand by the year 200 1.
7. The Department has prepared a futuristic document 'India IT Vision 20W-Action Plan' covering important areas of Infrastructure,
 Skill Development & Education, Finance & Marketing, Promotion & Applications Development, Technology R&D, Policy Support,
 and Indigenous Manufacture for self-reliance to make India a glooal information technology power and one of the largest generator
 and exporters in the world within ten years.
8. Keeping in view the recommendations of the Ninth Plan (1997-2002) Working Group on Electronics Industry set-up by the
 Planning Commission, the Department formulated certain nationally co-ordinated initiatives in 1997 which are under various stages
 of implementation. These incude: National Information Infrastructure for National Development: NIl 2000 Action Plan; National
 Software capability Enhancement Programme: SoftCap; Expand High Speed Datacom Facilities to enhance: Software Exports STPI
 Vision 2000; National Institute of Advanced Software Education and Research (NISER); Intellectual Property Rights (IPR)
 Promotion Programme, and Technology Information & Forecasting Support in IT (TechnolnFo).
9. Besides, pursuing the ongoing programmes, new programme proposed to be initiated by the Department durin, 1998-99 is,
 Technology Development Information Technology which aims at undertaking different Technology Development projects in
 information technology.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
10. After listening to the presentation made by the Secretary, DOE, the Committee examined the Demands for Grants of the
 Department for the year 1998-99 in the light of its mandate, objectives pursued by it and the targets achieved so far. 'The Budget
 provision for the Department of Electronics for the year 1998-99 is as under: Plan provision of Rs. 190 crores includes Rs. 7.75 crores
 towards book adjustment of external assistance being received under some programmes. 1be sector-wise break-up of allocation for
 attached offices, PSUs, Registered Societies, ongoing programmes/schemes and new schemes of DOE has been shown at Annexure.
11. The Committee wanted to know as to why there has been a substantial increase in the allocation on the plan side for the current
 financial year which is kept at Rs. 190.00 crores as against the B .E. of last year which was Rs. 135.60 crores. The Committee was
 informed that an additional amount of Rs. 50 crores has been allocated to fulfil the objectives of 1ndia IT Vision 201 O-Action Plan'.
 The Committee was further informed that the programmes which envisage substantial increase in the B.E. for 1998·99 compared to
 1997-98 are as follows:
 
The Committee examined the budgetary allocations made for different programmes of the DOE during the year 1998-99 and sought to
 know reasons for the variations wherever occured.
TECHNOLOGY DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL PROJECTS
12. The Technology Development Council (TDC) looks at general application based R&D projects in various sectors, inter-

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA 'RAJYA SABHA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20S%20and%20T,%20Env.%20and%20Forests/58%20Report.htm[29-08-2018 16:12:09]
disciplinary emerging technologies and other new initiatives. The allocation for the TDC projects during the current financial year has
 been reduced to Rs. 2.50 crores from Rs. 5.00 crores (R.E.) of 1997-98. The Committee wanted to know the reasons for this reduction
 in the outlay. The Committee was informed that the bulk of R&D funding comes through special Heads e.g., funding for Centre for
 Development of Advanced Computing (C-DAC), Society for Applied Microwave Electronics Engineering and Research (SAMEER),
 Centre for Materials for Electronics Technology (CMET), Centre for Liquid Crystal Research (CLCR), National Centre for Software
 Technology (NCST) and Electronics Research & Development Centre (ER&DC). Further, IT related R&D funding would be coming
 through NIT Head Projects like ATM Test Bed, IDIL Programme, etc. Besides, a provision of Rs. 10 crores has also been made for a
 new Programme "Technology Development in Information Technology and Other Programmes". The Committee was also apprised
 that many of the old projects funded through TDC route have fructified.       
13. Apart from many sources for the funding of the Technology Development Council Projects, the Committee learnt that the Central
 Government Departments have· also been advised by the Planning Commission to allocate 2 to 3 per cent of their outlay to promote
 Information Technology. The Committee recommends that the Department should constantly interact with various Ministries
 Departments of the Government to monitor that the allocation made by them to promote information technology is being used in the
 right direction. The Committee feels that in the absence of such a monitoring agency no checks can be imposed on the diversification
 of these funds for other purposes.
SOFIWARFJHARDWARE EXPORT PROMOTION
14. The programme aims at the creation of basic facilities for development and exports of software to data links and contributes
 towards achieving export targets, both for software and hardware. The Committee noted that there has been a substantial hike in the
 B.E. of 1998-99 under the head Software/Hardware Export Promotion from Rs. 2 crores, as was in the R.E. for 1997-98 to Rs. 10
 crores in the B.E. of the current year. The Committee enquired from the Department about the various schemes proposed to be
 undertaken to promote the integrated development of software hardware in the country for domestic as well as export market The
 Committee was informed that the export target for the terminal year of the Ninth Plan is Rs. 48,930 crores. In order to achieve this
 target there is need to upgrade promotional efforts and Quality Enhancement Programme. The Department proposes to initiate certain
 schemes to achieve this goal like the Project Soft QC/QM meant to promote quality culture amongst the software units; the scheme
 for the accreditation of software units as per the international standards; promotion -of Software Technology Parks (STPs); promotion
 plug and play facilities in existing STPs to facilitate new entrepreneurs and supporting schemes for building capabilities in software
 products and packages. Most of the software today is customised. There is a need to move up the value chain and undertake market
 and feasibility studies and launch export promotion campaigns.
15. The Committee notes with satisfaction that due to the efforts of the Department Indian software export has made a tremendous
 progress and has jumped to a left) of US$ 1.6 billion in 1997-98  The Committee is, however, constrained to observe that the
 Department has made relatively less progress in the hardware sector and recommends that definite plans schemes be chalked out for
 steady promotion and integrated development of hardware in the country for domestic as well as export market.
MANPOWER DEVELOPMENT FOR SOFTWARE EXPORT
16. The Committee was informed that allocation for Manpower Development for Software Export has been increased from Rs. 5.00
 crores as was in ~.E. of 1997-98 to Rs. 12.00 crores during the current financial year to achieve the software export target.
 Approximately, 20,000 professionals are required for every billion dollar of export and for generating new professionals, there is also
 a need for re-training of existing professionals, to take care of the technological obsolescence. Certain programmes envisaged in this
 area are: SOFTCAP which will include increase of intake in IITs and Regional Engineering Colleges (RECs) in collaboration with the
 Ministry of Human Resource Development (MHRD) and establishment of National Institute for Advanced Software Education and
 research (NlSER); promotion of Indian Institute of Information Technology (IIIT) through State Governments; upgradation of the
 capabilities of NCST; and promotion of Distance Learning.
17. The Committee observes that the manpower development for software export should be considered a priority area. Everything
 possible must be done to launch comprehensive programmes for updating the technological skills and knowledge of our software
 professionals so that India could compete in imitational software market with other world leaders in the area.
NATIONAL INFORMATION INFRASTRUCTURE (NIl)
18. With the convergence of Intonation Technology, Telecommunication and Entertainment, new vistas in the life of a common man
 have been opened. This technology would help in storage of information both text and multi-media, present and analyse in different
 ways/formats suitable to the circumstances for different purposes simultaneously at a umber of places. The allocation for Nll during
 1997-98 was Rs. 4.00crores while it has been in to Rs. 24.00 crores during the current year. 1be Committee wanted to know the
 reasons for the substantial hike of Rs. 20 crores towards allocation for the Nll in the B .E. of current year. 1be Committee was
 informed that during 1997-98 a nominal provision of Rs. 4.00 crores was made for Nll with the proviso that Nll blueprint would be
 prepared and approved and some initial follow up action will be initiated during 1997-98. Nll vision document and Nil 2000 Action
 Plan were both approved by the Committee of Secretaries and some progress was made towards implementation of the plan.
 However, the original Ninth Plan document had envisaged a much larger DOE initiative in this area with an outlay of Rs. 80 crores
 for the entire plan period. The year 1998-99, as stated by the Department may be seen as the first major year in which Nll initiative
 will make a real headway. 1be ongoing activities of the project initiated during 1997-98 itself would demand about Rs. 9 crores in the
 current year leaving about Rs. 15 crores for new initiatives as envisaged in the Nll2000 Action Plan.
RURAL PROJECTS (ELECTRONICS FOR RURAL/SOCIAL/AGRICULTURE/WATER SECTOR
19. In the sector of Rural and Social Applications of Electronics, the Committee was informed that the Department of Electronics
 strives to develop and demonstrate cost- effective applications of electronics for rural and social development including agriculture,
 watershed development, adult literacy, etc. The projects are usually implemented by R&D institutions, NGOs and field groups. To
 promote the utilisation of computers at the panchayat and block level. the Department of Electronics is also launching a few projects
 for establishing Village Level Information Centres (SAMADHAN Centres) that will be repositories of information on a variety of
 topics of interest to the local population. In addition, these centres could also be used as training and educational centres. The first of
 such projects has been initiated during 1997-98 in the Ramanathapuram District in Tamil Nadu.
20. The Committee was told that this programme aims at promoting and developing appropriate technologies based primarily on

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA 'RAJYA SABHA

 electronics which have variety of rural applications and help in production. The Committee wanted to know the reasons for
 practically no increase in the outlay for this sector, the allocation for which has been kept at Rs. 2.00 crores. The Committee wanted
 to know if the Department still considers this as one of its thrust areas. The Committee was informed that during the Eighth Plan,
 allocation for this sector averaged less than Rs. 50 lakhs. It was raised to Rs.2 crores last year and has been maintained at that level in
 the current financial year. The Committee was given to understand that through an allocation of 2-3 per cent outlay for Information
 Technology in all Central Government Departments which include the socio-economic Ministries and Departments there will be
 considerable additional resources for this Sector. During the last two years about 18 new projects have been initiated by the
 Department to promote electronics applications under this sector. One of the important areas that is being addressed is IT
 Applications for Watershed Development. Four projects have been sponsored in this area to develop software packages for the better
 implementation of watershed development projects.
21. While the Committee observes that the objectives of this programme are laudable, it however, fails to understand the reasons as to
 why the funds allocated under this Head during the year 1997-98 could not be fully utilised. The allocation for the programme during
 last year was kept at Rs. 2.00 crores while utilisation was Rs. 1.46 crores. The Committee recommends that all out efforts be made by
 the Department to see that the outlay earmarked this year for this important programme is fully utilised and the benefits of the
 schemes percolate down to a large segment of rural population.
UNDERUTILISATION OF FUNDS
22. The Committee has noted thai the allocations made for various schemes like Health, Electronics, Hi- Tech Power Electronics, lPR
 Promotion Programme and Environmental Management in Electronics during the last financial year (1997-98) were not used fully.
 The allocations for these schemes have either ~n increased or kept at the last year's B.E. level The Committee recommends that the
 Department should make concrete efforts for the utilisation of funds allocated for these schemes/programmes fully during the year
 1998-99.
OTHER PROGRAMMES
23. The Department has projected a demand of Rs. 22.37 crores (plan) in B.E. of current year for other programmes which include
 Foreign Trade, IPR promotion programme, etc. as against Rs. 12.70 crores in th.e B.E. of 1997-98 and Rs. 12.93 crores in R.E. of the
 same year. The Committee wanted to'know the reasons for this variation. The Committee was informed that a provision of Rs. 10.00
 crores has been earmarked for a new programme "Technology Development in Information Technology". The remaining provision of
 Rs. 12.37 crores is for the ongoing programmes which were initiated during the year 1997-98.
24. The Committee evinced a keen interest in the Supercomputer developed at the C-DAC and specifically enquired into the details of
 its economic aspects, particularly the savings it has led to. The Committee was informed that the C-DAC was established for strategic
 consideration, since the import of Supercomputer was hit by export Control mesures adopted by some developed countries. The C-
DAC has successfully developed Supercomputer through parallel processing technology and PARAM 1ססoo was unveiled in March,
 1998. Apart from Japan, no other country has this capability in Asia. Different configurations of the PARAM models have been
 supplied to various organisations mainly In Academic and R&D institutions in India. A few have been supplied to Russia, Canada
 and Germany. AII together 35 different systems have been supplied generating an income of Rs. 20 crores including Rs. 3 crores in
 foreign exchange. The Committee was further informed that under the Indo-Russian Technology Cooperation, an R&D collaboration
 by C-DAC with ICAD, Moscow has been established for development of new software for PARAM range of computers and this will
 enable greater use of the computers within India and abroad.
25. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department of Electronics has taken initiative and provided the needed. support to
 C-DAC which had successfully developed a supercomputer through parallel processing technology. The Committee would like to
 congratulate the scientists, engineers, technologists and others who were associated with this programme.
INDIA IT VISION 2010: ACTION PLAN
26. The Committee was given a brief outline of the programme 'India IT Vision 2010: Action Plan' which covers important areas of
 Infrastructure, Skill Development & Education, Finance & Marketing, Promotion & Application Development, Technology R&D,
 Policy Support, and Indigenous Manufacture for self-reliance to make India a global information technology power and one of the
 largest generators and exporters in the world within 10 years. The Committee was informed that in pursuance of the Prime Minister's
 Mission objective to make India an IT superpower and largest producer and exporter of software, the DOE IT Vision 201D-Action
 Plan was discussed in the Planning Commission and a tentative additional outlay of Rs. 50 crores has been allocated. The document
 has also been submitted to the National Task Force on Information Technology and Software Development This Task Force is
 required to submit a report on removal of bottlenecks to give a boost to Information Technology within 30 days and formulation of
 National Informatics Policy and Action Plan within 90 days. In the light of the recommendations of the National Task Force, the
 implementation of IT Vision 20JO will be undertaken.
27. Since the 'India IT Vision 2010: Action Plan' covers a wide range of activities which aim at making India a world leader in the
 software market and making India self-reliant in the field of information technology, the Committee would like the Plan to be
 implemented with focussed attention of the Department The Department may, therefore, consider appointing a high level Committee
 which should periodically review the progress of the projects initiated and target.;: achieved under the Plan.
COMPUTER EDUCATION
28. In the area of computer education the Committee was informed that in the non- formal sector (both private as well as public), the
 Department of Electronics has implemented a scheme viz., the Department of Electronics Accreditation of Computer Courses
 (DOEACC) under which the institutions/organisations in the non-formal sector meeting certain well-defined norms and criteria, in
 terms of faculty, software and hardware are given accreditation by the MHRD and AICTE, a Statutory Body, which provides
 accreditation to technical institutions. At present there are more than 600 institutions accredited under the scheme. Performance of the
 accredited institutes is monitored periodically. Besides, to ensure that the training under the DOEACC scheme is in keeping with the
 latest knowledge, the syllabuses of all the levels are revised periodically.
29. The Committee expresses its satisfaction that the Department has taken note of the prevailing obsolescence in the computer
 courses and has taken steps to update the computer education.
PHOTONICS

30. Photonics deals with the technology of generating and harnessing light and other forms of radiant energy the quantum unit of
 which is a photon. The range of applications of photonics extends from energy generating to detection, communication and
 information processing. The objective of the photonics development programme, according to the Department, is to develop core
 technologies and applications which are of critical importance for the present and next generation of electronics, computer and
 communication systems.
31. The Department of Electronics has taken major initiatives during the Eighth Plan which include projects in the areas of
 optoelectronics devices, components and sub-systems, .high speed fiber optic data links and interconnects, broadband (SDH/SONET
 communication systems, photonics switching, etc. The Department has implemented the programmes relating to the Fiber Optics
 Systems and Products Project; Optoelectronics Technology Project (OTP); Photonics Switching Development Programme (FSDP);
 and National Photonics Project (NPP).
32. The Department has also identified some new areas for the Ninth Plan period. The Committee was informed that a new project on
 Silica-on-Silicon based Integrated Optic components is expected to be initiated shortly.
PUBLIC SEctOR ENTERPRISES
33. There are three public sector enterprises, namely, Semiconductor Complex Ltd. (SCL) Computer Maintenance Corporation Ltd.
 (CMC) and Electronics Trade and Technology Development Corporation Limited (ET &n which come under the Department of
 Electronics. The Committee examined the demands of these Public Sector Enterprises and noted that the allocations on the Plan side
 have been reduced to Rs. 17.25 crores as against Rs. 26.50 crores in the B.E. of 1997-98. The Committee wanted to know the reasons
 for this variation. The Committee was informed that the Budgetary a1~ocation towards Plan Investment in the SCL is Rs. 15.00
 crores by way of equity and in the ET&T is Rs. 2.25 crores by way of loans and advances.
34. In case of SCL, the Committee was told that the Revised Cost Estimate-IT approved by the Cabinet, an outlay of Rs. 332.56 crores
 was envisaged for rebuilding of VLSI facility which constituted Rs. 289.97 crores as budgetary support out of which Rs. 165.86
 crores is by way of equity and Rs. 124.11 crores is by way of Grant-in- ­aid. The Committee was informed that an amount of Rs.
 134.935 crores has already been released as equity to SCL and for the balance amount of Rs. 30.925 crores, a sum of Rs. 15 crores is
 proposed to be released in 1998-99 and hence there is no reduction in the plan outlay for SCL.
35. In case of Electronics Trade & Technology Development Corporation Limited (ET&T the Committee was informed that a token
 provision of Rs. 2.25 crores has been kept for it during the current financial year 1998-99 because the Disinvestment Commission in
 its Sixth Report submitted in December 1997 has recommended closure of the company and the recommendations are under
 consideration of the Core Committee of Secretaries. ET &T has prepared another rehabilitation proposal which has also been sent to
 the Core Committee for consideration.
36. The Committee would like the Department to f'inalise its future programme with regard to the ET &T. Either this venture be
 closed down as recommended by the I investment Commission or a well thought out diversification plan should be prepared for the
 revival or the company. Uncertainty with regard to its future would prove costly to the public exchequer.
37. The Committee wanted to know whether there is any move to privatise CMC. The Committee was informed that there is no such
 move with regard to CMC. The CMC has. however, submitted a proposal to the Government wherein it envisages to raise the equity
 within the authorised share capital through private placement with financial institutions and mutual funds. The Government has not
 yet taken any decision in this regard.
38. After making a detailed scrutiny or the Demands for Grants of the Department of Electronics and assesing the progress of various
 important programmes and projects administrated by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 211.57
 crores, as sought by the Department or Electronics for the year 1998-99, under Demand No. 91 are in order and may be approved.

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and Forests, having been 
authorised by the Committee to present the report on its behalf, present this Fifty-Ninth Report of the Committee. 
This Report deals with the detailed Demands for Grants (1998-99) of the Department of Space (Demand No. 93). 
2. In the meeting of the Committee held on the June 26, 1998 the Secretary and other officers of the Depart­
ment of Space gave an overview of the various activities of the Department and the Committee sought clarifica­
tions on various aspects of the performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Department for replying to the clarifications 
sought by the Members and placing before it the required material to enable the Committee to scru tinise the 
Demands for Grants of the Department of Space. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on July 9, 1998 . 
NEW DELHI; 
July 9, 1998 
S.R. BOMMAI 1, 
Chairman, 
Committee on Science & Technology, 
Environment & Forests 

REPORT 
The Indian Space Programme, which had a modest beginning in the early sixt ies, is primarily aimed at 
promoti ng the development and application of space technology and space sciences for the socio-economic ben­
efits of the nation. Over the last three decades, the very challenging task of development of space technology and 
its utilisation, has not only graduated from establishment and expe rimental phase s to an operational era but also 
proved emphatically its potential to address the national needs. 
2. In tune with the goal of self-reliant use of space technology for national development, the main thrust 
areas of the Indian Space Programmes are:-
(a) satellite based communications for various applications; 
(b) satellite based remote sensing for resources survey, management and environmental monitoring; 
(c) meteorological applications; and 
(d) developm ent and operationalisation of indigenous satellites and launch vehicles for providing these 
space services. 
3. The Department of Space (DOS) is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space Commis­
sion. The policies are carried out through the Indian Space Researc h Organisation (ISRO) and the three Grant-in­
aid institutions, viz. the National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) and 
the National Mesosphere-Stratosphere -Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF). 
DEMANDS FOR GRANI'S (1998-99) 
4. The Committee was informed that the total expenditure of the Department during the Eighth Five Year 
Plan period was Rs. 3928.53 crores out of which the plan component was Rs. 3155.74 crores and the Non-Plan 
component was Rs. 772.79 crores. The Secretary, DOS, informed the Committee that most of the targets set for the 
Department during the Eighth Plan period were achieved. He also gave an outline of the proposed priorities of the 
Department for the Ninth Five Year Plan period. 
5. Analysing the performance of the Department on the basis of the information made available, the Com­
mittee found that during 1995-96, the Department had utilised the funds to the extent of 99.93 per cent. In 1996-
97, the fund utilisation level was about 99.83 per cent. The provisional expenditure for 1997-98 indicates utilisa­
tion of funds by•the Department upto 99.50 per cent of the revised estimates allocation. 
6. The Committee feels happy over the fact that the Department has made almost full use of funds allocated 
to it during 1995-96, 1996-97 and 1997-98. 
7. As regards the allocation projected by the Department and recommended by the Planning Commission for 
the Ninth Plan period, the Secretary, DOS informed the Committee that against a projected demand for Rs. 12,200 
crores sought originally (Plan Rs. I 1000 crores and Non-Plan Rs. 1200 crores) an outlay of Rs. 7100 crores has 
been decided and the total outlay for the Department during the entire plan period comes to Rs. 8300 crores. The 
non-plan component is thus kept at Rs. 1200 crores. As against the 14 Missions of the Eighth Plan, during the 
Ninth Plan period about 23 Missions (14 satellite and 9 launch vehicle missions ) have been identified. The Com­
mittee was informed that in view of the reduction in allocation, the missions envisaged for the Ninth Plan period 
have been reprioritised. The emphasis has been given to the realisation of missions/programmes essential to meet 
the projected user demands in the two operational systems viz .• IRS and INSAT besides development of indigenous 
launch capability. In this arrangement, however, a provision of Rs. 30 crores for Disaster Management System has 
been retained under the revised programmatic allocations for the Ninth Five Year Plan The Annual phasing of 
expendi ture has also been reworked and the annual revised estimates for 1997-98 (Rs. 1059.74 crores) and the 
budget estimatc l-.for 1~98 - 99 (Rs. 1607.83 crores) are in tune with this revised phasing of expenditure. The 

~nancial outlay of Rs. 8300 crores for the Ninth Five Year Plan represents II 0 per cent increase in outlay over the 
Eighth Five Year Plan expenditure at current prices . At 1991-92 prices, this increase will be about 55 per cent. 
8. The Committee was informed that consistent with the programme directions and targets envisaged for the 
Ninth Five Year Plan period, specific activities/projects to be undertaken during the current year have been care­
fully prioritised while arriving at the budget estimates for 1998-99. 1be budget estimates for 1998-99 work out to 
Rs. 1607.83 crores with a plan component of Rs. 1386.38 crores and non-plan component of Rs. 221.45 crores. 
The programmatic details of the plan provision is given in Annexure . 
8.1 The financial allocation for 1998-99 is largely towards projects which have already been ·approved by the 
Government. Out of a total budget of Rs. 1607.83 crores sought by the Department, the budget for the approved 
major projects is kept at Rs. 1067.60 crores which is approximately 66 per cent of the total budgetary outlay. 
INDIAN NATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEM (INSA'I) 
9. The Indian National Satellite System, which became operational with INSAT- tB, is a multi-agen cy, 
multi-purpose operatio nal satellite system which provides domestic long distance telecommunications, meteoro­
logical earth observation and data relay, nation wide direct satellite TV broadcasting to augmented TV receivers, 
nation wide radio networking, TV programme distribution and rebroadcasting to terrestrial transmitters, etc. The 
Department of Space is responsible for establishment and operation of INSAT space segment. 
9.1 The INS AT space segment at present consists of five satellites-INSAT-10, INSAT-2A, INSAT-2B, INSAT-
2C and INSAT-2DT acquired from ARABSAT Organisation, after INSAT-2D became inoperable on October 4, 
1997 following a power bus anomaly. 
9.2 The Committee was informed that during the Ninth Five Year Plan period continuation of INSAT Sys­
tem with enhanced capacity and capabilities will be an important target to meet the growing national needs and 
changing technology scenario. The Committee was also informed that it would be necessary to provide a space 
segment capacity of 135 transponders by the year 2001. Accordingly, INSAT-2E is scheduled to be launched 
during 1998-99 for communication and meteorological services. It will carry 17 C-band and lower extended C­
band transponders, a Very High Resolution Radiometer (VHRR) with an additional water vapour channel, etc. The 
sanctioned cost of the INSAT-2C D & E satellites, including launch services and acquisition of in-orbit Arabsat-C 
is Rs. 1439.80 crores and this year's financial requirement for it is kept at Rs. 58.10 crores. 
SATELLITE NAVIGATION 
l 0. Satellite navigation is a service which is expected to become operational in many advanced countries in 
the next few years. Notable among them are : United States, Japan, Europe, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. 
The International Civil Aviation Organisation has made Satellite navigation equipment mandatory on all civilian 
aircraft. To upgrade the existing Communications Navigation and Surveillance (CNS) and Air-Traffic Manage­
ment (ATM) system in India, the Airports Authority of India (AAI) is planning to make them adaptable to the 
Future Air Navigation System (FANS) through the introduction of Indian Wide Area Differential GPS (WADGPS) 
system. As a business plan AAI will phase out the existing navigational aids and will increasingly depend on 
satellite navigation by the year 2010. 
11. The Committee recommends that the Department of Space may provide aD necessary help to the Airports 
Authority of India (AAI) in setting up the satellite navigation infrastmcture to meet the national needs. 
INDIAN REMOTE SENSING SATELLITE (IRS) 
12. The Indian Remote Se4lsing (IRS), established with the launching of IRS-I A in March 1988, constitutes 
an important element of National Nlllural Resources Management System (NNRMS) providing continuously space­
based data for the management of resources. 
13. The Committee was informed that the Department proposes to undertake major initiatives in the use ofiRS 
data in the country for drought monitoring and assessment, water resources management, forests, environment 
and the resources sector, geology and mineral prospecting, agricultural applications, integrated land and water 
resource management, wasteland mapping, rural and urban development and coastal and ocean-related 
applications. 

14. The remote sensing applications in the country arc carried out under the broad umbrella of National 
Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS) . The nine NNRMS Standing Committees encompassing ma­
jor natural resources and developmental areas like agriculture. bioresource s and environment , urban develop ­
ment , etc. periodically review the status of utilisation of remote sen5ing in their respective fields and provide 
guidance for promoting remote sensing based activities. These Standing Committees are chaired by Secretaries 
to the Government of India of concerned Departments . Besides. the user interface at State level is facilitated 
through the State Remote Sensing Application Centres. 
WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENI' 
15. The Committee wanted to know about the application of remote s ensing data in finding out water 
resources and its use by the Department of Rural Development in providing water to village s. The Committee 
was informed that the National Drinking Water Mission and the remote sensing based maps and inputs were 
generated and used to locate ground water resources for drilling bore wells in about 1.6 lakh villages dur ing 
1987-91. In case of the Rajiv Gandh i National Drinking Water Mission which is operate d by the Dep artment of 
Rural Development, the inputs from the Depattment of Space include remote s ensin g data which would be 
coupled with the conventional techniques for identifying ground water sources in 4.3 lakh problem habitations. 
It has also been planned to identify sites for water harvesting for these habitations. A proposal in this regard is 
being worked out in consultation with the Mission. In Tamil N adu the DOS has taken u p a major project for 
identifying sites for water harvesting structures over the entire state. The study has also been com pleted for three 
districts and implementati on is going on in one district of Tamil N adu. 
16. The Committee expresses its concern over the receding water table in many parts of the country. High 
exploitation in a low availability ground water area is causing serious problem. There has to be a balance between 
the drawal of water from the surface and creation of water harvesting structures. The Committee is of the view 
that the Department is already doing a major project in Tamil Nadu for identifying sites for w ater h arves ting 
structures . If this experiment proves successful, the Committee would like that the similar requirem ents of other 
States may also be met by the Department. 
AGRICULTURAL APPLICATION 
17. The Committee evinced interest in the forecasting of agricultura l production by using space-based data 
and agrometeorological and land-based observations. The programme, Forecasting Agricultural output through 
Space, Agrometeorological and Land based Observations (FASAL) has been launched in the States of Assam, 
Andhra Pradesh, Haryana, Orissa and Uttar Pradesh. The Committee wanted to know about the experience of the 
Department in forecasting, agricultural output by usir.g Space-based and meteorological data and coupling it 
with the land-based observations. The Secretary, Department of Space informed that the Department has been 
using the space system for agricultural production and yield monitoring for the last seven or eight years and in 
th1s the Department is closely working with the Department of Agriculture. This works at 90 per cent accuracy 
and 90 per cent precision kind of data, one month before the harvest. The Department has established a method­
ology for this. The Department faces some problems with the methodology during the Kharif season because the 
sensor used in the space during the Kharif season cannot penetrate the clouds and this causes a problem in regard 
to looking at the ground. The Department of Space is working out a scheme with the Department of Agriculture 
10 taking into account the experience which it had acquired earlier at the t1me of kharif and rabi crops and it 
envisages the usc of agrometeorological information with the conventional knowledge like crop-cutting and 
other methods which the Department of Agriculture uses. The Department plans to extend FASAL to other States 
later. It is also contemplated by the Department of Agriculture and Cooperation to establish a National Centre for 
Crop Forecasting (NCCF). 
18. The Committee expressed its concern over the uncertainty and fluctuations in the climatic and weather 
conditions which have an adverse effect on agriculture. The Committee, particularly wanted to know from the 
Secretary about the Space-based data which may improve the weather forecastmg. 
18. I The Committee was told that a vast array of space-based meteorological data exists but wttat is lacking 
actually in accurate weather prediction is the need for improving modelling capability. Modelling in the tropical 
region is more complex than modelling in the temperate region. If one looks at the medium range capability in 
the Europ'ean Centre, they do it in seven or eight days earlier whereas because of complexities in atmospheric 
circul ation, we ha• a prof'llem of prediction cvrn two (I~ thr·,. thys earher Jb( Sccrt-tu'"''· • 1QS ··greed with the 
Committee that ac ·racy 1n predicting the weather cooJittons is an urgent need of the agricultu sector and the 
question would be examinc-.d further. 

INI'EGRATED MISSION FOR SUSI'AINABLE DEVELOPMENT 
19. The Committee was also informed that there -is the Integrated Mission for Sustainable Development 
(IMSD) to generate action plan for rural development The IMSD so far covered 175 districts in 25 States. This 
programme adopts a scientific and holistic approach for realistic planning for sustainable development and man­
agement of natural resources. For the generation of land and water resources action plans for developmental 
activities are also being initiated on I: 12,500 scales. The Department has also been doing waste land mapping for 
192 districts. 
20. The Committee is of the view that the programmes like IMSD and wasteland mapping should be en­
larged in scope so as to cover in a phased manner the entire country. 
URBANDEVELOPMrnNT 
21. Regarding urban development activities involving cities and towns, a high resolution data from Indian 
Space Research Organisation (ISRO) provides vital details useful for urban planning. The Department has already 
conducted urban sprawl study which was carried out for 12 major cities. Now under the aegis of the newly set-up 
NNRMS Standing Committee for Urban Development, it is planned to take-up base map updation for 24 selected 
towns, initially. It is also being proposed to take up studies for master plan development for 8 cities/metros. In 
Andhra Pradesh, studies towards preparation/updation of base maps is being taken up for 41 towns. 
BIO-DIVERSITY AND ENVIRONMENT 
22. India has rich biodiversity. The Committee was particularly interested in knowing if the Department has 
done anything to map the bio-diversity which exists in India. The Committee was of the view that many parts of 
India have still not been mapped. The Committee cited the example of Andaman and Nicobar which is rich in 
biodiversity but is yet to be mapped. 
22.1 The Committee was told that at the behest of the Department of Bio-technology (DBT), a project has 
been taken up towards characterising bio-diversity at landscape level. The three main bio-diversity rich regions of 
the country viz., North-East Himalaya, Western Ghats and North-West Himalaya are covered. The study aims at 
prioritising areas for bioprospecting and conservation. A nbmber of studies pertaining to Environmental Impact 
Assessment (EIA) of major developmental projects (mining, polluGing industries, power projects, etc.) and envi­
ronmental monitoring (mapping wetlands, coastal regulation zo~e), etc . .have been carried out under the aegis of 
the NNRMS Standing Committee on Bioresources and Environment. Few States have also taken initiatives to 
internalise EIA in case of polluting industries. The Forest Survey of India has been monitoring forest cover of 
entire country once in two years. 
~TIYGLOBALCHANGE 
23. On \he question of climate study and climatic changes the Committee was informed that the global 
climate chaqge is an important area of concern to the scientific community the world over and one of the important 
programm~ that the global scientific community has embarked on is the International Geosphere and Biosphere 
Programm4s 
23.f lSRO has been conducting studies and experiments that are specifically relevant to global change 
phenowtna over the Indian region. Data from remote sensing satellites and ground based and balloon borne 
experim·rl"tS•.are used for studing the processes relevant to green house warming and ozone depletion phenomena. 
An interesting constituent methyl bromide was measured during an ISRO-DLR balloon borne cryo sampler ex­
periments during 1990 which constitutes one of the important trace species which need to be monitored. ISRO has 
also initiated preliminary studies towards the definition of a climatesat satellite. A National Committee on Inter­
national Geosphere and Biosphere Programme is coordinating the activities at various institutions and Universi­
ties in this area. 
DTHMISSION 
24. The Committee was informed that the Direct-To-Home Mission has been removed from the plan sector 
because it was suggested to the Department that funding for this mission could be predominantly sought from users 
and private sector. Only seed money is kept in the Department of Space plan for participation in cooperative ven­
tures. The Department is in touch with few investors who would like to operate a satellite of that class. But this has 
to be looked into in the context of the Broadcasting BiH, particularly on the om. 

GEO-SYNCHRONOUS LAUNCH VEIDCLE (GSLV) 
25. The Geo-sync hronous Satell ite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) is configured by maximally utilising the models 
developed for Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV). GSLV is a three stage vehicle employing solid. liquid and 
cryo stages and is capable of placing 2500 kg. class communication satellites in Geo-synchronous Transfer Orbit 
(GTO). The Committee was informed that the development activities are progressing satisfactorily and the first 
launch of GSLV is expected in 1999. The total cost approved for GSLV project is Rs. II 05.30 crores. By the end of 
1998-99the cumu lative expend iture of the project would be Rs. 1004.37 crores which comes to approximately 91 
per cent of the total project cost. The financial outlay for 1998-99 for the project is Rs. 83.75 crores. 
CRYO-UPPER STAGE (CUS) PROJECT 
26. The Committee was informed that the indigenous development of cryogenic engine. the Cryogenic 
Upper Stage (CUS) Project, is a project with a total estimated cost of Rs. 335.89 crores. The cumulative expendi­
ture of this project by the end of 1998-99 would be Rs 238.24 crores which is approximately 71 per cent of the total 
project cost. The Budget estimates for 1998-99 is based on the programmatic target of realising the hardware for 
Engine and Stage component and testing of Cryo Engine. It is planned to use this engine in GSLV from 2000-01 
onwards. 
DISASTER MANAGEMENT 
27. Disaster Management System can be broadly classified into three phases, viz. (i) pre-disaster planning, 
consisting of steps leading to disaster prevention, disaster mitigation, and disaster preparedness (ii) the response to 
the disaster comprising the disaster warning and the emergency relief aspects. and (iii) the recovery phase consisting 
of rehabilitation and reconstruction. Space-based disaster management system provides valuable inputs in all the 
three phases, when appropriately integrated with the conventional ground-based systems. 
27.1 The Committee was informed that with the object of quick dissemination of weather warnings of impend­
ing disaster from approaching cyclones, specially designed receivers i.e., Cyclone Warning Dissemination Sys­
tems (CWDSs) have been installed within the vulnerable coastal areas to disseminate cyclone warning messages 
directly to the affected areas. The Indian Meteorological Department (IMD) has deployed 250 Cyclone Warning 
Dissemination System (CWDS) in various States along east and west coast of India. IMD has planned I 00 more 
CWDS receivers to be deployed during the Ninth Five Year Plan period. 
28. The Committee feels that there is a need to increase the network density in the coastal areas for direct 
transmission of cyclone warnings weU in advance and the Department should take up the matter with the India 
Meteorological Department in this regard. The Committee recommends that an Integrated Disaster Management 
System should be established with necessary facilities like control room with the latest equipments and technologies 
including satellite data reception and communication facilities for providing near real-time monitoring of the 
disasters. 
29. On a specific question regarding the recent cyclone in Gujarat, the Committee was told by the Secretary, 
DOS that the cyclone warning systems were working almost satisfactorily at the appropriate locations and this was 
confirmed by the India Meteorological Department. 
SECOND LAUNCH PAD AND COMMON FACILITIES 
30. The Committee was informed that the Second Launch Pad and Common Facilities project was sanctioned 
in October, 1997 with a total project cost of Rs. 289 crores. During the last year a token amount of Rs. I crore was 
allocated which is increased substantially toRs. 50 crores for the current financial year. 
31. The scope of the project is to establish a second launch pad at Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. The second 
launch pad will cater to the current versions of Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) and Geo-Synchronous Satel­
lite Launch Vehicte (GSLV). It will also have provision for suitable augmentation at a later date for GSLV variants to 
increase GTO payload to 4 tonne class and for advanced launch vehicles being studied to further enhance GTO 
payload above 6 tonne. The Committee was further informed about the various activities which the Department 
proposes to initiate during the period 1998-99.

study of ocean biological parameters and a Multi-frequency Scanning Microwave Radiometer (MSMR) for meas­
uring Sea Surface Temperature (SST) and meteorological parameters like atmospheric water vapour and sea sur­
face wind speed. The data obtained from this satellite will be used for deriving certain physical and biological 
parameters of relevance to ocean development including fisheries. Many user Departments are actively associated 
in the Oc~nsat-1 Utilisation Plan. The user related activities are coordinated by the Department of Ocean Devel­
opment. 
32.VThe Committee was informed that the IRS-P5 (Cartosat-1) and IRS-P6 (Resourcesat) Projects were 
approved in August, 1997 only and hence, the original financial allocation made in the budget estimates for 1997-
98 could not be fully utilised last year, as some of the procurement activities could not be completed on time. 
However, currently most of the procurement related activities relate to IRS-P5 particularly the materials, compo­
nents and high value contractual items have already reached an advanced stage and are expected to materialise 
during this financial year. It is expected that the spacecraft sub-systems development will also be completed this 
year as planned. In the case of IRS-P6, activities related to procurement of parts and materials as well as sub ­
system fabrication have been initiated. Hence it is anticipated that during the financial year 1998-99, the allocated

neurs/industries to provide value added services in the remote sensing and GIS.

B. Development and Educational Communication Unit (DECU) is engaged in mass communication soft ­
ware including television programmes with a developmental orientation, communications research and training 
programmes. 
33.1 The Committee was ir.formed that in 1998-99 financial allocation of Rs. 5.89 crores has been made for

37. The Committee was infonned that M/s Antrix Corporation of the Department of Space is marketing Indian

39. The Committee was told that the Indian Space Research Organisation has been encouraging active 
participation of Indian industries in the execution of space projects with a view to harnessing the potential existmg 
with the industry. The co-operative ventures with the industries have been promoted through transfer of technolo­
gies to industry, provision for technological Consultancy from space programme to industry and procurement of 
materials from Indian industry and fonning out fabrication contracts. So far, 231 technologies have been trans­
ferred to industries and more than 180 consultancy projects have been undertaken. Over 500 small, medium and 
large scale industries are involved including both Public Sector as well as Private Sector industries viz., HAL, 
BEL, BHEL, KELTRON, M/s. Godrej, L&T, Walchandnagar industries, Andlfra Sugars, etc.

40. The Committee wanted to know if there would be any effect of sanctions annou nced by the G-8 countries 
on the Department and whether any of its ongoing programme would suffer on account of these sanctions. 
40.1 The Committee was told that so far there has been no clarity on the details of the sanction and the response 
of US and European companies for the sanctions is yet to get crystallised. However, sanctions are not new to ISRO 
and space programme has placed thrust on self-relia nce through indigenous development of strategic items over 
the years. Already 23 different types of materials and about 24 types of passive electron ic components have been 
developed and qualified for use In our space programmes. Major efforts on development of critical items like 
CCDs, TWTAs, high efficiency Solar Cells, high power microwave devices, etc. are in progress. Efforts are also 
made on Identifying alternate sources for procurement for programme critical components for parallel ordering.

approximately). The ISRO has international cooperation agreement and joint international projects with several 
countries/space agencies like European Space Agency, French Space Agency, Gennan Aero Space Research Es­
tablishment, etc. which have not been affected.

for urban area town planning, etc. and wanted to know as to what the Department is doing for publicising its activi­
ties, particularly in the developmental and socio-economic sectors. The Committee was infonned that ISRO infor­

R E P O R T
General Background
 
1.         Science and Technology has had a long and rich tradition in India. Even in ancient times, India is known to have
 made pioneering contributions in the areas like mathematics, astronomy and chemistry. Iron-pillar situated near Qutab
 Minar is an eloquent testimony to the great advances made in the field of metallurgy in ancient India. From towards the
 end of the last century and during the first half of the present century, science in India witnessed a period of renaissance
 when India produced renowned scientists like J.C.Bose, S. Ramanujan, C.V. Raman, S.N. Bose, Meghnad Saha, P.C.
 Mahalanobis, Birbal Sahni, H.J. Bhabha, S.Chandrasekhar and others who are known for their path-breaking
 contributions in the areas of basic research.
 
2.         Spectacular achievements made in the field of science and technology during the last century brought about
 unprecedented economic growth and social transformation in the industrialised countries. This led to the creation of a
 favourable climate for science and technology being made a part of the national endeavour in developing countries as
 well. Governments in developing countries started paying increasing attention to science and technology on the
 assumption that an indigenous scientific and technological base would bring faster economic development and social
 transformation.
 
3.         After Independence, India also decided to use science and technology as a key instrument in the process of
 nation-building particularly through the vision and initiative of Jawaharlat Nehru. At the time of Independence, the
 scientific and technological base in India was neither properly organised nor capable enough to take on major national
 challenge. It was, therefore, decided to give special attention to create the necessary infrastructure for the development
 o4 science and technology in India. Various institutions and a network of laboratories for conducting research in
 specialised areas were established. Ministry of Scientific Research and Natural Resources was created by the
 Government of India in 1951 for organising and directing scientific research for national development.
 
4.         A symbol of the Government's forward-looking thinking in promoting science in the country was the adoption of
 the Scientific Policy Resolution in 1958 which aimed at securing for the people of the country all the benefits that can
 accrue from the acquisition and application of scientific knowledge. The Resolution aimed at producing research
 scientists of the highest quality in the country and introducing programmes for training scientific and technical
 personnel on a scale adequate to fulfil the country's need in areas like Health Education, Agriculture, Industry, Defence,
 etc.
 
5.         The Department of Science and Technology (DST) was, therefore, set up in 1971 with a view to providing a
 "nodal department for organising, coordinating and promoting science and technology (S&T) activities in which a
 number of institutions and Departments have interests and capabilities". This, of course, does not cover the specific
 programmes in fields such as atomic energy and space for which Government has specially set up Departments and
 Commissions. Major roles assigned to DST involve promoting new areas of science and technology and formulating
 policy statements and guidelines on S&T. The Department has since undertaken various projects and programmes for
 this purpose, such as providing support to basic and applied research; critical technology programmes; socially oriented
 S&T activities for
rural areas and weaker sections; and entrepreneurship development with a view to creating self-employment
 opportunities.

6.         In order to assess whether the DST is fulfilling its mandate effectively and efficiently, the Committee decided to
 study the various aspects of the functioning of the Department by analysing its Annual Report for the year 1992-93.
 
7.         The Committee was informed about various programmes and activities undertaken by DST for development of
 S&T and coordination of multi-institutional and inter-disciplinary activities at the national level. The Department also
 undertakes various societal programmes to help people in rural areas and weaker sections of society. It is also rendering
 scientific services such as collection and supply of meteorological .and seismic data to different user agencies and
 departments of the Government. Besides, these, the Department is also looking after various autonomous high quality
 research institutions and professional bodies throughout the country. The Department is promoting scientific research in
 frontline and priority areas of Research and Development (R&D) in various disciplines of science and technology by
 funding those through the mechanism of science and Engineering Research Council (SERC). SERC supports and
 monitors R&D efforts in new and inter-disciplinary areas by providing financial assistance, setting up of core groups
 and establishing national facilities required for promoting a given discipline of S&T. During the year 1992-93, SERC
 approved 155 projects costing Rs.22.96 crores in different areas of S&T. The Committee was informed about the
 'Young Scientists Scheme' meant for providing opportunities for pursuing exciting and innovative ideas 'by young
 scientists.
 
8.         The Committee was also given an idea about the multi-disciplinary activities of the National Centre for Medium
 Range Weather Forecasting and Development of Agro-meteorological Advisory Services which aim at the
 development of the capability of issuing medium range (3-10 days in advance) weather forecasting mainly for
 preparation of the weather based advisories for the farming community and dissemination of the same to the users.
 
9. The Committee was also informed about the support and facilities provided by the Department for science promotion
 through the initiation of several schemes such as the Regional Sophisticated Instrumentation Centres (RSICs),
 Sophisticated Instrumentation Facilities (SI Fs), National Coordination of Testing and Calibration Facilities (NCTC),
 support to State S&T Councils to professional bodies for various S&T activities. One Department also provides
 assistance for international travel to participate in scientific seminars and symposia.
 
10.       In the area of technology development, DST has evolved certain schemes intended to accelerate growth of
 indigenous capability such as Instrument Development programme, Robitics and Automation, Biomedical engineering,
 Cryogenics, Ceramics, etc. "Critical Technology Programme" is a new initiative to support selected activities conducive
 to strengthening technological capabilities of the country. The Technology Information Forecasting & Assessment
 Council (TIFAC) generates Technology Forecast and Technology Assessment documents in various areas. 'A number
 of technology forecasting, technology assessment and techno-market survey studies were conducted by the TIFAC in
 prioritised areas. DST has also set up a Science & Technology Advisory Committee (STAC) with a view to formulating
 long term S&T plans/ programmes relevant to concerned sectors.
 
11.       As regards the programmes involving international cooperation in scientific and technological fields the
 Committee was informed that DST has the nodal responsibility of coordinating international collaborations. Such
 programmes are in operation at bilateral, regional and multilateral levels. Agreement for cooperation in S&T has been
 signed with Hungary, Ukraine, Uzbekistan, Poland, Italy, Mangolia and Israel during the year 1992-93. Multilateral
 programmes on S&T including regional cooperation programmes and those involving UN and other international
 agencies are also being looked after by DST.
 
12.       Application of science and technologyfor the benefit of society is one of the important concerns of DST. Several
 experimental projects were undertaken by the Department in the past with a view to demonstrating the changes that
 could be brought about by S&T in improving the living conditions of the rural people and those of the women and other
 weaker sections of society.
 
13.       Activities connected with science communications and popularisation and National Science and Technology
 Entrepreneurship Development were also promoted by the
 Department. The Bharat Jan Gyan Vigyan Jatha (BJGVJ-92) communication event, which could directly address a
 large number of people in various parts of the country touching nearly a fourth of the population . The programme
 informed on some of the basic problems like water, nutrition; health, environment and literacy. The 144 - part radio

 14.       Besides, DST provides operational services in the field of meteorology and surveys
 through India Meteorological Department (IMD), Survey of India (SOI) and National Atlas

 the introduction of sophisticated equipments. With the help of widely distributed INSAT-based

 for defence mid developmental purposes. It has been carrying out geodetic and geophysical

 provides valuable services in the preparation of thematic maps. The Department also supports
 a number of autonomous research and academic institutions which are working in areas like
 medical science, plasma physics, palaeobotany, astronomy, astrophysics, geo-magnetism,
 Himalayan geology and climatology, etc.
 
Role of DST
 15.       When asked about the role and overall impact of DST in the promotion of S&T
 activities, the representative of the Department informed the Committee that DST was supposed to promote scientific
 research and development technology-related programmes and that it was also mandated to constitute the S&T inputs
 into society-related programmes. He informed the Committee that there was no single agency in the Government which
 was solely responsible for implementing society-related programmes. There are many departments/ agencies involved
 in it. In this regard Secretary, DST observed:
 
If we have to have the impact of demonstrations what is important is to make DST more effective in
 participating in the programmes of other departments .... there are large number of programmes. If coordination
 can be ensured, if effectiveness can be ensured whether it is the Ministry of Welfare or the Ministry of Rural
 Development, then we can make the impact.
 
In view of the observations made by the Secretary, DST, the Committee feels that the DST should dovetail its
 efforts not only with scientific departments but also with such Ministries/Departments like Railways, Defence,
 Communications, Commerce, Industry, etc. The Department should also coordinate its activities with the other socio-
economic Ministries. Whilst this is being attempted, the real success of S&T for national development will come about
 when this coordination can be made most effective.
 
Allocation of Funds :
 
16.       The Committee noticed that while the Annual Plans allocation for the DST during 1990-92 was Rs.274.20
 crores, actuals for the period were Rs.240.06 crores only. In other words, actuals were Rs.34.14 crores less than the
 allocation for this period. Attention of the Committee was drawn towards the fact that the allocation to the Department
 constituted just 0.2% of the total Central Sector outlay during the Sixth Plan. It went slightly up to 0.36% in the
 Seventh Plan. This share has further come down in the Eighth Plan. The Secretary, DST, also informed the Committee
 that of the total allocation made to the Department, a lion's share is being spent on the India Meteorological Department
 and Survey of India. Besides, DST is also required to support 13 autonomous research institutions like Raman Research
 Institute, Indian Institute of Astrophysics, etc. Thus, the remaining funds are not sufficient to fulfil the mandate
 assigned to it. The Committee, therefore, realises that the DST is working under severe financial constraints, and that
 with present level of allocation, it was difficult for the Department to promote effectively the mandate assigned to it.
 The Committee took particular notice of the financial paucity for carrying out R&D activities and various society-

related programmes. The Committee was told that any of the society-related programmes did not have more than Rs.4
 crores. Since these programmes are committed to supporting a large number of core groups, this amount is not
 sufficient. The Committee feels that there is need to spend more in the field of S&T. The Government should,
 therefore, make a realistic assessment of the financial requirements of the DST keeping in view the obligations which it
 has to fulfil and make suitable allocation to the Department.
 
17.       Survey of India and India Meteorological Department are huge organisations employing 17042 and 8307
 persons, respectively. This is needed in their cases as they are all India service organisations with considerable
 technical and field work. DST has a sanctioned strength of 757. The staff strength of DST, since it includes the
 personnel of IMD and SOI naturally conveys the impression that the Department is organised like any other
 administrative department of the Government rather than a scientific department which normally is expected to be very
 compact and highly scientific and officer-oriented. The Committee, however, is of the view that the ministerial strength
 of DST is also large for the role it has to play. The Committee, therefore, recommends that DST should organise itself
 in such a manner as may facilitate it to devote the bulk of its funds on scientific and research activities.
 
Technology Fee :
 
18.       The Committee is also of the view that a part of the fund could be raised from various beneficiaries of the
 technologies developed by DST. When asked about collecting something like development cess as was being done in
 the case of sugar and coal, the Secretary, DST had this to say :
 
"Fortunately for us we have what is known as technology fee which is being levied. Every import of
 technology requires a fee to be paid .... commodity cess is usually used by the corresponding socio-
economic Ministries more for the purpose of expansion of their activities. So, if we use the amount for
 the promotion of technology development and the DST has to perform that role, it will be very good.
 This is one cess to which we would like to have access. This is now being levied as part of the
 technology growth in the country. Industries are importing technology and in the liberalised
 environment, more and more imports will take place and there is a five per cent cess which is being paid
 towards those imports of technology. If we can have access to this, then we really don't have to trouble
 or burden the Planning Commission."
 
In view of the above, Committee feels that the Government may examine the feasibility of implementing the
 suggestion of allowing DST to have access to the technology fee; but there would have to be careful monitoring of the
 use to which funds' are put.
 
Research and Development (R&D) :
 
19.       Research and Development in various disciplines of S&T forms one of the important activities of the DST. Basic
 objectives of the R&D activities cover integrated research programmes in inter-disciplinary fields, frontier areas in
 science and engineering, encouraging brilliant young scientists and promoting general research capabilities in relevant
 areas of S&T. National R&D programmes are supported by DST involving a number of academic and research
 institutions, professional bodies and other socio-economic departments of the Government. Industrial R&D forms an
 important component of overall R&D activities in the country in which both the Public and the Private Sectors are
 involved. As regards the state of Industry-related R&D in India, the Committee was informed that of the total national
 R&D expenditure (Rs.4186.43 crores) during 1990-91, 68.9% came from Central Government, 7.9% from State
 Governments, 10.6% was contributed by public sector industries and 12.6% by the private sector industries. The major
 share of national expenditure on R&D was thus met from government sources (87.4%) and the rest 12,6% came from
 the private industries.
 
The Committee notices that this ratio is just the reverse in the developed economies such as Korea and Japan. In
 Korea, for example, in 1988, government share in the expenditure on R&D was just 18.1°/o and that of the private
 sector was 81.9%. Similarly, in Japan, this ratio was 20% and 80% respectively during the same year. The Committee
 feels that the share of private sector industries in R&D activities in India is far more less, particularly when the various
 incentives have been given to them. There is a need to raise standard of industrial research with a view to meeting the

 changing economic situation and to see that the country competes with others. Achieving this would certainly require
 substantial financial input which, as things stand today, is not possible, unless the private sector industries which are
 making use of expertise and technology developed by DST and its various centres, gives part of its cost back to the
 nation. The Committee, therefore, suggests that efforts should be made to motivate private industries to put more
 money into industry-related R&D activities. The Committee feels that by doing so a close linkage between Science-
industry-university can also be established.
 
Technology Information, Forecasting & Assessment Council:
 
20.       Technology Information, Forecasting & Assessment Council (TIFAC) has the primary mandate to generate
 Technology Forecasting (TF) and Technology Assessment (TA) documents in various technology areas and establish
 an on-line nationally accessible technology information system. The Committee noted the fact that according to the
 Department TA/TF studies have been completed in some areas like sugarcane and sugar production technologies,
 biotechnology, electronic technologies, aviation, etc., the tempo in implementing various programmes relating to
 TA/FF on an overall basis has not caught up; and even in the areas where work has been taken up, the depth is not
 adequate. The Committee is of the view that further major initiatives are required to be taken by the TIFAC to create an
 impact in this regard.
 
International Cooperation :
 
21.       On the question of international cooperation in the areas of science and technology, particularly at the bilateral
 level, the Committee was informed that such cooperation could play a prominent role in R&D activities at a relatively
 low cost. A great impetus can, therefore, be provided to S&T activities by seeking cooperation of the advanced
 countries. In this connection the representative of the Department gave the example of India's cooperation with Israel
 under which there would be a 3 million dollar Joint fund contributed equally by both the governments. It has been
 proposed that the projects to be taken up under this scheme should be decided by experts not by government officials.
 Similarly, a research centre has been set up in Hyderabad in cooperation with Bylorussia, where coating of blades of
 aircrafts has been started. This used to be earlier got done in England which involved a considerable amount of foreign
 exchange. In view of the benefits accruing from the international cooperation the Committee emphasises the need for
 building broad based R&D infrastructure even with foreign help and cooperation which would be advantageous to the
 country to make use of its comparatively inexpensive scientific manpower.
 
Brain Drain :
 
22.       Most of our young scientists and engineers who go abroad for higher study do not come back even after
 completing their studies. When Committee enquired about their number and employment profile, etc. it was informed
 that no such data was available with the Government. Department of Science & Technology, however, had sponsored
 some pilot-studies at IIT, Delhi and AIIMS, New Delhi yielding some estimates in this regard. For example, it was
 found that about 30% of the graduates from IIT had migrated abroad where most of them worked as practising research
 engineers and scientists. Similarly, the overall brain drain from AIIMS for the period 1956 to 1980 was 50% with a
 decreasing trend from 1971 onwards. The magnitude varied from 3% in 1980 to 89% in 1967. The field of work of
 those settled abroad had shown that 84% were in clinical practice, 30% in teaching and 19% in research, etc. The
 Committee feels that a poor country like India can ill-afford the drain of trained engineers, scientists and doctors,
 particularly when the country spends scarce money on training them. The Committee desires that the government
 should study the phenomenon of brain drain and evolve effective strategies to convince and motivate our scientists and
 engineers to come back after completing their studies abroad and furthermore, devise measures whereby we can make
 use of our scientists located abroad who desire to help in development of science and technology in our country and
 thereby contribute to the development.
 
Bharat Jan Gyan Vigyan Jatha (BJGVJ) :
 
23.       When asked about BJGVJ and post-Jatha activities, the Committee was informed in a written reply that during
 the Jatha period, over 400 Jathas in 375 districts touching nearly one-fourth of the population of the country were
 organised. Each district had its own Jatha covering 100 villages. Some 2500 volutarty agencies and other government

 activities and identifying local problems and mobilisation of people for the possible solution of the same. Thereafter, a
 Mass Action For National Regeneration would be launched. Programme planned for this might include, inter alia, basic
