54. Asked about the degree of precision in our weather forecast s as compared to 
western countries like UK and USA and whether our weather forecasts lack precision as 
compared to those countries, the Comm ittee was informed that the overall percentage 
accuracy of different types of short range weather forecasts i.e. forecast s valid upto 3 days 
including cyclone warn ings issued by IMD is of the order of 80%. Infact , the accuracy of the 
cyclone warnings with respect to its landfall points and associated disastrous weather is even ·· 
more and considered reasonably good. It was further stated that taking into account 

the excellence of cyclone forecasting by IMD, the World Meteorological Organization 
(WMO) has recognised New Delhi as a Regional Special ised Meteorological Centre on 
Tropical Cyclones alongwith Tokyo (Japan) and Miami (U.S.A.) 
55. The Long Range Forecast (LRF) of monsoon rainfall over the country has been 
found quite accurate every year since 1988 onwards when the indigenously developed LRF 
model was introduced by IMD. IMD is constantly striving to develop different LRF models 
for regional basis forecasts for different agroclimatic regions. 
56. UK & USA being extra-tropical countries are having more systematic weather 
phenomena as compared to the countries of tropical belt such as India. The tropical 
weather, which is dominated by meso-scale convective process, is difficult to forecast. Even ' 
in the case of countries like USA. there have been errors in forecasting stom1 tracks. 
Despite these limitations, India has been recognised by the developed coutnries including 
WMO that IMD's forecasting capabilities are one of the best in the world. 
57. In reply to a question whether it was a fact that some of the tragedies resulting from 
cyclones and hail storms etc. particularly in places like coastal areas of Andhra Pradesh 
could have been averted had our weather forecast been precise and timely; the Committee 
was informed that the cyclones are detected as soon as they form in the Indian seas with the 
help of INSA T series of satellites and constantly remain under surveillance till they approach 
Indian Coastline where they fall, in the grip of an overlapping chain of cyclone detection 
radars installed on east and west coasts of the country. No cyclone goes undetected with 
present system of observational netwnrk. 
58: The tragedies do occur sometimes bacause tropical cyclo111.:s particularly those of 
very severe intensity are natural phenomena with ext remely high potential for damage to 
property and Joss of life. The system is being constantly modernised with the latest state-of­
the-art technologies. Every effort is made by the State and Central Government agencies 
responsible for mitigation to reduce loss of life.

81. On a question on the revision of the Scientific Policy Resolution of 1958, the 
Committee was informed that the Scientific Policy Resolution does not require any major 
changes and is still valid. The Technology Policy Statement, however, requires some 
modifications keeping in view the changed scenario both at global and national level and the 
modifications required are under consideration. 
82. The Committee observes that the Government should have a comprehensive review of 
the Technt)JogicaJ· Policy Statement with a view to decide whether to have a consolidated 
technological policy or different Policies-~>ne for promotion of Science and the other for 
Technology. 
SCIENCE AND ·ENGINEERING RESEARCR COUNCIL (SERC) 
83. The Council ' was constituted with the primary objectives: 
(i) To promote research in newly emerging and front ier areas of science and 
engineer~ng including multidisciplinary fields. 
(ii) To selectively promote th~ genera~ resea rch capab ility in relevant areas of 
science a~d engineering taking int<> account. capab ility of the host institute. 
(iii) To 'enco~rage .y.oung scie~tists · to . take up challenging R&D activitie·s. 
·(iv) To give special encouragement ·.· to project s from less endowed university 
departments. 
(v) To encourage patenting facilities to scientists and technologies in the country 
for Indian and foreign patents on a sustained basis. 
84. The Science & Engineering Research Council is an apex body consisting of eminent 
Scientists from Universities, National laboratory and industry. 
... \ 
85. The Science and Engineering Research Council (S,eRC) continued to support 
research projects in challenging fields of Science and Eng ineering and encouraged Young 
Scientists .to take up research as a career. The programmes supported under SERC are 

distinctly different from those that are supported by specialised agencies. During the year 
under report, some of the important initiatives taken to promote R&D programmes are as 
fo11ows: 
• "SERC Students Fellowships" 
• "SERC Chairs" in key fields of Science and Engineering in Academic Sectors. 
Enhancement of Research Fellowships of JRF/SRFIRA 
• Funds for Improvement of Infrastructure in Universities and other Academic Sectors 
(FIST) 
• Kishore Vigyanik Protsahan Yojana 
86. The DST could spend Rs. 57.58 crores (Rs. 56.28 Plan and Rs. 1.30 crores Non­
Plan) in the year 1997-98. The allocation enhanced to Rs. 58.32 at BE stage (Plan Rs. 57.00 
crores and Non-Plan Rs. 1.32 crores) of the year 1998-99 with further enhancement to Rs. 
58.13 crores (Plan Rs. 56.94 crores and Non-Plan Rs. 1.19 crores) in RE of 1998-99. The 
Department has asked for an outlay of Rs. 70.54 crores (Rs. 69.25 crores Plan and Rs. 1.29 
crores Non-Plan) for the said programme for the year 1999-2000. 
87. The Committee notes that despite the increase in allocation for Science and 
Engineering Rese~rch Council (SERC) the number of projects supported by it has come 
down by about one third. The Department has explained this due to the change in rupee­
dollar parity increasing the cost of equipments and also due to increase in the fellowship­
amount and travel costs etc. 
88. The Committee feels that there is a need for quantum increase in funding for the 
SERC related activities to maintain the momentum in fundamental research. 
89. After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Science and 
Technology and assessing the progress of various important programmes and projects 
administered by it, the Committee recommends that the Demands for Grants of Rs. 654.63 
crores, as sought by the Department of Science and Technology, for the year 1999-2000 
under Demand No. 73, may be approved.

REPORT 
The Department of Ocean Development, since its inception in July, 1981, has directed its 
programmes towards development and use of science and technology for the sustainable and 
environment friendly exploration and exploitation of marine resources for the socio­
economic benefit of the country. Its technology development programmes are for future 
application~ with strategic, industrial and economic significance. 
2. The Department of Ocean Development is a nodal Department for orgamzmg, 
coordinating and promoting ocean development activities in the country. The national level 
R&D laboratories, educational institutions and industries assist the Department in carrying 
out its multi-disciplinary and multi-institutional plans and programmes of national 
importance. Further, marine research and capacity building is one of the key areas of the 
Department to promote basic research in marine science for self-reliance. 
3. The programmes of the Department which have been reoriented and revamped during 
the Ninth Five Yeur Plan period cover Polar (Antarctic) Science, Marine Living Resources, 
Marine Non-Living Resources, Ocean Observation & Information Services, Marine and 
Coastal Area Management, Marine Research and Capacity Building, Coastal Community 
Programmes, Ocean Awareness and International Cooperation. It has been stated that while 
formulating the research and development programmes, stress is laid on accelerated 
development of applied technology so that benefits continue to accrue to the society. 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
4. The Department proposed an outlay of Rs. 656 crore for the Eighth Five Year Plan 
period. But the Planning Commission allocated Rs. l30 crore only as indicative outlay. 
Later, based on the requirement!i of various programmes, a sum of Rs. 224 crore was 
provided against which the expenditure was about Rs. 200 crore. During the Eighth Five 
Year Plan, the strategic areas such as Antarctic Research, Polymetallic Nodules Programmes 
and International Cooperation Programmes received priority in terms of fund allocation 
amounting to a total of 66 per cent, followed by Societal Programmes 21 per cent, Scien:ific 
and Technological Development Programmes 8 per cent and Basic Research 5 per cent. 
5. The Secretary, DOD informed the Committee that the Ninth Five Year Plan has since 
been approved by the National Development Council (NDC). The Planning Commission, 
however, has informed that the Cabinet has approved an outlay of Rs. 510.62 crore in 
respect of the Department's Plan schemes for the Ninth Plan period. The break up of the 
outlay is given in Annexure-!. 
6. The Plan outlay for 1999-2000 is Rs. 90.00 crore and a Non-Plan outlay of Rs. 20.88 
crore. The Department would thus have a total outlay of Rs. 110.88 crore against the 
Rs. 107.41 crore (Plan as well as Non-Plan) allocated at RE stzge for 1998-99. Thus there is 
a marginal increase of Rs. 3.47 crore as compared to the anticipated expenditure for 
1998-99. The comparative figures in terms of actual expenditures for various programmes of 
the Department for 1996-97, 1997-98 and 1998-99 are given in Annexure- II and the financial 
allocations earmarked for 1999-2000 have been brought out in Annexure-III.

7. The Department projected an outlay of Rs. 140 crore which was reduced to Rs. 90 
crore by the Planning Commission, due to the resource crunch. Accordingly, the 
Department has revised the budget estimates by differing/scaling down some of the 
programmes/projects. The programmes likely to be affected are Antarctic Research, 
Metallurgy component of Polymetallic Nodules and Ocean Energy Mission of National 
Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT) and on Delineation of the outer limits of Continental 
Shelf. Thus, an additional outlay of Rs. 35.92 crore is required at revised estimates (RE) 
stage of the current financial year-Rs. 5.42 crore for Antarctic Research, Rs. 10 crore for 
Metallurgy Pilot Plant, Rs. 1.00 crore for Drugs from Sea, Rs. 5.00 crore for Ocean Energy 
Mission and Rs. 14.50 crore for Delineation of Continental Shelf. 
NON-PLAN EXPENDITURE 
8. The Non-Plan expenditure broadly falls under four heads, namely (i) ORY Sagar 
Kanya; (ii) FORV Sagar Sampada; (iii) Secretariat and Economic Services; and 
(iv) Administrative infrastructure. The major increase in the Non-Plan expenditure is against 
ORV Sagar Kanya which was acquired in 1984. It is a sophisticated research vessel which 
has been carrying out survey and exploration of marine non-living resources particularly in 
the field of physical and chemical oceanography, marine biology, meteorology, marine 
geophysics, marine geology, etc. It provides a common platform to the National Institute/ 
Laboratories in the field of Oceanographic research. 
9. The Committee was informed that during 1998-99 the ORY Sagar Kan ya conducted 
13 scientific cruises both in the Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal. The scientific investigations/ 
research carried out by ORY Sagar Kanya during 1998-99 include data collected from sea 
for validating satellite derived oceanic parameters; deployment, retrieval and servicing of the 
shallow and deep water data buoys in the Arabian Sea under the National Data Buoy 
Programme; bathymetric data collection in Arabian Sea for delineation of outer limits of 
continental shelf; multidisciplinary experiments under the INDOEX programme; BOBMEX 
pilot project in the Bay of Bengal for Monsoon Experimental studies; trial testing of various 
sub-systems of the crawler at shallow depth; and Lar}d Ocean Interaction in Coastal Zone 
(LOICZ) studies for comprehending climate change induced reactions in the coastal regions. 
10. The Secretary, DOD, informed the Committee that an enhanced budget provision in 
the Non-Plan sector would be required for operation and maintenance of ORV Sagar Kanya 
and FORV Sagar Sampada which were about 15 years old necessitating replacement of both 
the deck machinery and other essential equipment/instruments. The allocation of Rs. 9.48 
crore and Rs. 7.50 crore made for operation and management of ORV Sagar Kanya and 
FORV Sagar Sampada respectively during 1999-2000 is the barest minimum as against the 
required amount of Rs. 43.00 crore. This has resulted in accumulation of huge amounts of 
payments over the years to be made to Shipping Corporation of India, which run s the 
vessels. 
11. Th~ task of survey is to locate and map the resource potential of living and non-living 
resources by ORV Sagar Kanya and FORV Sagar Sampada. This will have to he continued 
for collection of enormous oceanographic data and information and exploration activity which 
are essential in or~er to understand various oceanographic phenomena. The Committee feels 
that an extra budgetary support is necessary for the programme to ensure continuity of the 
survey programme and avoid men and machinery being rendered idle. 

ANT ARCTIC RESEARCH PROGRAMME 
12. Tht: Indian Antarctic Programme and its scientific expeditions are held on annual basis 
with the launching of the first expedition to Antarctic in 1981. The first Indian research 
station , Dakshin Gangotri was commissioned in 1983 and replaced by the indigenously 
designed second Indian permanent station 'Maitri' in the Schirmacher Oasis in 1988. The 
Station 'Maitri' has adequate infra-structural facilities for conducting multi-faceted scientific 
research in Polar (Antarctic) Science::. While using An~m:tic a!\ a platform for conducting 
scientific experiments, India has always recognised the importance of preserving the pristine 
naturo.: of thi!\ remote and unique continent. In order to uphold thi!> commitment, India, an 
origin;tl 'otary of the Protocol on Environmental Protection to the Antarctic Treaty, has 
ratified thl.! Pn..Howl in April. 1996. 
13. The Committee was informed that so far 20 scientific expeditions have been 
launched on a regular basis whkh have carried research work in the thrust areas of polar 
sciem:t:, including an expedition to the weedell Sea and one for assessment of Antarctic 
Krill. During the year under reference the broad scientific and logistic activities planned to 
be undertaken are in continuation of studies on ozone, trace gases and aerosols of the 
Antarctic atmosphere using various state-of-the-art equipment; archival of meteorological 
parameters that can be employed for climatic modeling and prediction; experiments on solat 
terrestrial phenomenon like optical aurora and geo-magnetic perturbations; studies on 
adaptation techniques of human beings in adverse conditions; application and utiliz<ltioh of 
dean energy sources like wind and sun in Antarctica; experiments in Antarctic ice moss in 
relation to snowdrift patterns and snow albedo; up-gradation of communication facilities with 
special emphasis on real time picture transmission; and reorientation of waste discharge and 
handling facilities. Towards the end of 1999, the Nineteenth Indian Antarctic Expedition 
would be launched for carrying out contemporary research in the fields of atmospheric, 
geological, biological, environmental, medical sciences, engineering and commuRication. 
During the year 1999-2000, in order to continue the scientific activities, it would be 
necessary to continue the chartering of the ice-breaker along with other logistics in the 
research station. 
14. The Department proposed an outlay of Rs. 25.42 crore towards the annual 
expedition to Antarctica, scientific pro~rmnmes and strengthening the facilities at research 
station in Antarctica - "Muitri" and for facility augmentation and operation of the 
Antarctic Study Centre at Goa. Due w paucity of reso~rces outlay has been reduced to 
Rs. 20.00 crore by deferring some of the scientific programmes and phasing out some of the 
R&D facilities. The Committee was given to understand that an upward revision by Rs. 5.42 
crore at RE stage would help in promoting the interaction of our scientists with the scientific 
community abroad and in undertaking joint cooperative programmes. 
15. Antarctic Study Centre (ASC) at Goa, which had an attached office of the 
Department of Ocean Development, has been transformed into an autonomous institute 
from September, 1998. The Centre is responsible for in-house R & D activities in polar 
sciences and for coordinating expedition activities to Antarctic. Besides , the Centre is 
responsible for developing expertise in the field of polar sciences and logistics through 
activities such as coordination and execution of the entire scientific and logistic activities of 
the Antarctic expeditions, establish and maintain a research base in Antarctic and provide all 
operational and logistic support and encourage cooperative research both at national and 
international levels specially in the area of Global Change. 

16. A S rega rds in-hou se R&D activities, the Centre is conducting research on clima te 
modelin g, sea- ice-ocea n-atmosphere c oupling , monit oring all issues a rising o ut of the 
Environmental Protocol, develop ing a complete data base invento ry a nd rep osito ry for 
An tarctic a nd Arctic science and logistics, generatin g s pecialised manpowe r for polar science 
and logistics and cruise plann ing and management of,the Oceanograp hic resea rch vessels. 
17. Over the years the Antarctic Programme has generated valuable data w hich would be 
useful in future . Besides, the programm e has gained internation al importance in as much as it 
has provided internation al interaction among countri es to shar e their experience s in an 
atmo sphere of mutual friend ship. The Committee , therefore , feels that this programm e s hould 
not be allowed to suffer for wan t of funds. 
DRUGS FROM THE SEA 
18. The Na tional Project on "Drugs from the Sea" initiate d during 1990-91 is a multi­
institution al proje ct on devel opment of p oten tial dru gs and chemicals from marine organisms 
which was funded under R & D prog ramme till the end of Phase- 11 (1995-96). The 
Comm ittee was informe d tha t during the period 1998-99, 15 new marine flora and .53 fauna 
were collected for general biologica l s creening. I n order to confi rm biological activity and 
follow-up stud ies, repeat collect ion of 7 6 flora and 40 fauna was made which has yielded 
valuab le clues for develop ing potent dru gs. 
19. T he Depa rtment propose d an outlay of Rs. 3.00 crore for 1999-2000, it was reduced 
to Rs.1.60 crore due to financial crunch. The project has completed Phase-I II . It will enter 
the crucial Phase- IV from 1999-2000 onwards. In Phase-III, the resea rch activ ities have led 
to ide ntification of five marine organisms having potent ial properties as anti-d iabetic, anti­
viral, anti-anxiety, anti-cholesterol and larvicidal agents for develop ing new drugs du ring the 
Ninth Plan period. In Phase -IV, steps would be taken to investigate further and release new 
drugs developed from marine flora and fauna under Phase- Ill. Chemical trials are expected 
to be complete for anti-diabetic (CDR -134) drug. It has now been observed that the same 
lead has antidiabetic as well as anti-diarrhoeal propert ies. The Drug is as good as the 
standard antidiabetic drug like Phonformin and better than Tolbutamide. Also commercial 
work for patenting anti-cholesterol lead would be initiated. 
20. While the Committee appreciates the work being done by the Department in 
developing the drugs from Sea, it observes that a large number of multinational as well as 
Indian companies are engaged in researc h in this field in different systems of medicines. 
Medicines coming to market from these companies have largely a profit motive at th~ir back. 
The Committee therefore feels that a mere addition of a drug in the market would not serve 
the purpose. The country has a large potential of resources, be they in the form of herbs 
grown in forests or in other forms of natural deposits in the vast sea bed. A large number of 
diseases should be curable once for all. It should also be possible ~0 prevent the diseases by 
either preserving the natural force in the body or by restoring it with the help of medicines, 
as Hahneman, the founder of Homoeopathy put it. Our belief in Hahneman's principle of 
Similia Similibus Curenter (i.e. likes are treated by likes) is further strengthened because of 
the vast amount of natural resources available in our country. The Committee, therefore, 
observes that whatever number of drugs are taken up for research and development they 
should aim at excellence by curing the diseases once for all. The programme on research for 
these medicines should be time bound, well-knit to avoid delays and should not he allowed to 
suffer for want of funds otherwise it may lose its significance in the fast changing world. 

POLYMETALLIC NODULES PROGRAMME (PNP) 
21. In 1987, India was accorded the status of Registered Pioneer Investor and started 
the Polymetallic Nodules Programme (PNP). Considerable progress has since been made in 
the country in resource identification and evaluation, technology and manpower 
development towards exploitation of these resources. However, presently, this programme 
has been expanded to develop technologies for deep-sea mining and metallurgy for recovery 
of metals, etc . 
22. The major activities proposed to be undertaken during the current financial year are 
Survey & Exploration in the Central Indian Ocean Basin (CIOB) for spot sampling of 
nodules using grab sampler and updating of geo-statistical resource evaluation in the pioneer 
areas, ·Benthic disturbance and impact assessment studies in the Indian Pioneer Area', 
prepared on baseline benthic conditions. Besides, under Technology Development (Mining) 
programme activities would be undertaken for demonstrating shallow bed mining system 
along the coast. Also the work relating to development of manipulator for underwater 
operation and testing of materials for deep-sea operation would be undertaken including 
initiating a joint programme between NlOT and Russian Academy of Science, Moscow for 
design, development and testing of unmanned submersibles operational unto 6000 meter 
depth. An outlay of Rs.8.35 crore has been provided for this programme. 
23. Also initiatives will be made under Technology Development (Metallurgy) for 
carrying out demonstration campaigns to validate the data obtained from earlier campaigns 
and designing and development of semi-continuous demonstration pilot plant of 500 kg/day 
capacity at Hindustan Zinc Ltd. (Udaipur). Due to resource limitation, financial outlay for 
the Pilot Plant is kept at Rs.5.15 crore with a request to HZ Ltd. to advance the money and 
go ahead with the project. However, a final understanding is yet to be reached since the 
matter is under consideration of HZ Ltd. Thus, the Department will have to meet the entire 
expenditure of HZ Ltd. subject to the ceilings for which EFC approval exists. The activities 
proposed to be undertaken during the current year are part of the long-term activities 
planned under the programme fot which the tot ·1l financial outlay is Rs.14.05 crore. 
24. The Committee was apprised that Polymetallic Nodule Programme is still in 
experimental stage. Therefore, commercial exploitation of polymetallic nodules may not be 
feasible for some more time. However , the technology for exploration and exploitation has 
been demonstrated. Thus, development of technologies for nodule mining purposes for the 
deep sea may be viewed as contribution to a long term objective . 
25. The Committee observes that the long gestation period, rapidly changing technology, 
economic priorities of the countries and economic importance of the material likely to be 
extracted as also the cost of extraction are some of the factors which are liable to affect the 
viability of the programme. A critical assessment of all these factors was necessary before w 
planning the programme. At this stage, the Committee feels that the programme having · 
commenced, it should not be allowed to suffer because of the reduction in the budgetary 
support for such a reduction would disrupt continuity, may render some of the assets idle and 
thus, in turn, push up the cost of the . project.

ISLAND DEVELOPMENT PROGRAMME 
44. ln the Ninth Five Year Plan, the Island Development Programme envisages to give 
impetus for achieving various charters oi the Department of Ocean Development in the fielj 
of demonstration of technology having a bear ing on the socio-economic aspects of the Island 
community. Accordingly, the set object ives of the programme are to demonstrate the 
technology of enhancement of marine living resources; demonstration of the technology for 
fattening, sea ranching and sea farming of lobster; and introduction of technology 
development programmes for sea farming of sea bass, ornamental fish, mud crab, etc. 
45. With the commissioning of a sea-front laboratory at Neelankarai, Chennai, and with 
the availability of strengthened infrastructure fa<;ilities at NIOT and AN COD, all three 
components of the Enhancement of Marine Living Resources project, under the Island 
Development Programme, namely breeding and rearing of lobsters, fattening studies and 
sea-farming and sea-reaching would be accelerated. Besides, it is also envisaged to take up 
new programmes on Ocean Env ironment and Conservation of Living Resources including 
coral reefs. 
46. The Comm ittee feels that a new awakening needs to be infused in the islao~s through 
the techno logy such as the Ocean technology and other employment oriented programmes so 
that they do not carry a feeling of neglect by the mainland. 

MARINE RESEARCH AND CAPACITY BUILDING 
47. The Department has been implementing the Marine Research and Manpower 
Development Programme with the active participation of educational institutions, National 
R&D Laboratories, etc. The objectives of the programme are to encourage research on 
physical and chemical processes, which govern the seas of India; impact of natural 
anthropogenic sources on global climate change; to strengthen the infrastructure facilities in 
selected universitiesltnstitutes to carry out basic research in Marine Sciences; to create 
centres of excellence on ocean sciences at selected institutes/universities; to create a code of 
high class ocean scientists and trained personnel/users; and to create awiireness among the 
school children, public and coastal community on the usefulness of ocean resources and 
create scientific temper among the people on ocean science. 
48. The ongoing projects would be integrated for generation of a national project under 
Marine Living Resources Programme. Besides, funding of about 10 socially beneficial 
projects proposed to be taken up with a view to develop suitable technologies. Also, action 
wouid be initiated to bring uniformity in course curriculum for offering courses on Ocean 
Science & Technology in Colleges/Universities and to evolve a mechanism for upgrading and 
bringing uniformity in academic standards in all marine related course, including 
introduction of Ocean Science & Technology at secondary school level. 
49. The Committee observes the need to induct Ocean Science related courses at various 
levels of studies to mak~ the students more conversant with the developments taking place in 
the field of Ocean Sciences. 
50. After considering the Demands for Grants of the Department of Ocean 
Development and after reviewing some of the programmes and projects administered by it, 
the Committee recommends that the Demand for Grants of Rs.110.88 crore, as sought by 
tht Department of Ocean Development, for the year 1999-2000, under Demand No. 92, may 
be approved .

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Committee on Science and Technology, Environment and 
Forests, having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, 
present this Sixty-sixth Report of the Committee. This Report deals with the detailed 
Demands for Grants (1999-2000) of the Department of Biotechnology (Demand No. 75) . 
2. Ln the meeting of the Committee held on the 24th March, 1999 the Secretary and 
other Officers of the Department of Biotechnology gave an overview of the various activities 
of· the Department and the Committee sought clarifications on various aspects of the 
performance of the Department to enable it to scrutinise the Demands for Grants. 
3. The Committee expresses its thanks to the Officers of the Department replying to 
the clarifications sought . by the Members and placing before it the required material to 
enable the ·committee to scrutinise the Demands for Grants of the Department of 
13 iotechilOlogy. 
4. The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on 
April 20, 1999.

REPORT 
The field of bio-technology has made significant impact in the last decade on the growth 
of agricultural, industrial, plwrmaceutical and medical sectors. The scientific understanding 
at the cellular and molecular levels of biological systems and development of technologies 
based on these hus led to increase in the agricultural productivity, development of vaccines, 
diagnostics, drugs, improved animal husbandry practices, env ironment friendly technologies 
and ~evcral tools for conservation of biological diversity. 
2. In pursuan~:e of these goals, the Department of Bio-technology has provided 
sustained suppo rt to the research, application and commercialising of Bio-technology. The 
Department has made efforts for transferring of some innovations/Research leads to 
indu stry for comme rcia lizutio n and thus serves as a link between research institutions, 
academia and indu stry. Besides supporting basic research, the department has launched a 
number of projects for weaker section of the society. The mandate of the Department 
extends to providing support to R&D, setting up of centres of excellence, promotion of 
large-scal e use of biotechnology, human resource developm ent and manufacturing of 
biologicals. The Department also cremes infrastructural facilities to support Research and 
Production activities; it serves as a nodal point for the collection and dissemination of 
information reluting to biotechnology and evolves bio-safety guidelines. Manufacture and 
application of cell-based vaccines is also one of the major activity of the Department. 
3. It has been stated that during the year 1999-2000, basic research and product and 
process development would be major thrusts through identification of leads from ongoing 
R&D projects . Multi -institutional and multi-disciplinary projects having national impact 
would be pri01·tised and implemented in the areas of agriculture, phyto-pharmaceuticals, 
microbial products, animal biotechnology, infectious diseases and neuro-sciences. 
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION 
4. Based on the recommendation of the Working Group and the proposal submitted for 
Ninth Plan to the Planning Commission, the Department of Biotechnology proposed as 
outlay of Rs. 1026 crore for a period of five years (1997-2002) against which only an amount 
of Rs. 675 crore was sanctioned. Thus the final anrlllal budget was Rs. 85 crore during the 
first year of the 9th Plan (1997-98) against the allocated B.E. of Rs. 107.00 crore & 
projected plan demand of Rs. 129.50 crore (Annexur~-1). During 1998-99, the department 
proposed an outlay of Rs. 125.00 crore, but · the B.E. was kept at the level of last year i.e. 
107.00 crore and the revised estimates were pegged at Rs. 100.81 crore (Annexure-H). 
During the year 1999-2000 the Department has demanded a plan outlay of Rs. 139.00 crore 
while an outlay of Rs. 110.00 crore only has been sanctioned (Annexure-III). 
5. As regards the reasons for the yawning gap of 25% between what was demanded and 
what was actually spent, the Secretary, Department of Biotechnology, informed the 
Committee that every year the Department has been projecting demands based on the 
recom mendations of various Task Forces and Apex Committee on the projects and 
programmes to be planned for each financial year and also keeping in view the priorities of 
the nation and changing trends in the international scenario. The recommended budgetary 
support being released by the Planning Commission has been in the order of 10-15% over 
the R.E. level of previous year. 

6. The Committee has been given to understand that the Department has proposed a 
budgetary outlay of Rs. 1026 crore based on the recommendations of the work group 
constituted by the Planning Commission for preparing the 9th Plan proposals of the 
Department of Biotechnology. As against this amount Planning Commission has committeed a 
budgetary support of Rs. 675 crore. 
7. The Committee observes that the investments made in the area of biotechnology by the 
department for promoting research and development, human resource, establishment of 
infrastructure and autonomous research institutions, have given rich dividends in the form of 
new technologies, patents and publications, academic excellenced and large pool of expertise. 
It is therefore necessary to mount a major effort for bio-industrial development of the 
country . A priority agenda for the next millennium would be to ensure judicious utilisation 
and conservation of biological resources and to undertake mission mode programmes in the 
areas such as vaccines and diagnostics for communicable diseases, genomic anal ysis and to 
develop friendly technologies including transgenic plant research . This would bring about food 
security, nutritional security also diversification of our bread basket. The original proposal for 
9th Plan had more than 50% of the budgetary provision for basic and product oriented 
research with a view to developing products and processes. With the reduced allocation of Rs. 
675 crore, it may not be possible to complete many activities. Therefore, the additional 
allocation of Rs. 75 crore would be necessary to restore several of these important 
programmes for being taken up during the remaining three year (1999-2000). This amount 
would also facilitate conversion of many important R&D leads into products that enhance 
productivity and efficiency of the concerned sectors, provide easy to use, low cost, 
environmentally sound technologies specially for the health care system, for soil fertility, for 
environmental conservation and protection, aimed at sustainable development particularly for 
rural areas. 
8. The Committee is also of the view that Department should draw up its plans 
sufficiently in advance in order to ensure utilisation of allocated funds during a particular 
financial year. This would have an impact on the allocations made during the next financial 
year also. In case of scientific departments, assessment formula for suggesting mandatory cuts 
need not be based on the trend of expenditure during the first six months of the financial year 
as expenditure on programmes and proje~ts generally picks up after the first half of financial 
year. 
BASIC AND PRODUCT ORIENTED R&D 
9. Department of Bio-Technology supports research and development. Some of the 
institutions under the Depurtment e.g . the National Institute of Immunology and the Centre 
for Finger Printing have made some earnings from transfer of technology. The Department 
has earned royalties for its technology for development of monochronal anti-body. But the 
earnings are ploughed back for research , for the benefit of the animals, animal feed, clean 
conditions etc. The earnings have helped create e.g. animal house facility which is serving 
the entire community . 
lO.Thus the projects aim at creation of a strong R&D base and product development. 
These R&D proje cts mainly fall under (i) Basic research; (ii) Crop bio-technoogy; 
(iii) Medicinal and Aromatic Plants ; (iv) Tree and Woody Species, Tissue Culture; 
(v) Seribiote chnology; (vi) Biopro specting of biological wealth; (vii) Medical Bio-technology; 
(viii) Human Genetics and Gcnoms Analysis; (ix) Animal Bio-technology; (x) Aquaculture 
and Marine Bio-technology; (xi) Biodiversity Conservation and Environment. 

11. The allocation for Basic and Product Oriented R&D activities has been restricted to 
Rs. 45.35 crore against the demanded allocation of Rs. 53.50 crore in the current financial 
year as against Rs. 43.40 crore provided for in B.E. and later-on reduced to Rs. 40.63 crore 
at R.E. stage during the last financial year. In reply to a query as to how many projects! 
programmes evolved through Task Forces and Expert Committee for implementation during 
the last financial year were finally taken up for research, the Committee was informed that 
the Department as per its mandate, generates research projects in the priority areas 
identified by the respective Task Forces and Expert Committees and receives projects and 
programmes from individual scientists and team for support. Out of a total of 517 projects 
received during the year 1998-99 the Department has approved and implemented about 205 
projects based on scientific merit and techno-economic feasibility covering 20 different areas 
of specialisation including both basic and applied research. 
12. The Committee is of view that the projects and programmes designed for the benefit 
of farmers, persons belonging to weaker and back ward sections of the Society and the ones 
relating to bio-technologiclll innovations may be given wide publicity through the electronic 
media so that the sections of the sodety for "hich the programmes are intended can benefit. 
Besides, a mechanism should be evolved, for continuous evaluation and monitoring of the 
projects undertaken. 
13. The Department was aske~ whether Government were cosidering any proposal to 
ensure that the Research/non-earning ac~1demic type and other institute consider 
commercialising a part of their activities with a veiw to reduce dependence on budgetary 
support. The Committee was informed that the Department of Bio-technology has not only 
been advocating but ~llso promoting the reseurch orgunisations to consider commercialising a 
part of their activities with a view to reduce dependence on budgetary support. However, 
the Department would like such earnings to be used for improving the basic infrastructure, 
and giving incentives to young scientists. The programmes supported such as Repositories, 
Animal Facilities, Bioinformatic Centres, Pilot Plant to Tissue Culture and Bio-pesticides in 
various institutions have ulready been generating income through sale-proceeds for their 
service and materials. Industries have been involved in serveral R&D projects from the 
beginning to explore commercialisation of the leads during the course of the project. The 
Department also facilitates TechnologyTransfer in close co-ordination with NRDC and BCIL 
for commercialising the R&D leads: 
14. The Committee is happy to note that certain projects undertaken by the Department 
are already generating income. This would reduce their dependence on budgetary support. 
The Departments should ensure that earnings from the projects are commensurate with the 
inputs and are used for reinforcing the projects, by improving the basic infrastructure and for 
providing incentives to young scientists. 
AGRICULTURAL BIO-TECHNOLOGY 
(i) Biological Control of Plant Pests, Diseases and Weeds 
15. The Committee was informed that the projects undertaken by the Department for 
production of bio-pesticides and bio-fertilizers induded four new bio-pesticide technologies 
which are under feasibility studies for commercialisation mass production technologies of 
some of the bio-control agents like-Trichograma (developed by IARI), Trichoderma 
(developed by RRL, Jammu) and Beaveria bassiana and Verticillium lecam (developed by 
AAU, Assam) are being patented. Successful field demonstrations of the some of the bio­
control agents resulted in the recommendation for their use in various States. 

16. In case of Bio-fertilizers the Committee was informe d that a number of projects on 
crop specific bio-fertilizers have been supported. High nitrogen fixing stra ins of rhizobium 
and blue gree algae suitable for diffe rent agrodimatic regions were isolated and 
demonstrated in field conditions Technology for the mass production of mycorrhiza is being 
transferred to industry. Besides, a number of technologies have been developed by the 
department for large scale production of high quality bio-fe rtilize rs specially for rice, pulses, 
fodder, legumes and importa nt forests trees. These tech nologies have been demonstrated 
and are under transfer to field. The department has initiat ed a network programme i.e. 
Integrat ed Nutr ient and pest M anagement to develop a package of practices involving 
various bio-fertilizers for spec ific cropping systems and bio-pesticides. 
17. The Committee commends the work done by the Department in the field of bio­
control agents and bio-fertilizers. The Committee recommends that techniques de,•eloped be 
upgraded and transferred to industry for pilot level production. Besides, the achievements in 
the field of bio-control agents, bio-fcrtilizcr s, production of better quality seeds for 
improvement of crops may be widely disseminated for the benefit of the sections of the society 
which would benefit these achievements. 
(ii) Plant Tissue Culture 
18. As a part of Protocol refinement the Department has initiated a Programme on 
strengthening Tree Biology Research for tacking specific problem s of rege nerati o n and 
improvem ent of important temperate species, production of elite neem varieties at different 
location is continuing. 
19. As regard s the horticultural cro ps the technol ogy for complete plantl et regernerat ion 
of m ango varieties is being refi ned under a coordi nate d programme. Programmes on 
developing a complete package of technology for regeneru tion and extension of banana are 
in the field. Likewise, a project supporte d for the scale up and refinement of the techno lgy 
for Saffron and Kala Zira and a network programmes on Coffee Bio-technology have been 
developed. The test ing of the genetic variation in the tissue culture ruised plants is 
continuing . 
20. The Committee is of the vie'" the efforts be nwde to make use of the tissue culture 
and floriculture technology in areas which are a rich source of herbal heritage, and in areas 
including remote areas where proiJiem of' non-availability of man power is prevalent. 
Additional incentives could be thought of for persons willing to work in these areas to 
augment the man-power re<Juirements. 
SERI BIOTECHNOLOGY I 
21. The Commit!<.:<.: wanted to know the efforts being made to improve th e quality of 
silk , as produced in Chin a. Korea and othe r countr ies, from where we still import silk. This 
ts import an t to bring down the import of silk from ab road . 
22. Sericulture in India is an important agro-and forest-based cottage industry earning 
foreign exchange \\Orth alwut R!:.. 1000 nurc per :uu1um (1997-98) . Seri<:ulture is practi sed in 
about 59.000 villages in India . The indust ry em ploys more than 6 million persons of whom 
the majority are located in rm:tl <~ r ea~ and around -H>'Yo belong to SC I ST. Silk protllll.:tion 
has reached over 15.000 tonn<.:s (1997-98) and India b th<.: se<.:ond largest silk prodw.:cr (18% 
of world production) afte r Chim1 (69 °/.,) Even su. our present production falls very mU<:h 
short of the domestit· tlemand. 

23. The Department of Bio-technology has been supporting a focussed programme on 
the biotechnology of silkworms and host plants over the past few years covering a wide 
spectrum ranging from improvement of breeds to enzyme processing of silk. 
24. The newer techniques of molecular biology and genetic engineering provide 
promises in sericulture . The biotechnological I genetic engineering studies are necessary not 
only on silk worms , but also on their host plants. In pursuance of this, the DBT has 
identified in association with the Central Silk Board thrust areas in sericulture (both 
mulberry and non-mulberry) in which biotechnolgy can play a vital role in increasing 
productivity, enhancing silk quality and improvement of host plants. 
25. The Committee was informed that the on-going and completed project of the 
Dcpart":Ient in the field of sericulture aim at improving Silkworm Productivity by following 
methods:-
(i) Development of gene transfer systems in silkworm: Successful introduction of 
cloned foreign genes into silkworm is already a reality . Attempts now ongoing to 
introduce desirable foreign genes into silkworm. Such genes include those respons­
ible for quality silk yarn, resistance to viruses, bacteria, fungi etc. or "sturdiness". 
(ii) Using the silkworm as a bio-reactor: It would soon be possible to exploit silkworms 
to produce bio-molecules of commercial importance (e.g. vaccines interferons, 
interleukin - 3 etc). Leads already obtained by using recombinant baculovirus 
vactor show great promise in the expression of such products. 
(iii) Producing a molecular genetic map of silkworm: An ambitious project has been 
initiated to identify and map useful genes of silkworms using molecular techniques. 
This will help in breeding better silkworm. 
(iv) Use of diagnostic kits for detection of diseases: A study for the development of a 
diagnostic kit based on immunoassay technique has been completed at the field 
level for nuclear polyhedrosjs virus causing grasserie. A similar study has also been 
carried out for infectious flatchery disease and for pebrine disease. 
(v) Biocontrol of pests (uzifly): An integrated model comprising spraying uzicide 
(benzoci acid) unci release of parasitoid Nesolynx thymus for control of uzifly - a 
serious pest of silkworms has been developed at farmers' level and for Enhancing 
Silk Quality the following techniques are being adopted (i) Enzyme processing of 
silk: This is highly desirable in .view of its eco-friendly nature and its value addition 
to finished products; (ii) Molecular characterization of silk genes in non-mulberry 
silk worm: Molecular biological studies on silk protein (fibroin and sericin) genes of 
non-mulberry silkworms have been initiated; _ and (iii) Molecular studies on non­
mulberry silkworms: Attempts are being made to isolate and characterize the silk 
genes of non-mulberry silkworms for the purpose of introducing the same into the 
system. 
26. Besides, for improvement of Hot Plants, ongoing and completed projects include 
tissue culture propagation of mulberry and non-mulberry host plants, artificial feeds for 
rearing silk worms, induction of haploids and triploids in mulberry as well as geaetic 
tr:msfounution of mulberry. 

MEDICAL BIOTECHNOLOGY AND 1!\ll\IUNODIAGNOSTICS 
27. The Secretary, DBT informed the Committee that special efforts were being made 
to generate projects in the area of major communicable and non-communicable diseases 
namely HIV, tuberculosis, Japanese Encephalitis, cholera, leishmaniasis, malaria, Helicobac~ 
ter plyori and contraceptive vaccines. The funding of multi-institutional projects has yielded 
good leads in terms of targets and objectives. Three assay systems for detection of HIV 
infection were transferred to industry. The western blot test developed at CRI Bombay 
would be marketed by institution very soon. Three PCR based systems developed for early 
diagnosis of tuberculosis are in the advanced stage of validation. Reagents for lgM Mac­
ELISA test of dengue have been made available at NIV Pune for supplying to various 
hospitals for early detection of dengue cases. 
28. Phase I clinical trials of the first indigenously developed chokra vaccine, VA. 1.3 
have been initiated at various Hospitals in the country. The vaccine strain has been found to 
be genetically stable. 
29. A number of new vaccines are under development. A synthetic peptide vaccine has 
been designed for JEV. A DNA vaccine using envelope and non-structural core protein for 
JEV has produced good an tibody response in mice model and in generating T. cell memory. 
Recombinant BCGs using 6 antigens from Mtb and surface ant igen of Hcptatitis B and E 
virus have been develope d. 
30. As regards handicaps faced by the Depar tment in the commercial production and 
marketing of vaccines, the Committee was informed that there me two channels for

and once it is cleared by the Central Drug Controller the application is given to the state

31. The Committee was also informed that indigenous kits for Health care developed by 
the Department have no buyers, as they are costlier that the imported ones, though more 
accurate. 
32. The Committee is of the view that the information regarding TB control and leprosy 
control vaccines needs to be publicised widely on a regular basis. 
33. The Committee recommends that efforts be made by the Department to ensure that 
indigenous products in health care get priority over the imported ones and for this purpose 
improvements in quality should remain the main concern. At the same time the price of these 
kits could be subsidised temporarily to promote the sales. 
NATIONAL INSTITUTE OF IMMUNOLOGY 
34. The Institute has emerged as a centre of excellence in basic immunology, infectious

approaches for regulation of male and female fertility; to interact with industry for

recognised Universities and institutions of higher learning for the purpose of enabling 
research scholars to register for post-graduate degree to serve as a national reference centre 
for imm~nology and to provide consultancy services to medical and veterinary institutions , 

public health agem:ics and industries in the countries; provide and promote effective linkages 
between various scientific and research agcncieSitaboratories and other organisations in the 
field of immunology, vaccine development anti related areas; to collaborate with foreign 
organisations in relevant fields. The institute is a collaborating centre for national mission 
project of Cattle herd Improvement'. Several technologies related to diagnosis of AIDS virus, 
anti-leprosy vaccine, and contraceptive vaccines are under trial or transferred to industry. 
The Research leads made in the institute are transferred to industry for pilot level 
production. 
35. In reply to a question whether the Institute proposes to take new projects during the 
current year and how many leads made in immunology, infectious diseases etc., last year, 
were transferred to industry for commercialisation, the Committee was informed that the

67th Report on Demands for Grants of Department of Electronics
 
The Department of Electronics (DOE)  is responsible for the development of the electronics industry formulation,
 promoting application  of electronics and informative technology,  implementation and review of various programmes/schemes
 in the field of electronics.  These schemes are implemented both in-house as well as through PSUs /Societies  under DOE and
 also through various sponsored programmes being funded under R&D.
2.         The Department is a medium not only to provide a focal point of Government’s attention to electronics sector and also to
 function as a coordinator within and outside the Government, but is also responsible for bringing the benefits of electronics to
 every walk of life, and play a catalytic role to make the Indian Electronics Industry a global player  in the light of the new
 Industrial and Trade Policy.
3.         With delicensing of the entire electronics industry (except aerospace and defence electronics), liberalisation in foreign
 investment and Export-Import policies, the country is witnessing new investments, restructuring of existing activities,
 diversification of the product range and an intensely  competitive environment.  All the renowned global brands have either
 established production facilities in the country or are present in the market through technical/financial collaborations, thus
 giving consumer a wider choice in terms of product features, technology quality and competitive prices.
4.         The thrust , according to  DOE, during the Ninth Plan, would be on Export, Employment and productivity-led growth of
 Electronics and Information Technology.  The electronics and Information Technology sector has the propensity to increase the
 overall growth rate to higher level.
5.            Electronics is the fast growing sector of the Indian industry.  During the Eighth Plan, the electronics industry had a
 cumulative annual growth of 20 per cent in production and over 40 per cent in exports.  The electronics industry achieved a
 production level of Rs. 32,070 crores and an export performance of Rs. 9, 500 crores during the year 1997-98 and is likely to
 achieve a production level of Rs. 41,000 crores during the year 1998-99 registering a growth of over 28% and export
 performance of Rs.12800/- showing a net increase of 70 per cent.  A goal of annual electronics production of Rs. 1,38,350
 crores and exports of about Rs. 49,000 crores has been set for the terminal year of the Ninth Plan (2001-02), representing a
 growth rate of 39% and 52% respectively.
BUDGETARY ALLOCATION
6.         The Department was given an allocation of Rs. 791.78 for the entire 8
th Five Year Plan, out of which budgetary support
 was to the tune of Rs.  679.38 crores .  An allocation of Rs. 897.37 crores has been made available for the 9 th Five Year Plan
 (1997-2002) and Gross Budgetary support would be pegged at Rs. 542.37 crores.  .  During the first three years of plan Rs.
 769.57 crores  have been spent and left over allocation  is only Rs. 127.8 crores and the share of Budgetary support spent so far
 is Rs. 405.6 crores leaving a balance of Rs. 136.77 cores (Appendix –I).
 
 
7.            Budgetary support for the Department of Electronics for the current financial  year  is Rs. 208 crores (Rs. 180 crores
 Plan and Rs. 28 crores Non-Plan) against the revised estimate 1998-99 of Rs. 156.57 crores (Rs. 135 crores Plan and Rs. 21.57
 crores Non-Plan)(See Appendix –II).  The allocation for the year is thus Rs. 51.43 crores more than RE 1998-99.
8.         As regards the justification for  enhanced allocation the Committee was informed an enhanced outlay of Rs. 20 crores
 has been provided  for setting up of  an  IT Venture Capital Fund .  Besides, an amount of  Rs. 5.00 crores are likely to be spent
 for Electronic Governance. A sum of Rs. 5.09 crores has been provided towards  reimbursement of Central Sales Tax to
 STPs/EHTPs in accordance with the Exim Policy.    This scheme was being handled by Ministry of Commerce till 1996-97 and
 has subsequently been transferred to the Department of  Electronics.  TDC projects, STQC Labs/centre and Ernet India would
 require an additional outlay of Rs. 5.50 crores, 4.00 crores , 5.50 crores and 10.00 crores respectively for their plan expenditure
 and the additional allocation has been proposed  to give thrust to the technology development in the electronic sector  and to
 meet requirements of the approved projects
9.         The Committee finds that the Planning Commission has sanctioned a budget support of Rs. 300 crore for
 Information Technology to be spent during the Ninth Five Year (1997-2002) period.  The allocation has not been
 earmarked against any of the Ministry/Department of Government of India.  The Department is working on so many

 programmes/projects concerning Information Technology such as ERNET, NII, TDIL, Electronics Commerce,
 Electronics Governance, Venture Capital for Software etc. and the Planning Commission have not allocated sufficient
 funds for the said programmes/projects .  As DOE is responsible for promotion of Information Technology in the
 country   the Committee is strongly of the view that the amount of Rs. 300.00 crore provided by the Planning
 Commission to be spent during the Ninth Plan may be allocated under the administrative control of Department of
 Electronics and the Department may be designated  as  a  nodal agency in the field of information technology.
NATIONAL INFORMATION INFRASTRUCTURE FOR NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT

Sixty-Eighth   Report on Demands for Grants (1999-2000)
of the Department of Space
 
            India’s Space Programme, since its inception in the early sixties, has been guided by a vision which laid emphasis on the
 application of space technology for finding solution to the problems of man and society thereby establishing a viable & self
 reliant space programme.  From the very beginning, long-range plans have been drawn up to steer the programme effectively
 ensuring appropriate linkages among the application needs, satellite missions, launch vehicle capabilities and technology
 development.  Over the last three-and-half decades, significant progress has been made  in  space technology for building
 world-class satellites for communications and remote sensing; for launching the remote sensing satellites from India with
 indigenous launch vehicle; and providing the benefits of space technology to improve the quality of life at the grass root level,
 thus contributing to several areas of national development.
2.         In tune with the goal of self reliant use of space technology for national development, the thrust areas of the Indian
 Space Programme include:-
(a)        satellite  based communication for various applications.
(b)        satellite based remote sensing for resources survey, management and environmental monitoring;
(c)        meteorological applications; and
(d)        development and operationalisation of indigenous and launch vehicles for providing these space services.
3.         The Department of Space (DOS) is responsible for implementing the policies framed by the Space Commission.  The
 policies are carried out through the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO) and the three Grant in aid institutions, viz. the
 National Remote Sensing Agency (NRSA), the Physical Research Laboratory (PRL) and the National Mesosphere-
Stratosphere-Troposphere Radar Facility (NMRF).
4.         The cumulative expenditure on space research till the end of Eighth Plan period i.e. from the inception in 1962-63 to
 1996-97, is Rs.7431.67 crore.  During the Eighth Plan, most of the programmatic targets and missions planned have been
 achieved. The total expenditure incurred is Rs.3928.53 crore (Plan Rs.3155.74 crore and Non-Plan Rs.772.79 crore). The major
 missions achieved are INSAT-2B, INSAT-2C, INSAT-2D, IRS-1E, IRS-P2, IRS-1C, IRS-P3, SROSS-C1 and SROSS-C2.
 Besides, considerable progress in the areas like development of indigenous cryogenic engine and stage for the GSLV
 programme, technological development for indigenisation of strategic and critical sub-systems & components and setting up of
 facilities for realisation of inertial systems and electro-optical systems have been achieved. 
5.         The Committee was informed that the Planning Commission has allocated a Plan outlay of Rs.6511.72 crore, against
 their earlier communication of Rs.7100.00 crore and the Non-Plan outlay of Rs.1200 crore for the Ninth Plan period. Thus, the
 total outlay for the Ninth Plan is Rs.7711.72 crore. However, the actual Plan budgetary allocation would be decided annually
 based on the programmatic requirements.
6.         The programme directions and the programmatic targets for the Ninth Plan have been formulated after extensive
 interactions and consultations with user Ministries. The major missions planned for the Ninth Plan to realise the programmatic
 targets have been indicated in Annexure-I. While the basic vision would continue to be the large scale application of space
 technology for finding solutions to the problems of man and society, the programme would respond effectively to the dynamic
 and complex problems of the coming years. The   major programmes planned include (i) operationalisation of Geosynchronous
 Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) towards achievement of self-reliance in launching communication satellites;  (ii) providing
 additional and newer operational communication satellite services to meet the increasing national needs;  (iii) building earth
 observation systems for wide range of applications related to land, water and ocean resources as well as atmospheric
 observations; (iv) establishing the GRAMSAT programme for integrating the potentials of satellite communication and remote
 sensing for rural development including the tele-education and tele-health; (v) establishing new communication services for
 Digital Audio and Data Broadcasting and Direct to Home TV services; (vi) establishing a viable system for Disaster
 Management through Earth observation, satellite-based communications, conventional survey information and local networks;
 (vii) research and development as well as technology development; and (viii) enhanced interface between Indian industry and
 academia to give boost to the national space effort.
7.         The Committee observes that during 1996-97, the Department had utilised the funds to the extent of 99.83 per cent.  In
 1997-98, the fund utilisation level was about 99.13 per cent.  The provisional expenditure indicates maximum utilisation of

 funds by the Department of the RE allocation for 1998-99. The Committee notes with satisfaction that the Department has
 made maximum utilisation of the funds allocated to it during 1996-97, 1997-98 and 1998-99.
DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (1999-2000)
8.         The Committee was informed that keeping in view the Mission profile for Ninth Plan and specifically the programmatic
 needs/milestones targeted for realisation during the current year the budget requirements of the Department of Space has been
 drawn up. A significant part of the budgetary allocation sought for 1999-2000 is towards the ongoing projects  which have
 already been approved by the Government. Out of the total budgetary allocation (Net) of Rs.1755.00 crore and budgetary
 allocation (Gross) of Rs. 1759.82 crore,  the budget for approved major projects is Rs.1029.00 crore. The financial provision for
 BE 1999-2000 is given in Annexure-II.
9.         The major activities/milestones planned to be undertaken during the current year include launching and
 operationalisation of INSAT-2E, launching of IRS-P4 along with two foreign small satellites viz. KITSAT-3 from South Korea
 and DLR-TUBSAT from Germany on board the indigenous launch vehicle PSLV-C2, completion of Spacecraft
 assembly/testing and preparations for launching of INSAT-3A, first developmental flight of GSLV, and assembly, integration,
 testing and readiness of GSAT-1 satellite for GSLV-D1 flight.
10.        According to the Department of Space, the new activities which require  additional allocation of funds during the
 current year include: (i) completion of spacecraft fabrication, assembly & testing and launch & operationalisation of INSAT-
3B; (ii) completion of spacecraft assembly/testing and launch of INSAT-3A;  (iii) initiation of subsystem fabrication and testing
 for INSAT-3C; (iv) completion of procurement activity, spacecraft subsystem fabrication activity and payload development of
 IRS-P5 (Cartosat) spacecraft; (v) completion of procurement long lead items and subsystem fabrication of IRS-P6
 (Resourcesat) spacecraft; (vi) completion of preliminary & detailed design and civil works other than vehicle assembly bay of
 the second launch pad; and (vii) integration and testing of prototype engine and Initiation of hot test of the CUS project.
 Besides, some other new projects which necessitate additional funds include work on IRS-2 (advanced cartography) and
 GSAT-2&3 satellites for development flights of GSLV, etc.         
11.        In formulating the BE for 1999-2000 the important considerations have been the cash flow requirement for INSAT-3
 project including associated launch services.  During the current year, work on two of the INSAT-3 satellites viz. INSAT-3B
 and INSAT-3A are targeted for completion and substantial part of the work on subsequent satellite INSAT-3C is also to be
 completed for possible launch in 2000-01. Accordingly, the fabrication and procurement activities are being accelerated to meet
 this schedule.  The contract for procured launch services for INSAT-3A and 3C are also being concluded and milestone
 payments towards this are also due in 1999-2000.  The estimated cash flow requirement in the current year for INSAT-3 project
 (spacecraft and launch services) alone is Rs.565 crore.
12.        The major Space Applications programmes would require an outlay of Rs.748.92 crore during the current year
 essentially for the NNRMS/NRIS programme, Remote Sensing application development, Integrated Mission for Sustainable
 Development, GRAMSAT pilot project (Jhabua), GSAT-1 application projects, and other application programmes.  This also
 includes Rs.565.00 crore towards INSAT-3 Projects and for programmes like R&D applications, technical facilities
 augmentation/replacement, O&M of related Centres like Space Application Centre, DECU and RRSSCs as well as Grant-in-aid
 to NRSA.
INDIAN NATIONAL SATELLITE SYSTEM (INSAT)
13.        The  system (INSAT), which became operational with INSAT-1B, is a multi-agency, multi-purpose operational satellite
 system which provides domestic long distance telecommunications, meteorological earth observation and data relay, nation
 wide direct satellite TV broadcasting to augmented TV receivers, nation wide radio networking, TV programme distribution
 and re-broadcasting to terrestrial transmitters, etc. The system has enabled communication to and fro any part of India leading
 to training and awareness among rural masses on better agricultural practices, land and water resources management, family
 planning, health care and hygiene, disaster warning and rescue operations, etc.
13.1      The INSAT space segment, which is one of the largest domestic satellites in Asia, at present consists of five satellites
 namely NSAT-ID, INSAT-2A, INSAT-2B, INSAT-2C and INSAT-2DT acquired from ARABSAT Organisation, after INSAT-
2D became inoperable on October 4, 1997.
13.2      Secretary, Department of Space took the opportunity to inform the Committee that the indigenously designed,
 developed and tested INSAT-2E, was launched on 3
rd April, 1999 by the Ariane launch Vehicle of the European Space
 Agency. INSAT-2 is carrying 17 C-Band and lower extended C-Band transponders, a Very High Resolution Radiometer
 (VHRR), similar to that of INSAT-2A and INSAT-2B. It has an additional water vapour channel and a Charged Coupled
 Device (CCD) camera operating in visible, near infrared and short wave infrared bands with 1 km. resolution. Once INSAT-2E
 is operational it would beam television signals not only over India but also over other regions right from Australia on the

 eastern side to Europe on the western side. Eleven 36 MHz equivalent units of C-band capacity on INSAT-2E would be leased
 to INTELSAT. Secretary further informed the Committee that INSAT-2E health is normal and the satellite is expected to be
 ready for operational use by 1 st week of May after completion of all deployments, stabilisation and detailed on-orbit tests. The
 sanctioned cost of the INSAT-2CD & E satellites and 2DT is Rs.654.70 crore. In the current year, the financial requirement for
 these is kept at Rs.26.50 crore.
13.3      In response to a query raised  on the indigenous capability to launch INSAT category of satellites, the Secretary, DOS,
 informed the Committee that the Indian Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle (PSLV) has capability to launch 1000-1200 kg satellites
 into Polar Orbit and the IRS satellites are launched by PSLV.  The INSAT satellites are heavier weighing 2 to 2.5 tonnes in
 Geo-stationary transfer orbit and hence are being launched currently from foreign launchers.  The Geo-stationary Satellite
 Launch Vehicle (GSLV) programme which is already in advanced stages of development would provide India with the
 capability to launch INSAT type of satellites in future.
13.4      In view of INSAT-1D approaching its end of life and the growing user demand, it became necessary to augment the
 transponder capacity on a short-term basis by leasing seven transponders onboard Thaicom-3 satellite. Accordingly, the
 financial outlay in RE 1998-99 and BE 1999-2000 includes Rs.17.00 crore each for lease of transponders from Thaicom-3
 Satellite.
13.5      The INSAT-3 space crafts (INSAT-3A, 3B, 3C, 3D and 3E) have been planned for providing continuity in services,
 expansion of capacity and improving the capabilities of INSAT system for providing communication and meteorological
 services.   Consequent on the de-commissioning of the INSAT-2D, it has been decided to reconfigure and reschedule INSAT-
3B and launch it ahead of INSAT-3A during 1999-2000.  It is planned to launch INSAT-3A towards the end of 1999-2000.  The
 INSAT-3C and 3D are planned for launch during 2000-2002.
SATELLITE NAVIGATION
14.        Satellite navigation is a service  which is expected to become operational in many advanced countries like United
 States, Japan, Europe, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. The International Civil Aviation Organisation has made Satellite
 navigation equipment mandatory on all civilian aircraft. To upgrade the existing Communications Navigation and Surveillance
 (CNS) and Air-Traffic Management (ATM) system in India, the Airports authority of India (AAI) is planning to make them
 adaptable to the Future Air Navigation System (FANS) through the introduction of Indian Wide Area Differential GPS
 (WADGPS) system. Therefore, as a plan AAI would phase out the existing navigational aids and would increasingly depend on
 satellite navigation by the year 2010.
14.1      The Secretary, DOS, informed the Committee that the Department has prepared and sent a preliminary project report on
 satellite based navigation system to the Airports Authority of India (AAI). The AAI has sought certain technical clarifications 
 which are being studied by the Department. Accordingly, a revised proposal would be sent to AAI shortly. The national
 Steering Committee on communications, navigation and surveillance Air Traffic Management (CNS/ATM) is expected to
 review this proposal with the Department of Space for formalising the plan of action.
INDIAN REMOTE SENSING SATELLITE (IRS)
15.        The Indian Remote Sensing (IRS), started with the launching of IRS-1A in March 1988, is the mainstay of National
 Natural Resources Management System (NNRMS) providing continuously space-based data for the optimal utilisation of
 natural resources. At present the IRS system comprises IRS-1B, 1C, 1D and IRS-P3.
15.1      The  Department has undertaken initiatives in the use of IRS data in the country for drought monitoring and assessment,
 water resources management, forest, environment and the resources sector, geology and mineral prospecting, agriculture
 applications, integrated land and water resources management, wasteland mapping, rural and urban development and coastal
 and ocean-related applications.
15.2      The Remote Sensing applications are carried out under the broad umbrella of National Natural Management System
 (NNRMS). The nine NNRMS Standing Committees encompassing major natural resources and developmental areas like
 agriculture, bio-resources and environment, urban development, etc. periodically review the status of utilisation of remote
 sensing in their respective fields and provide guidance for promoting remote sensing based activities.
15.3      Currently the National (Natural) Resources Information System (NRIS) programme has been undertaken on a pilot scale
 in 30 districts spread over 17 states on 1:50,000 scale and in 4 states (Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, Maharastra and Gujarat) on
 1:250,000 scale with active participation from the concerned state governments. The progress made in these states/districts has
 been satisfactory and the systems would be operationalised in these districts and states in the current year.
15.4      The effective utilisation of IRS database on an operational basis is possible only when the states themselves establish
 appropriate mechanism to integrate the database with their developmental planning. In order to realise this objective, the

 establishment of State Natural Resources Management System (SNRMS) at state level has been conceptualised on the pattern
 of the existing NNRMS with the various state line departments closely interacting with each other for effective management of
 natural resources in the states. The SNRMS would be responsible for assessing information needs for natural resources
 management and developmental activities in the state and creating appropriate database and programmes, through the State
 Remote Sensing Centres which would act as the nodal agencies for SNRMS. The first of its kind has been set up recently by the
 Government of Uttar Pradesh. States like Madhya Pradesh, West Bengal, and Maharashtra are also in the process of
 establishing SNRMS in the near future.
 
 
16         The Committee agrees that effective management of natural resources is necessary for carrying out
 developmental activities. It is more so when the natural resources appear to be depleting in the years to come while
 demographic pressure are mounting up on the scarce natural resources. Establishment of State Natural Resources
 Management System (SNRMS) for optimal utilisation of natural resources in the states is a step in the right direction. 
WATER RESOURCES MANAGEMENT
17.        The Committee was informed about the application of remote sensing data in finding out water resources and its use in
 providing water to villages. The National Drinking Water Mission and the remote sensing based maps and inputs were
 generated and used to locate ground water resources for drilling bore wells in villages.
17.1      As regards the ground water survey, the Committee was informed that recently that the Ministry of Water Resources
 had requested the Department of Space to undertake the second phase of the Rajiv Gandhi Drinking Water Mission. Under this
 mission 4.5 lakhs habitats in the country would be covered. In the first phase, it has been decided to undertake this programme
 in five states i.e. Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Orissa and Maharashtra covering 1.5 lakhs habitats where the
 drinking water resources have to be identified.  At present,  the Department is engaged in developing the hydro-geo-
morphological maps for these 1.5 lakhs habitats. In Tamil Nadu  382 blocks have been identified by the Department with the
 help of this hydro-geo-morphological mapping. In the next three years  a total of 4.5 lakhs habitats are to be covered by the
 mapping.
18.        The Committee observes that amidst high exploitation and fast depleting  ground water table in the country is a
 matter of serious concern.  Therefore, there has to be a balance between the drawl of water from the surface and
 creation of water harvesting structures.  It is therefore necessary to pursue vigorously the project in Tamil Nadu for
 identifying sites for water harvesting structures.  If the exercise proves successful, the Committee would like the similar
 projects to be drawn up for other parts of the country.
WEATHER FORECASTING
19.        The Committee was informed that a vast array of space based meteorological data exists but what was lacking was
 accurate weather prediction system. Modelling in the tropical region is more complex than modeling in the temperate region
 due to complexities in atmospheric circulation for which it is difficult for us to predict even two or three days before. Therefore,
 accuracy in predicting weather conditions is an urgent need of the agricultural sector. Presently a small Committee has been
 constituted consisting of people from the DOS, DST and the India Meteorology Department (IMD). The Director-General of
 the IMD is the Chairman of the Committee to look into these specific issues relating to the weather forecasting.
19.1      In response to a query raised by the Members on the quality of weather forecasting on Doordarshan, the Committee was
 informed that the matter has been discussed with the Department of Science and Technology (DST),  Secretary, DST has
 formed a Committee with Director General, IMD as the Convenor and Members from DST, Doordarshan, DOS and Ministry of
 Information & Broadcasting to review and recommend innovative weather news on Doordarshan.  The Committee would
 specifically recommend measures to enhance the quality of Doordarshan weather news bulletins to international standards,
 suggest mechanism to monitor the news bulletin and ensure standards, recommend necessary software development, and
 maintain regularity of telecast.  Accordingly, necessary action would be initiated based on the recommendations of the
 Committee.        
19.2      The Committee expresses its concern over the lack of precision in  weather forecasts which have an adverse effect
 on agriculture. Besides, our inability to predict cyclones and other natural calamities plays havoc with human life. It is
 therefore necessary to improve our system of forecasting.
CLIMATE/GLOBAL CHANGE 
20.        On the question of climate study and climatic changes the Committee was informed that the global climate change is an
 important area of concern world over and is a complex study involving extensive observations/data collection, modeling and
